documents.section_title: From zero to your first event, in about five minutes
documents.title: From zero to your first event, in about five minutes
documents.content:
1. Quickstart

 

## From zero to your first event, in about five minutes

 

Ravensight is hosted. You do not run a server, you point your game at ours.

 

1. **Create an account.** Sign in at `https://app.ravensight.io` through RealitySE, the identity system Ravensight runs on. Use email and password, or one of the SSO providers: Apple, Google, Facebook, GitHub, Twitch, Xbox, or Steam.
 
1. **Create a project.** A project is one title, and it holds one game per environment. The first time you sign in the dashboard asks who your studio is, then a name, an id and an engine for your game, creates the project with its production environment, and waits for your first event. Every feature is available right away, no upgrade required. See [Projects and environments](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/projects/) for the shape.
 
1. **Copy the ingest key.** Each environment has its own. It is shown once on the confirmation screen and looks like `gt_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx`. A key that ships inside a build is not a secret: anyone with the build can read it. It can only create sessions, read the tracking on/off switch and the AI suggestions feed, submit player reports and submit doctor reports; it cannot read analytics or manage your account. If you lose it, rotate it from **Settings > Projects** for a new one. For a demo, a web build anyone can open or an open-source game, use a [public key](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/) (`gt_pub_`) with an event allowlist and a ceiling instead, and keep live keys on your own server when possible.
 
1. **Add the autoload.** Copy `Ravensight.gd` into your Godot project, e.g. `res://autoload/Ravensight.gd`. Open **Project > Project Settings > Autoload**, add the script, name it `Ravensight`, and enable it. Set `ingest_key` to the key from step 3 before Ravensight's `_ready()` runs: edit the default at the top of `Ravensight.gd`, or set it from an autoload listed above `Ravensight`. `api_url` already points at `https://api.ravensight.io`. Not on Godot? Install the SDK for your engine from the [SDK list](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/platform-support/) instead (Unity, Unreal, web, iOS, Android, C++, Odin or LÖVE), or call the [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/http-api/) directly from anything else.
 
1. **Send your first event.** Call `track_event()` from anywhere in your game.
 
1. **See the dashboard.** Pick your game in the switcher, and the environment beside it if the game has more than one. The SDK sends events in batches, 5 seconds after the first one waits, so they typically show up within a few seconds, no restart needed.

documents.section_title: From zero to your first event, in about five minutes
documents.title: Which environment does this key hit?
documents.content:
### Which environment does this key hit?

 

The SDK needs only the ingest key at initialization. The key alone decides which game and environment receive the events, so project and game ids do not belong in your app configuration; treat them as a release audit check instead. The free confirmation is `GET /api/v1/settings` with the key in `X-API-Key`, which returns the game's slug, name and environment (see [the HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/http-api/)), or `npx ravensight-doctor --live`, which from 0.4.2 prints `key belongs to <name> (<slug>, <environment>)`. Neither counts toward your usage.

 

Godot, res://autoload/ravensight.gd

 

```
Ravensight.track_event("level_completed", {
    "level": 3,
    "score": 15000,
    "time_seconds": 87.4
})
```

 

**Not on Godot?** The same account and ingest key work against the plain [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/http-api/): three headers and a JSON body from any engine or client that can make a POST request.

documents.section_title: One title, one project, one game per environment
documents.title: One title, one project, one game per environment
documents.content:
10. Projects and environments

 

## One title, one project, one game per environment

 

Your development build and your shipped build must not share an event stream, or a week of debugging quietly becomes your retention number. Ravensight keeps them apart by making each one its own game, and groups the games of one title into a project.

documents.section_title: One title, one project, one game per environment
documents.title: The three scopes
documents.content:
### The three scopes

 

| Scope | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| Environment, one game | Its own ingest key, its own tracking, history and weekly digest switches, and its own events, sessions, players, funnels, journeys, retention, reports and digests. The presets are production, early access, demo, beta, alpha, staging and development, and a project can also name its own, such as qa. At most one game per label per project. |
| Project, one title | Name and engine, the environments underneath it, and the studio records filed under it. Project-scoped pages read the project rather than one build. |
| Studio, your org | Members and roles, billing and the prepaid balance, the studio context graph, studio notes, cross-game analytics and the audit log. |

documents.section_title: One title, one project, one game per environment
documents.title: Picking one
documents.content:
### Picking one

 

The switcher at the top of the sidebar picks a project. Beside it in the header, on the pages whose numbers come from one build, an environment control picks which environment you are looking at. A project with a single environment needs no second choice, and the pages that belong to the whole project do not show the control at all.

 

The switcher also offers **All games**. Brainstorm, Strategy matrix, Design, Dashboards, Muninn, Marketing, Sales, Pulse, Publishers and Studio data follow the selection: one game shows that game's records, and All games shows every game's, along with records that have no game. There, each record can be moved to a game with Move to game. Every other page shows one game at a time and asks you to pick one under All games. This is a filter inside your studio, not a change in who can see what: every member still sees every game.

documents.section_title: One title, one project, one game per environment
documents.title: Managing them
documents.content:
### Managing them

 

**Settings > Projects** is where projects are renamed, merged, and given new environments. Because every existing game was migrated into a project of its own, two environments of the same title can start out as two projects. Ravensight proposes the merge when their names normalize to the same thing and their environment labels do not collide, and nothing is merged until you accept the proposal. Dismiss one and it stays dismissed. You can also move a single environment from one project to another, or delete a project once it is empty.

 

Creating, renaming, merging and deleting all need an admin role or above. Everyone in the studio can read the list.

 

Analytics queries are still keyed on one game, which is why a number on screen always belongs to exactly one environment. A project-level or studio-level number is the same per-game query asked of several games and summed, never a new aggregation with its own rules.

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: Where the SDKs run
documents.content:
4. Install an SDK

 

## Where the SDKs run

 

Every SDK ships as source and speaks plain HTTPS to the same four endpoints. There is no prebuilt binary in any of them. The platform specific code is small: the LÖVE SDK's HTTPS transports, and the app background handling on iOS and Android. The C++ and Odin SDKs link libcurl for the HTTP calls. The LÖVE SDK runs on the desktop, and on the web through the JavaScript SDK; see the [LÖVE SDK reference](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/love-sdk/). A cell says Untested where no build of that SDK has been run on that platform yet.

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: Support matrix
documents.content:
### Support matrix

 

| SDK | Desktop | iOS | Android | Web | Console |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Godot | Yes | Untested | Untested | Yes, on the web export | Untested, subject to cert |
| Unity | Yes on macOS, in the Unity 6 Editor and a macOS player. Windows and Linux untested | Untested | Untested | Untested, on WebGL | Untested, subject to cert |
| Unreal | Untested. Mac editor and game targets build on Unreal Engine 5.8.3, no packaged game has run yet | Untested | Untested | No web target in UE5 | Untested, subject to cert |
| JavaScript (web and Node) | Yes, in Electron or Node | Untested, in a web view | Untested, in a web view | Yes | Not applicable |
| C++ | Yes on macOS, C++17 plus libcurl. Linux in CI, Windows untested | Untested | Untested | Not applicable | Untested, subject to cert |
| Odin | Yes on macOS, via libcurl. Windows and Linux untested | Untested | Untested | Not applicable | Untested |
| LÖVE | Yes on macOS. Windows and Linux untested | Not supported yet | Not supported yet | Through ravensight-js and the love.js bridge | Not supported yet |
| iOS native Swift | Yes, macOS 12+ | iOS 15+. Tests pass on the iOS Simulator, untested on a device. tvOS 15+: tests pass on a tvOS simulator | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| Android native Kotlin | Not applicable | Not applicable | minSdk 24. Tests pass under Robolectric, untested on a device or emulator. Meta Quest runs Horizon OS, which is Android, so the same SDK runs there unchanged | Not applicable | Not applicable |
| Any engine via HTTP | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, subject to cert |

 

These are honest cells, not a marketing grid. A Yes here means a build of that SDK has run there, and Untested means it has not yet. What we have not done is ship a title on every one of them, so treat even a Yes in the mobile and console columns as "nothing in the way" rather than "verified in a submitted build". Each SDK's README lists exactly what was run.

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: Consoles
documents.content:
### Consoles

 

Nothing in any SDK is blocked on a console. What is blocked is everything else about console networking: each platform holder requires that outbound traffic, privacy disclosure, and any data collection be declared and approved as part of certification, and NDA restrictions mean we cannot ship console specific code publicly anyway. Ravensight is an ordinary HTTPS call from your title's own network stack, and passing cert with it is the developer's responsibility, exactly as it would be for a leaderboard or a patch notes fetch.

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: Mobile privacy
documents.content:
### Mobile privacy

 

Ravensight does not touch an advertising identifier. Every SDK generates its own random device id on first run and stores it locally. The Godot and LÖVE SDKs write 32 lowercase hex characters, a hyphen and the OS name, so `3f9ac2e17b5d4c0e8a61f2b9d7c04e5a-android` is what one looks like. The Unity, C++, Odin, iOS and Android SDKs write `dev_` and 32 hex characters from 16 random bytes; Unreal writes `dev_` and a random UUID, and the JavaScript SDK writes `dev_` and a random UUID where the browser or Node offers one, else 32 hex characters. No IDFA on iOS, no Android advertising id, no hardware identifier, and no IP based fingerprinting. That id is meaningless outside your game's own data, and nothing in Ravensight ever joins it to a name, an email or an account, because the SDK has no field for any of those.

 

An event row holds the game id, the device id, the session id, the event name, a timestamp, and the level, platform, version and payload you sent. Unless you switch them off, it also holds the country the session connected from and the device model, OS version and GPU the SDK sent (see [country and device](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/platform-support/#country-device)). It holds no IP address, no user agent and nothing finer than a country, and it is deleted after 90 days. To detect abuse, a keyed hash and a masked form of the address a session connects from are kept for 30 days, or for as long as you keep that address blocked, never the full address (see [traffic sources](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/traffic/)). Two things outlive that window: one record per game and device with the first day it was seen, kept for the game's lifetime so lifetime and new-player counts stay correct, and any feedback text a player typed, kept until you delete it or the game.

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: Country and device
documents.content:
### Country and device

 

Two more things are collected by default, and one switch per game turns both off: **Record country and device fields** on the game's card under **Settings > Projects**, or `countryDeviceEnabled: false` on `PATCH /api/v1/games/:gameId`.

 

- **Country.** When a session starts, the server looks up the country of the address the request connected from, in an offline database bundled with the server, so no request leaves Ravensight to answer it. Only the two-letter country code (such as `US`) is kept, on the session and on each of its events. The address itself is never stored. A private or unknown address gives an empty value, and the SDK cannot send or change the country. IP geolocation by [DB-IP](https://db-ip.com), used under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
 
- **Device.** SDK builds that support it send an optional `device` object when a session starts: `model` (the device model name, never a serial or other unique id), `osVersion` (the version only, since the platform already names the OS) and `gpu` (the graphics adapter name). Each is trimmed and cut to 128 characters, and a value with a control character is stored as empty. An SDK sends only what its engine exposes without a permission prompt: Godot 0.5.0, Unity 0.5.0 and Unreal 0.5.0 send all three, C++ 0.5.0 and Odin 0.6.0 send the values your game sets in their config, iOS 0.6.0 and Android 0.5.0 send the model and OS version, and LÖVE 0.7.0 sends the GPU name. A Meta Quest headset reports its model as `Meta Quest 3`, and so on, to tell it from a phone.

 

With the switch off, new sessions store empty values for all four, the game's live sessions are cleared, and every batch that arrives after the switch is written without them. Events already accepted and waiting to be written at the moment you switch it off may still carry them. Events written before the fields existed, or while the switch was off, read as unknown: nothing is filled in afterwards.

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: Tracking prompt, opt-out and reset
documents.content:
### Tracking prompt, opt-out and reset

 

**No App Tracking Transparency prompt is required for Ravensight.** Apple defines tracking as linking data collected from your app about a user or device with data collected from other companies' apps, websites or offline properties for targeted advertising or advertising measurement, or sharing it with a data broker. Ravensight does neither: the id is yours alone, it is never combined with another company's data, and nothing reaches an ad network or a data broker. So on Ravensight's account you do not need to call `requestTrackingAuthorization`. If something else in your app does track across companies, that decision is unchanged by this.

 

Two SDK calls exist for studios that show their own consent screen. Ravensight ships no consent UI; wire these to your own settings menu if your audience or your lawyer wants one.

 

- **The opt-out** stops the SDK sending anything: queued events are dropped and no further request is made, not even the startup check. Every SDK except JavaScript saves the choice locally, so it survives a restart until the player turns it back on. The JavaScript SDK does not store it: keep the choice in your own settings and apply it before the first event on every launch.
 
- **The reset** saves a new random id and opens a new session under it, so a player can start a fresh analytics identity from your game's own settings. Rows already stored under the old id are not rewritten; they expire with the game's selected raw-event window (90 days by default, or 180 or 400 days with extended retention), or sooner if you delete the game.

 

| SDK | Opt-out | Reset |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Godot | `Ravensight.set_tracking_enabled(false)` | `Ravensight.reset_device_id()` |
| JavaScript | `rs.setEnabled(false)`, not saved | `await rs.resetDeviceId()` |
| LÖVE | `ravensight.setTrackingEnabled(false)` | `ravensight.resetDeviceId()` |
| Unity | `Ravensight.SetTrackingEnabled(false)` | `Ravensight.ResetDeviceId()` |
| Unreal | `SetTrackingEnabled(false)` on the subsystem | `ResetDeviceId()` |
| C++ | `client.set_tracking_enabled(false)` | `client.reset_device_id()` |
| Odin | `rs.set_tracking_enabled(client, false)` | `rs.reset_device_id(client)` |
| iOS | `Ravensight.setTrackingEnabled(false)` | `Ravensight.resetDeviceId()` |
| Android | `Ravensight.setTrackingEnabled(context, false)` | `Ravensight.resetDeviceId()` |

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: Store disclosures and the privacy manifest
documents.content:
### Store disclosures and the privacy manifest

 

You do still have disclosure obligations, and they are yours rather than ours, because Apple and Google ask the publisher of record. The answers below cover what Ravensight collects on its own account; add whatever your own events carry on top, and if you send something personal, disclose it.

 

- **App Store privacy details.** Declare **Device ID** under Identifiers and **Product Interaction** under Usage Data, both under **Data Not Linked to You**, purpose **Analytics**, and answer **Data Not Used to Track You**. With the country and device fields on (the default), also declare **Coarse Location** under Location and **Other Diagnostic Data** under Diagnostics, the same way. Add **Crash Data** under Diagnostics only if you send crash events.
 
- **Apple privacy manifest.** With any SDK other than the Swift package, add the `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes` entries below to your `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`, with `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked` false and `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking` false on both, and `NSPrivacyTracking` false. The required-reason entries depend on the SDK. The Swift package ships its own `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`, which Xcode merges into your app's privacy report: it declares `NSPrivacyAccessedAPICategoryUserDefaults` with reason `CA92.1`, tracking false, and Device ID and Product Interaction as collected, so you do not add those two yourself. With the country and device fields on, add `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeCoarseLocation` and `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeOtherDiagnosticData` to your app's own manifest with any SDK, the Swift package included, linked false, tracking false, purpose Analytics. Unity's `PlayerPrefs` is `UserDefaults` on iOS, so a Unity game's manifest must declare `NSPrivacyAccessedAPICategoryUserDefaults` with `CA92.1` if the engine's own manifest does not already. Godot and Unreal store a file in the app's own container and add no required-reason entry of their own, so leave whatever your engine's export already declares exactly as it is.
 
- **Android.** The `android.permission.INTERNET` permission is the only one any SDK needs. No `AD_ID` permission, and nothing that triggers a runtime permission dialog. In the Play Console Data safety form declare **Device or other IDs** and **App interactions** as collected, not shared, for Analytics, not for advertising, and with the country and device fields on also **Approximate location** and **Diagnostics** the same way; answer yes to encrypted in transit, because every request is HTTPS; and answer yes to a deletion path, which is the reset call above plus deleting the game. With the native Android SDK, merge its Auto Backup rules so the device id and the saved opt-out stay on the device rather than following the player's cloud backup to a new phone.

 

PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy, the Ravensight entries

 

```
<key>NSPrivacyTracking</key>
<false/>
<key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes</key>
<array>
  <dict>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataType</key>
    <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeDeviceID</string>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposes</key>
    <array>
      <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposeAnalytics</string>
    </array>
  </dict>
  <dict>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataType</key>
    <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeProductInteraction</string>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposes</key>
    <array>
      <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposeAnalytics</string>
    </array>
  </dict>
  <!-- With the country and device fields on -->
  <dict>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataType</key>
    <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeCoarseLocation</string>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposes</key>
    <array>
      <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposeAnalytics</string>
    </array>
  </dict>
  <dict>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataType</key>
    <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeOtherDiagnosticData</string>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeLinked</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeTracking</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposes</key>
    <array>
      <string>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypePurposeAnalytics</string>
    </array>
  </dict>
</array>
```

 

**What our sub-processors see**, so your "shared with third parties" answer is honest. The event stream is stored with our cloud, event database and operational database providers, who process it only to run Ravensight for you. When you use the AI analyst, the model provider receives the text a player typed into feedback and the rows and totals the analyst's tools queried, under contract; it never receives a player's report image. The embedding provider receives feedback text so you can search it. A product analytics service runs in the dashboard and on this website, never inside a game. Nothing reaches an ad network or a data broker, and nothing is sold. Both stores treat a service provider acting on your instructions as your own processing rather than sharing, which is why "not shared" is the correct answer. The [privacy policy](https://www.ravensight.io/privacy/) names every provider.

 

Ravensight itself is the processor here, not the controller. What ends up in an event payload is entirely what you chose to put there, so if you send something personal, disclose it.

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: What your privacy label can say
documents.content:
### What your privacy label can say

 

These are the answers for a game that uses Ravensight and nothing else that collects data. Each row says why, against the store's own definition, so you can defend it in review. Apple's rule for "not linked": direct identifiers are stripped before collection and you never try to link the data back to a person afterwards. Ravensight never collects a direct identifier in the first place, and there is no account to link to.

 

App Store privacy details

 

| Data type | Answer | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identifiers: Device ID | Collected. Analytics. Data Not Linked to You. Data Not Used to Track You. | A random per-install id that is never joined to a name, email or account, and never combined with another company's data, so it meets neither the "linked" test nor the tracking definition. |
| Usage Data: Product Interaction | Collected. Analytics. Data Not Linked to You. Data Not Used to Track You. | Event names, levels and session timing from your own game only, stored against the same unlinked id and used for nothing but your dashboard. |
| Diagnostics: Crash Data | Only if you send crash events. Same answers as above. | Ravensight has no crash reporter; a crash you report as an event is Product Interaction unless it carries a stack trace, in which case declare Crash Data too. |
| User Content: Other User Content | Only if you enable player feedback or Player Reports. Analytics. Not Linked. Not Used to Track. | Free text a player types and any image they attach are stored under the device id until you delete them; disclose what your players can type. |
| Contact Info, Location, Financial Info, Health, Browsing History, Search History, Purchases | Not collected. | The SDK has no field for any of these, and the privacy policy commits that it never will. |

 

Google Play Data safety

 

| Question or data type | Answer | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Device or other IDs | Collected. Not shared. Analytics. Not used for advertising or marketing. | The random per-install id above; it leaves your game only for Ravensight's own storage, which Play treats as your processing, not sharing. |
| App activity: App interactions | Collected. Not shared. Analytics. | Your gameplay events, under the same id, used only for your dashboard. |
| App info and performance: Crash logs | Only if you send crash events. | Ravensight has no crash reporter of its own. |
| Messages or other user-generated content | Only if you enable player feedback or Player Reports. | Text a player types is stored until you delete it and reaches the model provider for analysis under contract. |
| Is the data encrypted in transit? | Yes. | Every SDK talks to Ravensight over HTTPS only. |
| Is there a way to request deletion? | Yes. | The SDK's reset call (see the table under Mobile privacy) severs the player from their history and the old rows expire under the game's selected raw-event retention (90 days by default, optionally 180 or 400); deleting the game removes its stored gameplay data. |
| Is collection required or optional? | Optional if you wire the SDK's opt-out call (see the table under Mobile privacy) to a setting, otherwise required. | The switch sends nothing while off, and every SDK except JavaScript saves it; Ravensight ships no consent screen, so this one is your call. |

 

For a game that runs no ads, the one sentence this lets you put on your store page, and mean it: **"No ads, no tracking, no account needed."** If you later add an ad network, an attribution SDK or a sign-in, revisit every row above, because the first two are exactly what the tracking definition is about.

 

A public demo that asks before it sends keeps the player's opt-in choice on the player's own device, in the game's save folder or the browser's storage, so clearing it asks again. A random device id is still an identifier: it is not linked to a person, but it is collected, so declare it as the rows above do.

documents.section_title: Where the SDKs run
documents.title: SDK repositories
documents.content:
### SDK repositories

 

| SDK | Status | Repository |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Godot | Stable | [ravensight-godot](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-godot) |
| JavaScript | Stable | [ravensight-js](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-js), [ravensight on npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ravensight) |
| Unity | Beta: verified in the Unity 6 Editor and a macOS player | [ravensight-unity](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-unity) |
| Unreal | Beta: compiled and spec tested on Unreal Engine 5.8.3 | [ravensight-unreal](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-unreal) |
| C++ | Beta | [ravensight-cpp](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-cpp) |
| Odin | Beta | [ravensight-odin](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-odin) |
| LÖVE | Desktop, web through the JavaScript SDK | [ravensight-love](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-love) |
| iOS | Beta | [ravensight-ios](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-ios) |
| Android | Beta | [ravensight-android](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-android) |

 

Beta means the SDK meets the same contract as the others and its own tests pass, but no released game has shipped with it yet; it becomes Stable when one does.

 

Every SDK implements the common ingest protocol, and its batching and retry logic is tested with a fake network rather than the live API. For the 0.2.0 releases these suites were run: the Godot behaviour tests, headless on macOS and in CI; the Unity SDK's engine-free core tests in CI and, for 0.2.1, its 58 EditMode and 4 Play Mode tests in the Unity 6000.6.5f1 Editor, plus a macOS player run end to end; the Unreal plugin for 0.2.1, built on Unreal Engine 5.8.3 with warnings treated as errors, its 78 automation specs run headless in the editor, and the Mac editor and game targets built, though no packaged game has run yet; the C++ and Odin suites on macOS; the Swift package's tests on macOS and the iOS Simulator; the Android SDK's JVM and Robolectric tests; and the LÖVE SDK's suite (`luajit spec/run.lua`). Each SDK's README names the commands and toolchain versions. If your engine is not here, the [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/http-api/) is three headers and a JSON body.

 

Current SDK versions are Godot 0.5.0, JavaScript 0.7.0, LÖVE 0.7.0, Unity 0.5.0, Unreal 0.5.0, C++ 0.5.0, Odin 0.6.0, iOS 0.6.0 and Android 0.5.0. They include typed event helpers, opt-in performance sampling, remote config and experiment exposure, and from these versions every one keeps a saved queue across launches, compresses large requests (C++ when built with zlib, Odin on macOS and Linux), signs requests on a public key, and sends ad and attribution events. JavaScript 0.7.0, Doctor 0.5.1 and skills 0.2.2 are available from npm. Native SDKs are available from their linked repositories and version tags. The engine results above describe earlier versions. Each repository's validation notes record the current checks and remaining platform limits.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Ravensight.gd
documents.content:
5. Godot SDK reference

 

## Ravensight.gd

 

One autoload script. It owns device identification, session creation, batching, retries, and the offline queue, so your game code only ever needs to call `track_event()`.

 

Code samples scroll horizontally when needed. Focus a sample and use the arrow keys, or swipe to read a long line.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Options
documents.content:
### Options

 

Set these before Ravensight's `_ready()` runs: edit the defaults at the top of `Ravensight.gd`, or set them from an autoload listed above `Ravensight`.

 

| Property | Type | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_url` | String | `https://api.ravensight.io` | With or without `/api/v1`, with or without a trailing slash. Empty means the default. `api_base()` returns the normalised root. |
| `ingest_key` | String | `gt_live_your_ingest_key_here` | Your game's ingest key. It ships in your build and is not a secret. For a web export, a demo or an open-source game, use a public key (`gt_pub_`); keep live keys on your own server when possible. See [Public builds](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/). |
| `game_version` | String | `1.0.0` | Sent with every session. |
| `enabled` | bool | `true` | `false` turns the SDK off for this run: no request of any kind, nothing queued, no `game_started`, until `set_enabled(true)`. Never saved. `set_tracking_enabled()` still saves the player's choice while it is `false`. |
| `max_queue_size` | int | `500` | Unsent events kept. The oldest are dropped first; a queued `game_started` is kept. |
| `flush_interval` | float | `5.0` | Seconds an event waits so it can go out with others. 50 waiting events go at once. |
| `handle_quit` | bool | `true` | The SDK sets `auto_accept_quit` to false, flushes on a close request (and the Android back button when `quit_on_go_back` is on), then calls `get_tree().quit()` itself within 1.5 seconds. Set false if your game has its own "really quit?" dialog; the SDK then only flushes on a close request, and your dialog calls `Ravensight.quit()`. |
| `session_timeout` | float | `1800.0` | Android and iOS only: seconds in the background after which the session counts as over. See Automatic events. |

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Public functions
documents.content:
### Public functions

 

| Function | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `track_event(event_name: String, data: Dictionary = {})` | Queue an event. It only queues: events go out in batches of up to 50, `flush_interval` seconds after the first waiting event, at once when 50 are waiting, on `flush()`, when the app goes to the background, and on quit. Safe to call from any autoload, even before Ravensight's own `_ready()`. |
| `flush()` | Send what is queued now instead of waiting for the timer. Cuts a backoff wait short; a server's Retry-After wait still holds. |
| `quit(exit_code = 0)` | Send `game_exited` and the queue, then quit. Call it from your own Quit button instead of `get_tree().quit()`. |
| `submit_feedback(message: String, category: String = "", rating: int = 0)` | Send player feedback. `category` is optional and one of `FEEDBACK_CATEGORIES`: `bug`, `suggestion`, `complaint`, `praise`, `playtest`, `other`. `rating` is 0 to leave it out, or a whole number from 1 to 5. Anything else fails at once with `invalid_category` or `invalid_rating` and no request is made. Needs an open session; unlike `track_event()`, a call made before one exists fails immediately rather than queueing. |
| `set_tracking_enabled(on: bool)` | The player's opt-out, saved across launches. See Player privacy below. |
| `is_tracking_enabled()` | `true` while events are collected: enabled, not opted out, kill switch on. |
| `reset_device_id()` | Start a fresh analytics identity for this install. Returns the new id. |
| `set_enabled(on: bool)` | The game's own switch for this run (see `enabled`). |
| `get_status_reason()` | Why nothing is being sent, or `""`. See Startup and failures. |
| `api_base()` | The API root requests go to, for example `https://api.ravensight.io/api/v1`. |
| `is_playtest()` | `true` in a run driven by the Ravensight playtest runner. |
| `set_playtest_context(ctx)` | Puts a running game into playtest mode. The SDK already does this from the playtest runner's variables, so a game never needs to call it by hand. |
| `track_ad(network, format, result, options = {})` | Queue an ad lifecycle step as an [`ad` typed event](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events). Returns `false` and sends nothing when a field is malformed. |
| `track_ad_revenue(network, format, placement, revenue_micros, currency)` | Queue a paid impression (result `shown`). Revenue is a digit string of whole micros. |
| `micros_from_decimal_string(text)`, `micros_from_revenue(value)` | Revenue as a micros digit string, without multiplying a float. |
| `set_attribution(attribution)` | Queue where this install was acquired, once per install. |
| `get_device_id()` | This install's random device id, for an attribution partner's customer user id. |
| `get_delivery_stats()` | Events let go of since launch: `dropped_overflow`, `dropped_too_old` and `dropped_refused`. |
| `fetch_suggestions()` | Experimental. Answers on `suggestions_received`; while tracking is off nothing is requested and it answers with an empty list. |

 

`Ravensight.tracking_enabled` is read-only and gives the same answer as `is_tracking_enabled()`. `Ravensight.session_token` is the open session's token, or `""` until one opens. If your game server should report into the player's session, hand it this token and have it send it as `joinToken` when it opens its own session (see the [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/http-api/)). The SDK never computes a session id itself.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Signals
documents.content:
### Signals

 

| Signal | Fires when |
| --- | --- |
| `session_ready` | A session is open. |
| `session_failed(reason: String)` | Opening a session failed: `"invalid_key"` for a refused key, otherwise the server's error code or `"offline"`. Retried for you unless the key was refused. |
| `tracking_disabled(source: String)` | `"server"` for the kill switch, `"player"` after an opt-out, `"init"` when `enabled` is `false` or after `set_enabled(false)`. |
| `status_changed(reason: String)` | `get_status_reason()` changed. |
| `events_flushed(count: int)` | A batch was accepted. `count` is the number sent, which can be more than the server stored: an event timestamped more than 90 days ago is dropped (see [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/http-api/)). |
| `flush_failed(reason: String)` | A batch failed. It is retried for you, except events the server refuses with a 400, or one event refused with a 413, which are dropped. `"event_too_large"` for an event whose data is over 8,192 bytes as JSON, dropped before it was queued. |
| `feedback_submitted` | Feedback was accepted. |
| `feedback_failed(reason: String)` | Feedback failed: `"disabled"`, `"empty_message"`, `"invalid_category"`, `"invalid_rating"` or `"no_session"` before sending (no request is made), or the server's error code. |
| `suggestions_received(suggestions: Array)` | Experimental. Carries the result of `fetch_suggestions()`. |
| `event_tracked(event_name: String, data: Dictionary)` | Every time `track_event()` queues an event, with the data actually queued (playtest tags included in a playtest run). Use it to mirror tracked events elsewhere in the running game. |

 

```
func _ready():
    Ravensight.session_ready.connect(func(): print("ready"))
    Ravensight.session_failed.connect(func(reason): print("session failed: ", reason))
    Ravensight.tracking_disabled.connect(func(source): print("tracking off: ", source))
    Ravensight.status_changed.connect(func(reason): print("status: ", reason))
    Ravensight.events_flushed.connect(func(count): print("sent ", count, " events"))
```

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Automatic events
documents.content:
### Automatic events

 

The SDK sends exactly two events by itself:

 

- **`game_started`**, once per session. It is queued at launch, first in the queue with the launch time, and sent once the kill switch check allows it. It is never queued while the SDK is disabled or the player has opted out; a game enabled later in the run queues it then, once.
 
- **`game_exited`**, once, when the game quits through `Ravensight.quit()`, or through the window close or the Android back button when the SDK handles that quit (`handle_quit`). Losing focus on a desktop is not an exit: it only sends what is queued.

 

**Android and iOS.** Going to the background tries to send what is queued and saves a small marker (`user://ravensight_bg.save`); no event is sent. Back in the foreground within 30 minutes (`session_timeout`), nothing happens. After 30 minutes or more, the old session gets `game_exited` stamped with the moment the app went to the background, and a new session starts with `game_started`. If the player swipes the app away while it is in the background, the next launch sends that `game_exited` from the marker (one attempt, before anything else) and deletes the marker.

 

**Web export.** The browser gives a Godot web game no close notification, so a web build never sends `game_exited`. `game_started` and everything you track are sent as usual.

 

From your own Quit button, call `Ravensight.quit()` instead of `get_tree().quit()`, which quits at once and sends no `game_exited`:

 

```
func _on_quit_pressed() -> void:
    Ravensight.quit()
```

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Startup and failures
documents.content:
### Startup and failures

 

`get_status_reason()` says why nothing is being sent, and `status_changed` fires when that changes.

 

| Reason | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `""` | Nothing is wrong: a session is open, or opening normally. |
| `disabled` | `enabled` is `false`, or the player opted out. |
| `invalid_key` | The server refused the ingest key (401, or a 403 that is not one of the codes below). Logged once as `Ravensight: ingest key refused (invalid_key), sending stopped for this run. Check your gt_live_ key.` Nothing more is sent or retried this run; the queued events stay on disk for the next launch. A 401 on a batch is an expired session instead: the SDK opens a new session once, and a second 401 in a row waits for the backoff. |
| `tracking_disabled` | The kill switch is off for your game. Nothing more is sent this run; the queued events stay on disk. |
| `offline` | No answer (no connection, or no reply within 15 seconds). Retried after 10 seconds, doubling up to 5 minutes, each wait multiplied by a random factor from 0.5 up to 1; events are kept. |
| `rate_limited` | The server said slow down (429, or 503 with Retry-After). The SDK waits exactly the Retry-After time. |
| `session_failed` | Opening a session failed for another reason (retried with the same backoff), or a playtest token was refused. |
| `playtest_job_closed` | The playtest job this run belongs to has closed. Nothing more is sent. |

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Delivery
documents.content:
### Delivery

 

- **Saved queue.** Unsent events are written to `user://ravensight/queue-<16 hex>.json`, one file per ingest key, through a temporary file renamed over the old one. The file is read once when sending starts. At most 500 events are kept across launches, oldest dropped first, and events older than 89 days are dropped when it is read. An event leaves the file only after a 2xx answer, or a 400 that refuses it. `get_delivery_stats()` counts what was let go.
 
- **Device backups.** Godot gives a script no way to keep a file out of Android and iOS backups, so the game does it. The [README](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-godot) gives the export option and backup rules. Desktop builds need nothing.
 
- **Origin.** Each session's events are saved with that session's `origin`, so events a later launch sends are filed under the session, build and platform they happened in. Timestamps are unix milliseconds, so events in one second keep their order.
 
- **Errors behind gameplay.** Gameplay events, a game's own `track_error` included, go before captured errors, also after the queue is read from disk. A capture evicts only the oldest capture, never a gameplay event, and an error's `rs_trail` is never written to the file.
 
- **Compression and signing.** A request body of 1,024 bytes or more is sent gzip compressed; a 415 is sent once more uncompressed. When the session answer has `signing` ([public keys](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/)), every batch carries `X-Ravensight-Timestamp` and an HMAC-SHA256 `X-Ravensight-Signature`. The secret is never written to disk.
 
- **Refusals.** A 400 naming one event by `index` drops that event and resends the rest. Only `batch_too_large` and 413 halve the batch. Any other 400 drops the request's events, reported on `flush_failed`.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Kill switch
documents.content:
### Kill switch

 

On boot, the SDK calls `GET /api/v1/settings` once with `ingest_key`. If tracking is off for your game, it goes idle for that run: no session is created and nothing is sent, and the `tracking_disabled` signal fires with source `"server"`. A `403 tracking_disabled` from any request has the same effect mid-run. Flip `trackingEnabled` from the dashboard's game settings and it takes effect on the game's next launch, no update required.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Levels and deaths
documents.content:
### Levels and deaths

 

Ravensight builds the level funnel, per-level deaths and journeys from your event names, with no configuration: names containing `died`, `destroyed` or `killed` count as deaths, `start`, `begin` or `enter` as level starts, and `complet`, `finish`, `win` or `clear` as completions. The `level`, `location` or `track` field says where. To say what an event means instead, set `rs_kind` in its data to `level_start`, `level_complete`, `death` or `none`. It is read before the name, and `none` opts an event out. Keys that start with `rs_` are reserved for Ravensight.

 

```
Ravensight.track_event("boss_phase_begin", {"level": "castle", "rs_kind": "none"})
Ravensight.track_event("run_over", {"level": "castle", "rs_kind": "death"})
```

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Typed events and performance
documents.content:
### Typed events and performance

 

Four helpers send the [typed events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events) without you writing the reserved keys. Each builds the `rs_` properties and calls `track_event()`, so queueing, retries and the player's opt-out are unchanged. Every helper takes an optional last `options` dictionary.

 

| Function | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `track_purchase(item_type, item_id, amount, currency, options)` | A purchase. `amount` is whole minor units and the currency is upper-cased. `options` takes `cart` and `transaction_id`. Event name `purchase`. |
| `track_resource(flow, resource, amount, options)` | A resource gained (`"source"`) or spent (`"sink"`). `options` takes `item_type` and `item_id`. Event name `resource_source` or `resource_sink`. |
| `track_progression(status, p1, options)` | A progression step: `"start"`, `"complete"` or `"fail"`. `options` takes `p2`, `p3` and `score`. Event name `progression_start`, `progression_complete` or `progression_fail`. |
| `track_event_at(event_name, position, data)` | An event with a position for [Level heatmaps](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/): `position` is a `Vector2` in your game's units, sent as `rs_x` and `rs_y`. A component that is not finite sends the event without a position. Since 0.6.0. |
| `track_error(severity, message, options)` | An error. The message is cut to 200 characters and the stack (`options.stack`) to 2000. Event name `error`. |
| `performance` option | Off by default. When on, the SDK samples the frame rate once a second and sends one `health` event per session, on background (Android, iOS), page hide (web) or quit (desktop). |

 

`options.data` adds your own properties (the reserved keys win if they clash) and `options.event_name` replaces the default event name. The helpers never throw: a wrong value becomes an event the server flags.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Player privacy
documents.content:
### Player privacy

 

The device id is 16 random bytes from the operating system's secure random source, as hex, plus the OS name, generated on first run and saved in `user://`. `set_tracking_enabled()` writes the choice at once and can be called at any time, even from an autoload that runs before Ravensight's `_ready()`, or while `enabled` is `false`. A saved opt-out wins over `enabled = true`: on the next launch nothing is sent, not even the kill switch check. Turning it off drops the queue and deletes the saved queue file. `reset_device_id()` saves a new random id, drops the queue (and its file), the session and the attribution flag, and returns the new id. In a playtest run both do nothing but print one line.

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Telling players
documents.content:
### Telling players

 

You do not need a permission prompt, but saying what the game sends is good manners. A paragraph your game can show, in a settings screen or on its store page:

 

This game sends anonymous gameplay events (what happens in the game, never who you are) to Ravensight so we can improve it. You can turn this off in Settings at any time.

 

And the toggle behind "turn this off":

 

```
# an "Analytics" switch in your settings screen
func _on_analytics_toggled(on: bool) -> void:
    Ravensight.set_tracking_enabled(on)  # remembered across launches

# a "Forget me" button: a fresh random identity from now on
func _on_forget_me_pressed() -> void:
    Ravensight.reset_device_id()
```

documents.section_title: Ravensight.gd
documents.title: Player Reports
documents.content:
### Player Reports

 

Add an optional in-game form that captures the current game screen, lets players highlight or hide an area, and sends a short message. Bind the reporting action to a key, controller input or pause-menu button. The dashboard groups reports into issues and tracks fixes through verification.

 

Download [Ravensight.gd](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/godot/Ravensight.gd), [RavensightReports.gd](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/godot/RavensightReports.gd) and [RavensightReportOverlay.gd](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/godot/RavensightReportOverlay.gd). Add the latter two as children of the Ravensight autoload, named RavensightReports and ReportOverlay. Bind `ravensight_report` in Input Map. The overlay captures only the game viewport and never pauses multiplayer.

 

Reports draw from your included events and prepaid balance automatically. A text report counts as 1 event on the event meter; a screenshot adds 20,000 events to the meter, covering processing, storage and delivery. There is no separate screenshot budget to configure. Failed or canceled uploads release their reserved usage. Retention and file limits are listed in Settings. Text-only reporting remains available if capture or upload fails. Screenshots are not automatically sent to AI providers.

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.content:
6. JavaScript SDK reference

 

## The ravensight package for browser games and Node

 

One zero-dependency client for browser games and Node 18 or newer, shipped as both ESM and CommonJS. It owns sessions, batching, the offline queue, rate limits and the server-side kill switch, so your game code calls `init()` once and `track()` from then on.

 

Code samples scroll horizontally when needed. Focus a sample and use the arrow keys, or swipe to read a long line.

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: Install
documents.content:
### Install

 

```
npm install ravensight
```

 

There is no build step for consumers. It suits Phaser, PixiJS, three.js, Excalibur and hand-written canvas games. Godot HTML5 exports use the [Godot SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/godot-sdk/) instead.

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: Quickstart

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: Options
documents.content:
### Options

 

Pass these to `new Ravensight(options)`.

 

| Option | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ingestKey` | required | Your game's key: a public key (`gt_pub_...`) in a web page, a `gt_live_...` key only on a server. See [Public builds](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/). |
| `apiUrl` | `https://api.ravensight.io/api/v1` | `/api/v1` is appended if you leave it off. |
| `gameVersion` | `'1.0.0'` | Reported with the session. |
| `platform` | auto | `'web'` in a browser, `node-<platform>` in Node. |
| `autoFlushMs` | `15000` | Flush interval. `0` flushes only on demand. |
| `maxQueueSize` | `500` | Offline queue cap. The oldest events are dropped first. |
| `persistQueue` | `true` | Keep the queue across a reload, a crash or a lost network: one `localStorage` entry per ingest key in a browser, one file per key in Node. `false` keeps it in memory only. |
| `queueDir` | `~/.ravensight` | Node only: the folder the queue file is written to. |
| `maxSessions` | `64` | Sessions cached at once, one per device id. The least recently used is dropped first, never the current id, and reopens on that device's next event. |
| `storage` | auto | Anything with `getItem` and `setItem`. Holds the device id. |
| `deviceId` | auto | Overrides the generated device id. |
| `enabled` | `true` | Pass `false` to start opted out. |
| `autoEvents` | `true` | Send `game_started` and `game_exited` for you, in a browser only. A client that starts with `enabled: false` sends neither. |
| `fetch` | global | Inject a custom fetch. |
| `debug` | `false` | Logs SDK activity to the console, and warns about reserved `rs_` keys. |
| `performance` | `false` | Sample the frame rate and send one `health` event per session on page hide. Browser only. See [typed events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events). |

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: Methods
documents.content:
### Methods

 

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `await rs.init()` | Reads the kill switch from `GET /api/v1/settings`, then opens a session. Resolves with `{ trackingEnabled, sessionReady, reason }` and never throws on a network failure. `reason` is `null` when the session is ready, otherwise one of the values in the table below. If tracking is off for your game, nothing further is sent. |
| `rs.track(event, data?, { deviceId }?)` | Queues an event and records its timestamp at the moment of the call. Safe before `init()`. Returns `false` when tracking is off. `deviceId` sends this one event as another device, under that id's own session, so one Node client can serve many players. It must be a non-empty string or `track()` throws a `TypeError`. |
| `rs.trackPurchase({ amount, currency, itemType, itemId, cart?, transactionId?, data?, event? })` | A typed purchase. `amount` is whole minor units, an integer or a digit string, and the currency is upper-cased. Event name `purchase`. Returns what `track()` returns. |
| `rs.trackResource({ flow, resource, amount, itemType?, itemId?, data?, event? })` | A resource gained (`'source'`) or spent (`'sink'`). Event name `resource_source` or `resource_sink`. |
| `rs.trackProgression({ status, p1, p2?, p3?, score?, data?, event? })` | A progression step: `'start'`, `'complete'` or `'fail'`. Event name `progression_start`, `progression_complete` or `progression_fail`. |
| `rs.trackAt(event, { x, y }, data?, { deviceId }?)` | An event with a position for [Level heatmaps](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/): sets `rs_x` and `rs_y` from `x` and `y` in your game's units, then sends it like `track`. A coordinate that is not a finite number sends the event without a position. Since 0.11.0. |
| `rs.trackError({ severity, message, stack?, data?, event? })` | An error. `severity` is `'debug'`, `'info'`, `'warning'`, `'error'` or `'critical'`; the message is cut to 200 characters and the stack to 2000. Event name `error`. |
| `rs.trackAd(network, format, result, { placement, revenueMicros, currency }?)` | An [`ad` typed event](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events). Revenue is a digit string of whole micros, sent only with `shown` and always with a currency. Returns `false` and sends nothing for a value the server would flag. |
| `rs.trackAdRevenue(network, format, placement, revenueMicros, currency)` | A paid impression. `microsFromDecimalString('0.0015')` and `microsFromRevenue(0.0015)` both give `"1500"` without multiplying a float; `adFormatFrom` maps a mediation format name. |
| `rs.setAttribution({ source, network, campaign, adset, creative, touchTime })` | One `attribution` event per device id; every later call returns `false`, across restarts. In a browser the SDK sends one for you on the first load of a new device id when the landing URL has a UTM parameter. |
| `await rs.flush()` | Sends what is queued now and resolves with `{ sent, queued }`. Concurrent calls are safe. It cuts a backoff wait short, never a server `Retry-After`. |
| `await rs.submitFeedback(message, category?, rating?)` | Sends player feedback. `category` is one of the values below, exported as `FEEDBACK_CATEGORIES`. `rating` is an integer from 1 to 5. Leave either out with `undefined`, `null` or an empty string. Anything else is invalid and throws before any request is made, with code `invalid_category` or `invalid_rating`; an empty message throws `empty_message`. |
| `rs.setEnabled(bool)` | Local opt in and opt out. `false` stops sending and clears anything queued. The SDK does not store the choice: keep it in your own settings and call this before the first event on every launch. |
| `await rs.setDeviceId(id)` | Changes the device id, for example after a player signs in on a shared machine. The switch is immediate: nothing is flushed or waited for. The new id is stored and its session opens on the next flush. Events already queued keep the id they were tracked under and go out under that id's own session, so nothing is ever sent under the wrong id. Resolves with `{ previousId, queuedUnderPreviousId }`. Setting the current id again changes nothing. |
| `await rs.resetDeviceId()` | The same with a fresh random id, which it resolves with. Use it for a reset analytics id button. |
| `rs.joinSession(token, { deviceId }?)` | Joins a session opened elsewhere, normally the browser's `rs.sessionToken`, so the next session opened for `deviceId` (default: the client's own id) shares its analytics session. Any session already cached for that id is dropped, and the token is used once. See Joining the browser's session below. |
| `await rs.dispose({ flush = true, timeoutMs = 2000 })` | Shuts the client down and resolves with `{ sent, dropped, kept }`. The timer and page listeners stop at once and `track()` returns `false` from that moment. The queue is then flushed by default, bounded by `timeoutMs`, even if `init()` was never called; in a browser, whatever is still queued after that goes out in one last keepalive or beacon request. With the persisted queue on, anything left stays stored for the next launch and is counted as `kept`; with `persistQueue: false` it is counted as dropped. Events in a request that timed out are counted as dropped, even if it later lands. Pass `{ flush: false }` to discard the queue. After dispose, `setDeviceId()` and `resetDeviceId()` reject with code `disposed`. |
| `await rs.fetchSuggestions()` | Experimental. The AI-generated design suggestions for your game, empty until a weekly digest has run. The shape may change, so do not build game logic on it. |

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: Why a session is not ready
documents.content:
### Why a session is not ready

 

| Reason | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `invalid_key` | The key was refused (`401`, or a `403` other than the kill switch) by the settings check or `POST /session`. The run ends, because a retry cannot fix a revoked, rotated or wrong key: the queue is cleared, the timer stops, `track()` returns `false`, and `init()` and `flush()` do not try the key again. It warns once on the console. |
| `tracking_disabled` | Tracking is switched off for this game. Nothing is sent. |
| `disabled` | The client is opted out (`enabled: false` or `setEnabled(false)`). `init()` makes no network call. Call `setEnabled(true)` and then `init()` to start. |
| `offline` | No answer from the network. Retried with backoff. |
| `rate_limited` | `429`. Retried after `Retry-After`. |
| `session_failed` | Any other answer. Retried with backoff. |

 

`rs.stats.lastError` holds the last failed request as `{ code, status, at }`, from the session, settings or batch requests, or `null`. Read it when events are not arriving. It can show `session_expired` after a routine `401` the SDK has already recovered from, so read it together with whether the queue is draining.

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: How delivery works
documents.content:
### How delivery works

 

- **Batches of 50.** The server's limit per request. A flush keeps sending batches until the queue drains.
 
- **Persisted queue.** On by default. In a browser the queue lives in one `localStorage` entry per ingest key; in Node it is one file per key under `~/.ravensight` (or `queueDir`), written through a temporary file and a rename. It is read back once at start. At most 500 events are kept, the oldest go first, and anything older than 89 days is dropped at start. Two tabs of the same game share one entry, so the last tab to write wins.
 
- **Removed only once delivered.** An event leaves the queue only after a `2xx`, or a `400` that names it by `index`. Each event remembers the `origin` of the session it was tracked under, so an event sent on a later launch is stored under the session, build and platform it happened in. Timestamps are unix milliseconds of the moment it was tracked.
 
- **Errors behind gameplay.** Gameplay events go ahead of queued automatic error captures. In a full queue an incoming capture evicts the oldest capture, or is dropped, and never evicts gameplay. `rs_trail` is never written to storage, and `resetDeviceId()` and an opt-out delete persisted captures.
 
- **One device per batch.** Each request carries the leading run of queued events that share one device id, under that id's own session, then the next run.
 
- **Answers.** A `400` with `index` drops that event and resends the rest; `400 batch_too_large` halves the batch; any other `400` drops the request's events. A `401` opens one new session for that device and resends; a second `401` in a row waits for the backoff. A `403` on a batch keeps the events and stops sending until the next launch. `413` splits the batch, `415` resends once uncompressed, and `429`, or `503` with `Retry-After`, waits exactly the server's time.
 
- **Backoff.** From 10 seconds, doubling to 5 minutes, each wait multiplied by a random factor between 0.5 and 1. `flush()` cuts a backoff short; nothing cuts a `Retry-After` short.
 
- **Compression and signing.** A request body of 1,024 bytes or more is sent gzip compressed; page-hide sends never are. When `POST /session` answers with `signing` ([public keys](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/)), every batch carries `X-Ravensight-Timestamp` and `X-Ravensight-Signature`, an HMAC-SHA256 over the uncompressed body. The secret is kept in memory only; a beacon carries a signed body envelope instead.
 
- **Page hide.** When the page goes hidden the SDK sends one last batch, preferring `fetch` with `keepalive`. Where that is unavailable it falls back to `navigator.sendBeacon`, which cannot set headers, so the session token travels in the JSON body as `sessionToken`, never in the URL. Those events stay in the persisted queue marked unconfirmed; the next launch resends them if it comes within 23 hours, inside the server's 24 hour duplicate window.
 
- **No re-send while in flight.** The SDK never sends a batch again while it is still in flight, so a batch cut off by a real page unload can be lost rather than counted twice. A batch whose response is lost, from a network error or a 5xx after the server already stored it, can be sent again on the next flush, and ingest does not remove duplicates.

 

Session creation and tracked events are rate limited per game, not per client. See [Usage, billing and limits](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/limits/).

documents.section_title: The ravensight package for browser games and Node
documents.title: What the dashboard reads
documents.content:
### What the dashboard reads

 

The dashboard gives meaning to some fields and event names. Name your events with these in mind.

 

- **One place per event.** `level`, `location` and `track` in the event data fold into one place, and the first non-empty one wins, in that order. The level funnel, per-level deaths and journeys only see events that have a place.
 
- **Event names.** A name containing `start`, `begin` or `enter` is a level start; `complet`, `finish`, `win` or `clear` is a completion; `died`, `destroyed` or `killed` is a death. These are lowercase substring matches.
 
- **`rs_kind` overrides the name.** Set `rs_kind` in the event data to `level_start`, `level_complete`, `death` or `none` and it is read before the name. `none` opts an event out, so `checkout_started` is not a level start. An unknown value falls through to the name match. Keys that start with `rs_` are reserved for Ravensight. The SDK exports the four values as `RS_KINDS`, and with `debug: true` it warns once per event and key about an `rs_kind` outside that list or an `rs_` key Ravensight does not read. It never throws and still sends the event. The server counts the same two mistakes on the Implementation health card.
 
- **Potentially stuck** is one event repeated 10 or more times at the same level in a session of fewer than 20 events. The same event at a new level each time is movement, not stuck. Events with no place are grouped together, so ten repeats of a placeless event in a short session count; send a place or accept it.

 

```
rs.track('boss_phase_begin', { level: 'castle', rs_kind: 'none' });
rs.track('run_over', { level: 'castle', rs_kind: 'death' });
```

 

The full rules, including the player flags, are in [how the built-in detections read your events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#detection-rules).

documents.title: Campaign links
documents.content:
### Campaign links

 

A [campaign link](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/campaign-links/) that points at a web page adds `rs_link` to the address. From 0.8.0, the SDK reads it from `location.search` once, when it starts, and sends it with the first session it opens, so the Campaign links page can count the players and sessions each link brought. There is nothing to call. Later sessions do not send it, nothing is stored, the page address is left as it is, and consent applies as to everything else.

 

Outside a web page (a desktop or mobile app built on the SDK), read `rs_link` from the address your deep link, universal link or App Link handler received and pass it to `rs.setCampaignLink(id)` (0.12.0 or later). It returns `true` for a link id and sends it with the next session, once, the same way; anything else returns `false` and changes nothing. See [Campaign links](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/campaign-links/#campaign-links-players).

documents.title: Privacy
documents.content:
### Privacy

 

The SDK generates a random device id and stores it under `ravensight_device_id`. It collects no hardware identifier, advertising id or personal data, only the events you send. If you pass your own `deviceId`, as on a server, make it a pseudonymous player id your game generates, never an email or account name. The row by row answers for the App Store and Google Play forms are in [what your privacy label can say](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/platform-support/#privacy-label).

documents.section_title: Web games: your website and your game
documents.title: Web games: your website and your game
documents.content:
Web games

 

## Web games: your website and your game

 

A browser game usually shares a domain with its own website: a landing page, a pricing page, a sign in page, then the game. If the game SDK starts on every page, every visitor opens a game session and counts as a player, and your player numbers stop meaning players. Keep the two apart: the website tracker on your site, the game SDK inside your game.

documents.section_title: Web games: your website and your game
documents.title: Two trackers, two jobs
documents.content:
### Two trackers, two jobs

 

Ravensight has two separate ways to measure a web game, each with its own key, and they are meant to run on different pages.

 

| Where | Use | Key | What it counts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Public pages: landing, marketing, pricing, blog | The [website tracker](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/websites/), `createSiteTracker()` | Your website key, `gt_site_...` | Visitors, page views, sources and goals, with no player identity |
| Inside the game, for a player who is playing | The [game SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/javascript-sdk/), `new Ravensight()` | Your game's public key, `gt_pub_...` | Players, sessions, retention, funnels and everything else on the dashboard |

 

A key shipped in a web page is public, because anyone can read it from the page: use a public key with an event allowlist and a monthly ceiling, and keep `gt_live_` keys on your own server. See [Public builds](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/).

 

In a browser the game SDK sends `game_started` as soon as the client is created and `game_exited` when the page is hidden. That is right inside a game and wrong on a landing page: a visitor who reads one page and leaves becomes a player with a two event session. Two of our own web games did exactly this: over 30 days, more than 80% of their new players were really website visitors.

documents.title: How Ravensight tells you
documents.content:
### How Ravensight tells you

 

The Data quality card on your game's Health page, and `visitorSessions` in the [`get_data_quality`](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/mcp/#get-data-quality-game-id-from-to) tool, check for this on every web game. They look at the devices first seen in the selected range (30 days by default) that sent a web event, real players only, and count how many never sent more than 3 events in any session: a session start and very little else. Events your game server sends into the browser's session count toward that session.

 

- **Flagged** when we are 95% sure at least 60% of those devices did nothing past a session start. The card shows a warning with the fix and a link to this page.
 
- **Clear** below that. A game where even half its new players leave at once stays clear.
 
- **Too few to read** with fewer than 10 new web devices.

 

Players who open your game and leave at once look the same as visitors, so a flag means "check where your site starts the SDK", not proof. After you fix it, the check reads only devices first seen since then, so it clears as the range moves past the fix; choose a shorter range on the Health page to see it sooner. Events already stored are not rewritten, so earlier visitors stay in your history.

 

To check by hand, open a public page in a private window with your browser's network panel open. Nothing should go to the `/session` endpoint and no `game_started` event should be sent until you sign in and open the game.
