documents.title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.content:
7. LÖVE SDK reference

 

## The ravensight folder for LÖVE games

 

Pure Lua for LÖVE 11.x and 12.x on Windows, macOS and Linux. It owns the device id, sessions, batching, retries and the offline queue, and it sends requests from a background thread, so a slow network never costs a frame. There are no native files to bundle, sign or notarize.

 

Code samples scroll horizontally when needed. Focus a sample and use the arrow keys, or swipe to read a long line.

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Install
documents.content:
### Install

 

Copy the `ravensight` folder from [ravensight-love](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-love) into your game, next to `main.lua`. It can live in a subfolder too (`lib/ravensight`); require it by that path. The same files are published here: [init.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/init.lua), [core.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/core.lua), [config.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/config.lua), [errors.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/errors.lua), [hmac.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/hmac.lua), [json.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/json.lua), [reports.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/reports.lua), [transport.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/transport.lua), [typed.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/typed.lua), [web.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/web.lua) and [worker.lua](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/worker.lua), the love.js bridge [ravensight-love-bridge.js](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/ravensight-love-bridge.js) (only for a web build, it goes on the page, not in the game), the [README](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/README.md) and the [MIT license](https://www.ravensight.io/sdk/love/LICENSE).

 

```
my-game/
  main.lua
  conf.lua
  ravensight/
    init.lua
    core.lua
    config.lua
    errors.lua
    hmac.lua
    json.lua
    reports.lua
    transport.lua
    typed.lua
    web.lua
    worker.lua
```

 

Set an identity in `conf.lua`, so the SDK has a save folder for its device id:

 

```
function love.conf(t)
  t.identity = "my-game"
end
```

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Use
documents.content:
### Use

 

```
local ravensight = require("ravensight")

function love.load()
  ravensight.init({
    apiUrl = "https://api.ravensight.io",
    ingestKey = "gt_live_...",   -- from your game's page in the dashboard
    gameVersion = "1.0.0",
  })
end

function love.update(dt)
  ravensight.update(dt)
end

function love.quit()
  return ravensight.quit()
end

-- anywhere in your game
ravensight.track("level_start", { level = "forest_1" })
ravensight.track("level_complete", { level = "forest_1", seconds = 74, deaths = 2 })
```

 

`game_started` is sent for you on launch and `game_exited` on quit. `ravensight.quit()` returns `true` the first time, which tells LÖVE to wait while the last events are sent; the SDK quits again by itself once they are answered, or after 1.5 seconds. If your game already has a `love.quit`, return its answer from your own handler, or pass `handleQuit = false` so the SDK never delays a quit.

 

```
function love.quit()
  if not saveGame() then return true end
  return ravensight.quit()
end
```

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Options
documents.content:
### Options

 

Pass these to `ravensight.init(options)`.

 

| Option | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ingestKey` | required | Your game's ingest key. It ships in your build and is not a secret. For a web build, a demo or an open-source game, use a public key (`gt_pub_`); keep live keys on your own server when possible. See [Public builds](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/). |
| `apiUrl` | `https://api.ravensight.io` | With or without `/api/v1`. |
| `gameVersion` | `1.0.0` | Sent with every session. |
| `enabled` | `true` | `false` sends and queues nothing for this run, and is not saved. The player's opt out is `setTrackingEnabled`. |
| `maxQueueSize` | `500` | Unsent events kept. The oldest are dropped first. |
| `flushInterval` | `2` | Seconds an event waits so it can go out with others. 50 waiting events go at once. |
| `handleQuit` | `true` | Hold the quit up to 1.5 seconds to send the last events. |
| `transport` | automatic | `"https"`, `"winhttp"`, `"libcurl"` or `"curl"` to try first, or `"web"` for the love.js bridge (chosen for you in a web build). |
| `timeout` | `15` | Seconds per request. |
| `debug` | `false` | Print informational messages too. Warnings always print. |
| `performance` | `false` | Sample the frame rate once a second and send one `health` event per session, on quit. Call `update(dt)` every frame. See [typed events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events). |

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Functions
documents.content:
### Functions

 

| Function | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `track(name, data)` | Queue an event. `data` is a flat table of strings, numbers and booleans. Safe before the session is ready. |
| `purchase(amount, currency, itemType, itemId, opts)` | A typed purchase. `amount` is whole minor units and the currency is upper-cased. `opts` takes `cart`, `transactionId`, `props` and `name`. |
| `resource(flow, resource, amount, opts)` | A resource entering (`"source"`) or leaving (`"sink"`) the economy. `opts` takes `itemType` and `itemId`. |
| `progression(status, p1, opts)` | A progression step: `"start"`, `"complete"` or `"fail"`. `opts` takes `p2`, `p3` and `score`. |
| `error(severity, message, opts)` | An error or warning, with an optional `opts.stack`. The message is cut to 200 characters and the stack to 2000. |
| `trackAd(network, format, result, opts)` | An [`ad` typed event](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events). Returns `true`, or `false` and the reason when a field is malformed (nothing is sent). |
| `trackAdRevenue(network, format, placement, revenueMicros, currency, opts)` | A paid impression (result `shown`). |
| `microsFromDecimalString(text)`, `microsFromRevenue(number)` | Revenue in micros as a digit string, without multiplying a float. |
| `setAttribution(attribution)` | Where this install was acquired, sent once per install. |
| `getDeliveryStats()` | Desktop: events let go of since launch, `dropped_overflow`, `dropped_too_old` and `dropped_refused`. |
| `flush()` | Send what is queued now. It cuts a backoff wait short, never a server Retry-After. |
| `submitFeedback(message, category, rating)` | Send player feedback. `category` and `rating` (1 to 5) are optional. Needs an open session. |
| `setTrackingEnabled(enabled)` | The player's opt-out, remembered across launches. `false` drops the queue and sends nothing, not even the startup check. |
| `isTrackingEnabled()` | `false` when the player opted out or tracking is switched off for your game. |
| `resetDeviceId()` | Start a fresh analytics identity for this install. |
| `getDeviceId()` | This install's random id. |
| `getTransport()` | How requests are sent here, or `nil` if nothing works. |
| `on(event, fn)` | Listen for an SDK event. Returns a function that stops listening. |
| `update(dt)` | Call every frame. Delivers answers and runs retries. |
| `quit()` | Return it from `love.quit`. |

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Events
documents.content:
### Events

 

| Event | Arguments | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `session_ready` | none | A session is open. |
| `session_failed` | `reason` | Opening a session failed. It is retried for you. |
| `tracking_disabled` | `source` | `"server"` when tracking is switched off for your game, `"player"` after an opt-out. |
| `events_flushed` | `count` | A batch was accepted. |
| `flush_failed` | `reason` | A batch failed. It is retried for you. `"event_too_large"`: one event's data was over 8,192 bytes as JSON and the event was dropped, not retried. |
| `feedback_submitted` | none | Feedback was accepted. |
| `feedback_failed` | `reason` | Feedback failed, including `"no_session"` when sent too early. |
| `event_tracked` | `name, data` | Every queued event, with the data actually queued. |

 

```
ravensight.on("tracking_disabled", function(source)
  print("analytics off:", source)
end)
```

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: How requests are sent
documents.content:
### How requests are sent

 

LÖVE 11 has no built-in HTTPS, and the API only accepts HTTPS, so the SDK uses the first of these that works. Nothing native is bundled.

 

1. **`require("https")`**: built into LÖVE 12, or the lua-https library if you added it to an 11.x game.
 
1. **WinHTTP** on Windows, the HTTP library every Windows version ships, called through LuaJIT's FFI.
 
1. **libcurl** on macOS and Linux, the system's own copy, through the FFI.
 
1. **The `curl` command** on macOS and Linux, if libcurl would not load.

 

If none of them works, the SDK prints one warning, keeps events queued, saves them when the game quits and tries again next launch. `getTransport()` tells you which one is in use. The libcurl and `curl` paths have been run against the live API on macOS. The WinHTTP path and Linux are written but not yet verified in a shipped build.

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Delivery
documents.content:
### Delivery

 

On the desktop; a love.js build delivers through the page's JavaScript SDK.

 

- **Batches of 50.** Up to 50 events per request.
 
- **Saved queue.** Unsent events are written to `ravensight/queue-<16 hex>.json` in the save folder, one file per ingest key, whenever the queue changes, through a temporary file renamed over the old one. At most 500 events are kept, oldest dropped first, and events older than 89 days are dropped when it is read. An event leaves the file only after a 2xx answer, or a 400 that refuses it. The 0.5 `ravensight_queue.json` is read once and removed.
 
- **Device backups.** On macOS the SDK excludes the file from Time Machine itself. On Android and iOS the game does it; the [README](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-love) says how.
 
- **Origin.** Each session's events are saved with that session's `origin`, so a later launch sends them under the session, build and platform they happened in. Timestamps are unix milliseconds.
 
- **Errors behind gameplay.** Gameplay events, a game's own `error()` included, go before captured errors. A capture evicts only the oldest capture, never a gameplay event, and an error's `rs_trail` is never written to the file.
 
- **Compression and signing.** A request body of 1,024 bytes or more is sent gzip compressed; a 415 is sent once more uncompressed. When the session answer has `signing` ([public keys](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/)), every batch carries `X-Ravensight-Timestamp` and an HMAC-SHA256 `X-Ravensight-Signature`, computed in `hmac.lua`. The secret stays in memory.
 
- **Backoff.** A failed request is retried after 10 seconds, doubling up to 5 minutes, each wait multiplied by a random factor from 0.5 up to 1. A `429`, or a `503` with `Retry-After`, waits exactly the server's time. A batch `401` opens a new session once, then waits for the backoff.
 
- **Refusals.** A `400` naming one event by `index` drops that event and resends the rest. Only `batch_too_large` and `413` halve the batch. Any other `400` drops the request's events. An event whose data is over 8,192 bytes as JSON is dropped before it is queued.
 
- **Refused key and kill switch.** Either stops the SDK for the rest of the run; the queued events stay on disk for the next launch. Turning tracking off as the player, or `resetDeviceId()`, deletes the saved queue.

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Privacy and the opt-out
documents.content:
### Privacy and the opt-out

 

The SDK generates a random device id per install: 32 hex characters, a dash and the OS name, from the operating system's random source on first launch, saved in your game's save folder. It is not derived from hardware or an account, and `resetDeviceId()` replaces it. Each event carries a timestamp, your game version and the OS. There is no advertising identifier, and no field for names, emails or accounts, so a game using it needs no tracking permission prompt. The row by row store answers are in [what your privacy label can say](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/platform-support/#privacy-label).

 

Ravensight ships no consent screen. If your game shows one, wire it to `setTrackingEnabled(false)`, which is saved and holds across launches, and `resetDeviceId()`.

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Public builds
documents.content:
### Public builds

 

For a demo, a web build or an open-source game, ship a [public key](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/) with ravensight-love 0.3.0 or later. Without a key, `init` is inert: it writes no files, makes no requests, and `ravensight.enabled()` returns `false`; pass `optional = true` to silence its one warning. With `consent = "opt_in"` nothing happens, no device id, no queue and no settings call, until the player turns analytics on with `setTrackingEnabled(true)`, and that choice is saved. The `distribution` option is sent on the session, and every event carries an `rs_event_id` so a resend is never stored twice. A `401` or `403` on the settings check or the session stops the run instead of retrying a revoked key. On the web, `installRavensightBridge(null, Module)` installs a sink for a page with no key: the game's tagged lines are swallowed and the game never knows, and the bridge's opt-in check defaults to off when storage is missing or blocked.

 

Keep the key out of your repository. A tracked example file with placeholders sits beside an untracked config file that your ignore list excludes; your release job writes the real config from a CI secret when it builds a release. A clone or a fork has only the example, so its builds run with analytics off.

 

```
-- analytics.config.example.lua (tracked)
return {
  ingestKey = "",               -- written by the release job, never committed
  distribution = "native-dev",
}

-- main.lua: analytics.config.lua is untracked, and absent in a clone
local file = "analytics.config.lua"
local config = love.filesystem.getInfo(file) and love.filesystem.load(file)() or {}
ravensight.init({
  ingestKey = config.ingestKey ~= "" and config.ingestKey or nil,
  distribution = config.distribution or "native-dev",
  optional = true,
  consent = "opt_in",
  gameVersion = "1.0.0",
})
```

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Shipping to the web
documents.content:
### Shipping to the web

 

A love.js build cannot make requests from Lua, so the page does the sending. Load the [JavaScript SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/javascript-sdk/) (0.4.0 or newer; 0.5.1 or newer for the bridge to report experiment exposure, and 0.7.0 for millisecond timestamps) on the page and install `web/ravensight-love-bridge.js` from the repository before `Love(Module)` runs. The Lua SDK notices the web build by itself and hands every `track`, `submitFeedback`, `setTrackingEnabled` and `flush` to the page, whose SDK owns the session, the device id and the two lifecycle events. The snippet and the details are in the README's [shipping to the web](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-love#shipping-to-the-web-lovejs-itchio) section.

documents.section_title: The ravensight folder for LÖVE games
documents.title: Not supported yet
documents.content:
### Not supported yet

 

Android and iOS are not supported yet. Ravensight Playtest plays a love.js build like any web build, in the cloud or locally with `--build-dir` (see [Which builds play where](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-engines)); a desktop build driven through the experimental desktop adapter (with an automation server you run yourself) or a custom bridge reads the `RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST_TOKEN` and `RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST_RUN_ID` variables, so its persona sessions are tagged synthetic.

 

Where each SDK finds a playtest run: Godot, LÖVE, Unity (desktop), Unreal, C++ and Odin read `RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST_TOKEN` and `RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST_RUN_ID`; iOS reads them from the launch environment; Android reads the intent extras `ravensight_playtest_token` and `ravensight_playtest_run_id`; the JavaScript SDK reads the page global `__RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST__`. The table below has the other sources each one accepts.

documents.title: The Ravensight Swift package for iOS, tvOS and macOS
documents.content:
8. iOS SDK reference

 

## The Ravensight Swift package for iOS, tvOS and macOS

 

One Swift package for iOS 15 or newer, tvOS 15 or newer and macOS 12 or newer, with no third party dependencies and a URLSession transport. It owns the device id, sessions, batching, the offline queue, rate limit handling and the server kill switch, and it sends player feedback and Player Reports with a screenshot.

 

Verified so far: the package's tests on macOS, on the iOS Simulator and on a tvOS simulator. On tvOS the saved queue and pending crash records live in Caches, the only folder a tvOS app may keep files in, so the system can purge them under storage pressure. It has not yet run inside a shipping app or on a physical device, so read the code before a release build. The source and the full README are at [ravensight-ios](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-ios). Code samples scroll horizontally when needed.

documents.section_title: The Ravensight Swift package for iOS, tvOS and macOS
documents.title: Install
documents.content:
### Install

 

Swift Package Manager only. In Xcode choose File > Add Package Dependencies, paste the repository URL and add the `Ravensight` library to your app target. Or declare it in `Package.swift`:

 

```
dependencies: [
    .package(
        url: "https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-ios.git",
        from: "0.6.0"
    ),
],
targets: [
    .target(name: "YourGame", dependencies: ["Ravensight"]),
]
```

documents.section_title: The Ravensight Swift package for iOS, tvOS and macOS
documents.title: Initialise
documents.content:
### Initialise

 

Call `start` once, early, from the main thread (your `App` init or `application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)`), with your game's ingest key from the dashboard. It queues `game_started`, reads the kill switch, opens a session, sends batches every 5 seconds and hooks the app lifecycle so the queue is flushed when the player leaves. The key ships inside your app, so it is not a secret: anyone with the app can read it, though it can only write events. For a demo or an open-source app use a public key (`gt_pub_`) with an event allowlist and a ceiling, and keep live keys on your own server when possible. See [Public builds](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/).

 

```
import Ravensight

Ravensight.start(ingestKey: "gt_live_your_key")

Ravensight.track("level_completed", data: ["level": 3, "deaths": 2])

// Or the full configuration:
var configuration = RavensightConfiguration(ingestKey: "gt_live_your_key")
configuration.gameVersion = "1.2.0"
configuration.persistQueue = true      // the default; false keeps the queue in memory
Ravensight.start(configuration)
```

 

On iOS a session ends by time in the background: a player who comes back within `sessionTimeout` (30 minutes by default) carries on the same session, and one who comes back later, or after the app was swiped away, gets the old session's `game_exited` stamped with the time they left, then a new session.

documents.section_title: The Ravensight Swift package for iOS, tvOS and macOS
documents.title: Xcode configuration
documents.content:
### Xcode configuration

 

Keep the ingest key out of source and give each build configuration its own: an ignored `.xcconfig` with per-configuration keys, an explicit `Info.plist` template that substitutes `$(RAVENSIGHT_INGEST_KEY)`, suppression under XCTest and SwiftUI previews so tests and canvases send nothing, and a check of the built bundle before you ship. The steps are in the SDK repo's [`docs/XCODE_SETUP.md`](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-ios/blob/main/docs/XCODE_SETUP.md). To confirm which environment a build's key reaches, see [Which environment does this key hit?](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/quickstart/#which-environment)

documents.section_title: The Ravensight Swift package for iOS, tvOS and macOS
documents.title: Timing and privacy
documents.content:
### Timing and privacy

 

The SDK stamps events with wall clock time. If your app reads `systemUptime` (or another boot-relative clock) for its own timing, Apple treats that as a required-reason API, so your app needs its own privacy manifest declaration for it. Send elapsed in-app intervals, such as seconds spent in a level, as event data, and never raw uptime, which can be used to tell devices apart.

documents.title: Playtest tagging, and why a synthetic id is never mirrored
documents.content:
### Playtest tagging, and why a synthetic id is never mirrored

 

A Ravensight Playtest run identifies itself with a token and a run id, from `RavensightConfiguration.playtestToken` and `playtestRunId`, or else from the `RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST_TOKEN` and `RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST_RUN_ID` launch environment variables (on the Simulator, `xcrun simctl launch` passes a variable through when you prefix it with `SIMCTL_CHILD_`). With a token, every request carries the `X-Ravensight-Playtest` header and the run sends the device id `pt-<runId>`, held in memory only and exposed as `playtestDeviceId`. The persisted queue is not used. A token without a run id never runs as a real player: nothing is sent.

 

`Ravensight.deviceId` always returns the durable id, never the synthetic one, and `resetDeviceId()` never returns a synthetic id either, so an app that copies the id into its own storage or its own server is safe. Never copy `playtestDeviceId` anywhere that outlives the run. A mirrored `pt-` id would come back on a later launch: a real player's events would then be filed under a persona's run and left out of every report that hides playtest sessions, and your own records would count a persona as a player. `Ravensight.isSynthetic` tells you which kind of run this is. Leave the token and run id unset in a build for real players.

documents.section_title: The Ravensight Swift package for iOS, tvOS and macOS
documents.title: The persisted queue
documents.content:
### The persisted queue

 

By default (`persistQueue`; set it to `false` to keep the queue in memory only) the queue is mirrored to one JSON file under Application Support, excluded from backups: at most the newest 500 events, written atomically through one temporary file, coalesced over a quarter of a second, and read right after the client is created. Restored events go out under the current session, each with the `origin` of the session it was tracked in and its original timestamp, and events older than 89 days are not restored. Session tokens, signing secrets and an error's `rs_trail` are never written. The file is deleted on an opt-out, on `stopAllTelemetry`, on `resetDeviceId`, on the kill switch and when the queue drains, and a playtest run never reads or writes it. It narrows the window in which events can be lost; an event tracked a moment before a crash may not have been written yet.

 

From 0.6.0 timestamps are unix milliseconds, a request body of 1,024 bytes or more is sent gzip compressed, a session that answers with `signing` signs every batch with an HMAC-SHA256 whose secret stays in memory, and `trackAd`, `trackAdRevenue` and `setAttribution` send the [ad and attribution events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events). `sendDeviceInfo` (on by default) sends the model and OS version on the session.

documents.content:
### What each SDK supports

 

Read from each SDK's own source. A cell that says not in this SDK is a feature that SDK does not have. No SDK has a journeys call: journeys are built by the server from the place on the level events you track, with any SDK, on deployments with journey graphs configured.

| JavaScript | `submitFeedback` | `submitReport`, from 0.5.1, with `captureScreenshot` for a canvas | Yes | `setEnabled(false)`, not saved by the SDK | `persistQueue`, on by default, from 0.7.0 | Not in this SDK |
| Godot | `submit_feedback` | `submit_report` and an optional capture overlay, from 0.3.1 | Yes | `set_tracking_enabled(false)`, saved | Always on, from 0.5.0 | Not in this SDK |
| LÖVE | `submitFeedback` | `submitReport` with PNG bytes, from 0.5.0 | Yes | `setTrackingEnabled(false)`, saved | Always on, desktop, written on every change from 0.7.0 | Not in this SDK |
| Unity | `SubmitFeedback` | `SubmitReport`, from 0.3.1 | Yes | `SetTrackingEnabled(false)`, saved | Persist Queue, on by default, from 0.5.0 | Not in this SDK |
| Unreal | `SubmitFeedback` | `PrepareReport` and `SubmitReport`, from 0.3.1 | Yes | `SetTrackingEnabled(false)`, saved | Always on, from 0.5.0 | Not in this SDK |
| C++ | `submit_feedback` | `submit_report`, from 0.3.1 | Yes | `set_tracking_enabled(false)`, saved | `persist_queue`, on by default, from 0.5.0 | Not in this SDK |
| Odin | `submit_feedback` | `submit_report` with PNG bytes, from 0.4.0 | Yes | `set_tracking_enabled(client, false)`, saved | Always on, from 0.6.0 | Not in this SDK |
| iOS | `submitFeedback` | `submitReport`, from 0.3.0 | Yes | `setTrackingEnabled(false)`, saved, plus `stopAllTelemetry()` | `persistQueue`, on by default from 0.6.0 | Not in this SDK |
| Android | `submitFeedback` | `submitReport`, from 0.3.1 | Yes | `setTrackingEnabled(context, false)`, saved | `persistQueue`, on by default, from 0.5.0 | Not in this SDK |

 

Where each SDK finds a playtest run is in the [SDK comparison table](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/love-sdk/#sdk-compare).

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.content:
9. HTTP API

 

## Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot

 

Building for the web or Node? The [JavaScript SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/javascript-sdk/) wraps everything below in a zero-dependency client with batching, an offline queue, and tab-close flushing. Unity developers use the [Unity SDK](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-unity), and LÖVE games use the [LÖVE SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/love-sdk/). Everything else speaks plain HTTP.

 

Sending from your own backend into your website analytics, such as an account created or a payment confirmed? That is not game ingestion: use [server events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/server-events/), with the website's secret server key.

 

The Godot SDK is a client for this same surface. If you're on Unity, Unreal, a browser game, or anything else, this is what to call directly. The ingest endpoints answer any web origin, so browser games on GitHub Pages, itch.io or your own site need no CORS setup.

 

Base URL

 

```
https://api.ravensight.io
```

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: POST /api/v1/session
documents.content:
### POST /api/v1/session

 

Opens a session for a device. Auth: `X-API-Key` (your ingest key). The game identity comes from the key, never from the body.

 

Request

 

```
POST /api/v1/session
X-API-Key: gt_live_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "deviceId": "3f9ac2e17b5d4c0e8a61f2b9d7c04e5a-windows",
  "gameVersion": "1.4.2",
  "platform": "Windows"
}
```

 

Response, 201

 

```
{
  "token": "st_9f2c...redacted",
  "expiresAt": "2026-08-29T16:00:00.000Z",
  "expiresIn": 86400
}
```

 

Errors: `400 missing_device_id` when `deviceId` is absent, `401 invalid_api_key` or `missing_api_key`, `403 tracking_disabled` when the game's kill switch is off, `429 rate_limited` at more than 60 session creations per minute for the game.

 

A live key is never refused over what a device sends here, because an SDK would resend the same request for ever. A `platform` or `gameVersion` loses any control characters (line breaks, tabs, escape codes) and is then cut to 128 characters, one that is neither text nor a number is left out, and a `deviceId` past 256 characters is stored as a short id derived from it by hash, so the same device stays one device.

 

**Distribution.** The body may carry an optional `distribution`, a string of at most 40 characters naming where the build was distributed, such as `native-release` or `web-itch`, with no control characters. It is stored on the session as the client declared it and added to each of the session's events as a `distribution` property unless the event sends its own (`400 invalid_distribution` for anything that is not such a string).

 

**With a [public key](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/)**, `/session` can also answer `403 key_expired`, `403 key_paused`, `403 origin_not_allowed` when the key enforces its origin list, `403 origin_required` when it also requires one and the request sends no `Origin`, `403 version_not_allowed` when `gameVersion` is missing or not on the key's version list, `403 public_key_forbidden` for a doctor session or a playtest run, which need the game's live key, `400 invalid_device_id` for a device id that is not text or over 256 characters, `400 invalid_platform` or `invalid_game_version` for one past 128 characters, not text, or holding a control character such as a line break or tab, and `429 rate_limited` from the key's own session limits. The session token lives the key's `session_ttl_seconds`, or until the key's expiry date if that comes first.

 

**Joining a session.** Send `joinToken`, the token of a live session from the same game, instead of a `deviceId`, and the new session shares that session's analytics session id and device id. Use it when a second client of the same player, such as your game server, should report into the player's session. The new session keeps its own `platform` and `gameVersion` and never outlives the one it joined. The answer carries the same `token`, `expiresAt` and `expiresIn` plus `joined: true` and `synthetic`, which the server decides from the session that was joined, so your game server can rely on it instead of a flag the browser sends. A fresh session's answer carries neither field. A `deviceId` in the same body never becomes the new session's device id. A join from a synthetic (playtest) session stays synthetic: the new session belongs to the same run, its events are marked synthetic and are never metered, and feedback sent through it is marked synthetic too. It keeps the playtest's own platform whatever the body says, and once the run or its job has finished, its events and feedback answer `403 playtest_job_closed`. When a join from a synthetic session also sends the player's own `deviceId`, that device's real sessions in the same game from the last 15 minutes join the run too, their events are marked synthetic, and the answer adds `adopted` with how many. Events they sent before the join were already counted on the event meter and are not refunded, so have your game server open its session with the browser's session token as `joinToken` before it tracks the sign-up, and nothing is tracked as real first.

 

```
{
  "joinToken": "st_9f2c...redacted",
  "gameVersion": "1.4.2",
  "platform": "dedicated-server"
}
```

 

A join from a playtest session that adopted one earlier session answers:

 

```
{
  "token": "st_41ab...redacted",
  "expiresAt": "2026-10-15T19:30:00.000Z",
  "expiresIn": 3600,
  "joined": true,
  "synthetic": true,
  "adopted": 1
}
```

 

A token that is unknown, expired, revoked, from another game, or from a doctor session answers `401 invalid_join_token`, the same answer for each, so a token's existence never leaks; so does a join sent with `"platform": "doctor"` or a playtest header. A `platform` or `gameVersion` that is not a string or number answers `400 invalid_platform` or `invalid_game_version` on a public key join; a live key joins, stores a number as text and leaves anything else out. Joins count toward the same 60 a minute.

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: GET /api/v1/settings
documents.content:
### GET /api/v1/settings

 

Reads the tracking kill switch, and names the game the key belongs to, so a client or the doctor can confirm it ships the key for the game and environment it meant. Auth: `X-API-Key`.

 

Response, 200

 

```
{
  "trackingEnabled": true,
  "game": { "slug": "nebula-drifter", "name": "Nebula Drifter", "environment": "production" },
  "key": { "kind": "live", "label": null }
}
```

 

`slug` is the key's own game id, never another game's, and the answer never includes the key or its hash. `key` says which kind of key answered: `live` for the game's `gt_live_` key, or `public` with the label you gave a [public key](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/).

 

An address on the game's block list gets `403 ip_blocked`, and more than 30 reads a minute from one address on one key get `429 rate_limited` with a `Retry-After` header.

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: POST /api/v1/track
documents.content:
### POST /api/v1/track

 

Sends a single event. Auth: `X-Session-Token` (from step above).

 

Request

 

```
POST /api/v1/track
X-Session-Token: st_9f2c...redacted
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "event": "level_completed",
  "data": { "level": 3, "score": 15000, "time_seconds": 87.4 },
  "timestamp": <unix milliseconds, within the last 90 days>
}
```

 

Response, 202

 

```
{ "accepted": 1 }
```

 

`timestamp` is optional and defaults to the time the server receives the event. Send unix milliseconds, so that events in one second keep their order in funnels and sessions. A value below 100,000,000,000 is read as unix seconds and stored on the whole second, so a client that sends seconds keeps working exactly as it did, and funnels read its events in one second by step. A timestamp in the future is stored as now. For timestamps in milliseconds, a clock up to a minute ahead moves its whole batch back by that much instead, so the batch keeps its order. An event whose timestamp is more than 90 days old is dropped: it is not stored and not charged, and it is counted as `timestamp_too_old` on the Implementation health card. The request still succeeds, so `accepted` can be lower than the number of events you sent, on this endpoint and on `/track/batch`.

 

A [typed event](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events) that breaks its contract is stored with `rs_invalid` rather than refused, and the 202 body adds `"invalid": n` only when there was one. A purchase of 4.99 US dollars, in minor units:

 

```
{
  "event": "gem_pack_bought",
  "data": {
    "rs_kind": "purchase",
    "rs_amount": 499,
    "rs_currency": "USD",
    "rs_item_type": "gems",
    "rs_item_id": "gem_pack_small"
  }
}
```

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: POST /api/v1/track/batch
documents.content:
### POST /api/v1/track/batch

 

Sends up to 50 events in one call. Same auth as `/track`.

 

Request

 

```
POST /api/v1/track/batch
X-Session-Token: st_9f2c...redacted
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "events": [
    { "event": "level_started", "data": { "level": 3 } },
    { "event": "checkpoint_reached", "data": { "idx": 2 } }
  ]
}
```

 

Response, 202

 

```
{ "accepted": 2, "duplicates": 0 }
```

 

`duplicates` counts events skipped because their `rs_event_id` was already stored for that device on this game within the key's dedupe window (at least 24 hours by default); they are not stored twice and not charged (see [duplicates and retries](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/#public-timestamps-retries)). A public key always answers both fields. The live key adds `duplicates` only when an event in the request carried an `rs_event_id`; otherwise its answer is `{ "accepted": 2 }`.

 

Errors: `400 invalid_batch` when `events` is missing or empty, `400 batch_too_large` above 50 events or past the 512 KB body limit, so an SDK splits the batch and sends again, `400 missing_event` if any entry lacks an `event` name.

 

**With a [public key](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/)**, the key's policy adds these `400` answers, each naming the `index` of the first event that broke it (0 on `/track`): `missing_event`, `event_not_allowed` (the name is not on the allowlist), `event_too_large` (above `max_event_bytes`), `invalid_event_data`, `too_many_properties`, `payload_too_deep`, `string_too_long`, `invalid_number` (a number that is not finite), `reserved_key` (an `rs_` key Ravensight does not read, or an `rs_kind` outside its values) and `invalid_event_id`. `batch_too_large` (above `max_batch`) refuses the whole batch and has no index. A session whose key was paused, revoked or expired answers `401 public_key_inactive`: open a new session. It can also answer `429 public_key_ceiling` when the batch would take the key past its optional monthly ceiling; the whole batch is refused and `Retry-After` runs to the start of the next UTC month. On any key, `429 quota_exceeded` with `reason: "needs_funds"` means the included allowance is used and the prepaid balance cannot buy the next block of events. Add funds to keep accepting events. None of these refusals is charged.

 

Keys that start with `rs_` in event data are reserved. An `rs_kind` that is not one of the nine kinds, `level_start`, `level_complete`, `death`, `none`, `purchase`, `resource`, `progression`, `error` or `health`, and any other `rs_` key Ravensight does not read, is stored as sent and counted as `rs_kind_unknown` or `rs_key_unknown` on the Implementation health card. One is the server's own: `rs_link`, the [campaign link](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/campaign-links/#campaign-links-players) a session arrived by. Send it as `campaignLink` on `POST /session`, never in event data: one in event data is replaced by the session's, or dropped.

 

**What the dashboard reads from your events.** `level`, `location` and `track` in `data` fold into one place, and the first non-empty one wins. The level funnel counts three kinds at a place: `level_start`, `level_complete` and `death`. Set `rs_kind` to say which one an event is; without it the kind is read from the event name. An event with a place and none of those kinds is shown as navigation only, stays out of the funnel, and is counted as `place_without_kind` on the Implementation health card. Send `rs_kind: "none"` when the place is intentional. The full rules are in [how the built-in detections read your events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#detection-rules).

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: GET /api/v1/agent/suggestions
documents.content:
### GET /api/v1/agent/suggestions

 

Experimental, machine-readable design suggestions from your weekly digest. Auth: `X-API-Key`. Returns an empty array until a digest has run for your game.

 

```
{ "suggestions": [] }
```

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: GET /api/v1/doctor/ping/:nonce
documents.content:
### GET /api/v1/doctor/ping/:nonce

 

The read-back for [the doctor's live check](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/doctor/). Auth: `X-API-Key`. A session opened with `"platform": "doctor"` lives ten minutes, gets a device id the server chooses, and may send only `ravensight_doctor_ping`, ten a minute per game (`400 doctor_event_only` for any other name, and for feedback and player reports). Its events are kept out of your analytics and your event usage. This endpoint answers whether the ping whose `rs_doctor` value is `:nonce`, 32 lowercase hex characters, was stored for the key's game in the last 15 minutes.

 

Response, 200

 

```
{ "found": true, "acceptedAt": "2026-10-10T12:00:01.250Z" }
```

 

`404 {"found": false, "error": "ping_not_found"}` until the event is stored, which can take a few seconds while it is batched. `400 invalid_nonce` for a malformed nonce, `429 rate_limited` above 30 reads a minute for the game, `503 storage_unavailable` when event storage is down. A nonce sent by another game reads as not found.

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: POST /api/v1/feedback
documents.content:
### POST /api/v1/feedback

 

Auth: `X-Session-Token`.

 

Request

 

```
POST /api/v1/feedback
X-Session-Token: st_9f2c...redacted
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "message": "Level 3's second checkpoint feels unfair.",
  "category": "suggestion",
  "rating": 4
}
```

 

Response, 201

 

```
{ "id": "66c1f2a9d4e8b0021f9a7c31" }
```

 

`category` and `rating` are both optional. When present, `category` must be one of `bug`, `suggestion`, `complaint`, `praise`, `playtest`, or `other`.

documents.section_title: Ingestion for anything that isn't Godot
documents.title: Errors
documents.content:
### Errors

 

| Status | Error | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | `missing_device_id`, `missing_event`, `invalid_batch`, `batch_too_large`, `event_name_too_long`, `event_too_large`, `invalid_event_data`, `missing_message`, `message_too_long`, `invalid_category`, `invalid_feedback`, `doctor_event_only`, `invalid_nonce`, `invalid_distribution` | Malformed request body or a payload ceiling (see Limits). |
| 400 | `missing_event`, `event_not_allowed`, `batch_too_large`, `event_too_large`, `invalid_event_data`, `too_many_properties`, `payload_too_deep`, `string_too_long`, `invalid_number`, `reserved_key`, `invalid_event_id` | A public key's policy refused an event. The answer carries the `index` of the first offending event (none for `batch_too_large`, which refuses the whole batch). Drop that event and never retry it. |
| 400 | `invalid_device_id`, `invalid_platform`, `invalid_game_version` | On a public key's `/session`: a device id that is not text or over 256 characters, or a platform or game version over 128 characters, not text, or holding a control character. A live key stores bounded values instead of refusing. |
| 401 | `missing_api_key`, `invalid_api_key`, `invalid_join_token`, or a missing/expired session token | Bad or absent credentials for the header the endpoint expects, or a `joinToken` that cannot be joined. |
| 404 | `ping_not_found` | The doctor's ping is not stored yet, or was never sent for this game. Only returned by `GET /api/v1/doctor/ping/:nonce`. |
| 403 | `tracking_disabled` | The game's server-side kill switch is off. Only returned by `POST /api/v1/session`. |
| 401 | `public_key_inactive` | The public key that opened this session is paused, revoked or expired. Open a new session, which answers the key's real state. |
| 403 | `key_expired`, `key_paused`, `origin_not_allowed`, `origin_required`, `version_not_allowed`, `public_key_forbidden` | A public key is expired or paused, its policy refused the origin, a missing origin or the version, or it called an endpoint public keys cannot use. Stop for this run. |
| 429 | `rate_limited` | Per-game ceiling hit: 60 session creations or 600 tracked events per minute, or one of a public key's own limits per key, session or device id. Carries a `Retry-After` header in seconds. |
| 429 | `quota_exceeded` | Monthly event quota reached for this account. Carries a `Retry-After` header, in seconds until the quota resets at the next UTC month. With `reason: "needs_funds"`, the prepaid balance cannot buy the next block of events: add funds to keep accepting events. |
| 429 | `public_key_ceiling` | A public key reached the optional monthly ceiling its owner set. Carries a `Retry-After` header to the next UTC month. Nothing in the refused batch was stored or charged. |
| 503 | `storage_unavailable` | Event storage is temporarily unavailable. Carries `Retry-After: 60`; nothing was accepted or charged against quota. |

documents.section_title: Send events from your own servers
documents.title: Send events from your own servers
documents.content:
Server events

 

## Send events from your own servers

 

Server events let your own backend send events, such as an account created, a payment confirmed or a nightly job finished, into the analytics of one of your websites: a title's Game website or your company website. Your server sends them over HTTPS with the website's secret server key, and they have their own Server events report, kept apart from what visitors do in the browser.

documents.section_title: Send events from your own servers
documents.title: When to use server events
documents.content:
### When to use server events

 

Send each event from the place that knows first that it happened.

 

| What happened | Send it with |
| --- | --- |
| A visitor opened a page or clicked on your website | The [website snippet](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/websites/#websites-setup) in the browser, with the website's public key |
| Your server did something: created an account, confirmed a payment, received a webhook, finished a scheduled job | Server events, with the website's secret server key |
| A player did something in your game | The [SDK for your engine](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/platform-support/) or the [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/http-api/), with the game's ingest key |

 

Server events belong to a website, not to a game. They need no game, environment or session, and they never appear in a game's reports. When the event is about a player in your game, such as a purchase your game server confirms, send it to the game instead: your game server can [join the player's session](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/http-api/#post-api-v1-session) and track the event there.

 

Server events show only in their own report. They never change any other website report, so visitors, page views, events, goals and funnels stay what the browser saw (see [where the events show](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/server-events/#server-events-reports)).

documents.section_title: Send events from your own servers
documents.title: Create the server key
documents.content:
### Create the server key

 

Each website has at most one server key. Owners, admins and members, the roles that can configure a website, can create, replace and revoke it.

 

1. Open the website's setup. For your company, open website setup from the Company website card on Company home. For a title, select its project and open Live data > Game website, then Setup. Collect website activity must be on: while it is off, the key is refused.
 
1. In the Server key card, choose Create server key. The key starts with `gt_srv_`.
 
1. Copy it straight into your server's secret settings, for example an environment variable named `RAVENSIGHT_SERVER_KEY`. The key is shown this once. Ravensight stores only a one-way hash of it and cannot show it again.

 

Afterwards the card shows the key's first characters, when it was created and when your backend last used it. Replace key makes a new key, shown once, and the old key stops working at that moment, so update your server straight away. Revoke removes the key, and requests that carry it are refused from then on. Removing the website removes its key.

 

Server events do not mark the website as installed. Verify installation still waits for the browser snippet; the key's last use is what shows your backend is sending.

 

**Keep the key on your server.** Anyone who holds it can add events to your website, and those events count toward your studio's usage. Never put it in a web page, a game build, a mobile app or a repository; the website snippet's public key is the one made for browsers. A request that carries an `Origin` header, as every browser request does, is refused with `403 server_only`, so a server key never works from a web page. No MCP tool or agent token can read or change it.

documents.section_title: Send events from your own servers
documents.title: Send a request
documents.content:
### Send a request

 

Request

 

```
POST https://api.ravensight.io/api/v1/site/server-events
Authorization: Bearer gt_srv_...
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "events": [
    {
      "eventId": "7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7",
      "name": "account_created",
      "timestamp": 1795076742620,
      "actorId": "account-48213",
      "properties": { "plan": "free", "method": "password" }
    }
  ]
}
```

 

One request carries 1 to 50 events. The JSON body may be at most 512 KB, counted after any gzip is undone, and you may send it compressed with `Content-Encoding: gzip`. Send no cookie and no `Origin` header. The body holds only `events`, and each event only the five fields below. It never names a website, studio or game: the key alone decides which website the events join and which studio's usage they count toward.

 

| Field | Rules |
| --- | --- |
| `eventId` | Required. 8 to 128 letters, digits, `_`, `.`, `:` or `-`. Make a new one when the event happens, such as a random UUID, and keep it for every retry (see [retries and duplicates](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/server-events/#server-events-retries)). |
| `name` | Required. A letter, then up to 79 letters, digits, `_`, `.` or `-`, such as `account_created`. |
| `timestamp` | Required. When it happened, as a whole number of Unix milliseconds. At most 5 minutes ahead and 90 days back. |
| `actorId` | Optional. Your own opaque id for the person or device the event is about, 8 to 128 letters, digits, `_`, `.`, `:` or `-`. Never an email address. Leave it out for an event about your backend itself. |
| `properties` | Optional. Up to 24 flat keys and values (see [actors and properties](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/server-events/#server-events-actors)). |

 

The whole batch is checked before anything is stored or charged. One event that breaks a rule refuses the request with a `400`, and nothing in it is recorded.

 

**Limits.** 600 requests a minute for each key, and 6,000 events a minute for one website. Past either, the answer is `429 rate_limited` with a `Retry-After` header.

documents.section_title: Send events from your own servers
documents.title: Actors and properties
documents.content:
### Actors and properties

 

`actorId` says who or what the event is about: the id your own database already uses for an account, a player or a device. It must be opaque. An email address, a name or a phone number is never an actor id, and the allowed characters leave no room for an email address. A short number needs a prefix to reach 8 characters, such as `account-42`.

 

Ravensight never stores the id you send. It stores a keyed one-way hash of it, made separately for each website, so the same id sent to two websites counts as two different actors, and your id cannot be read back. The report counts how many different actors sent each event. Events sent without an `actorId` belong to your backend itself and are never counted as an actor.

 

Properties follow these rules:

 

- At most 24 keys. A key is a letter, then up to 63 letters, digits or underscores.
 
- Some keys are reserved, in any letter case: keys that start with `rs_`, `history_` or `ravensight_`, and the keys `context`, `identity_kind`, `session_provenance` and `profile_provenance`.
 
- A value is a string of at most 200 characters, a finite number, `true`, `false` or `null`. No lists and no nested objects.
 
- All of an event's properties together are at most 4 KB as JSON.
 
- A string that looks like a person or a credential is refused: one that holds an `@`, a label such as `password=`, `token:` or `Bearer` followed by a space, a signed web token, a Ravensight key, or 80 or more letters and digits in a row.

 

A property that breaks a rule is answered with `400 invalid_properties`. Keep identifiers in `actorId`, never in properties.

documents.section_title: Send events from your own servers
documents.title: Answers and errors
documents.content:
### Answers and errors

 

Response, 200

 

```
{
  "accepted": 2,
  "duplicates": 1,
  "conflicts": 0,
  "refused": 0,
  "acceptedIds": ["7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7", "...", "..."],
  "conflictIds": [],
  "refusedIds": [],
  "paused": false
}
```

 

Every event in the request is counted once:

 

- `accepted`: stored now.
 
- `duplicates`: already stored with the same `eventId` and content, so not stored or charged again. `acceptedIds` lists both of these.
 
- `conflicts`: an `eventId` already stored with different content. Only those events are refused, listed in `conflictIds`; the rest of the batch is stored.
 
- `refused`: stopped by a pause, listed in `refusedIds`. Collection pauses when your studio's included events are used up and the prepaid balance cannot cover more. The answer then has `"paused": true` and a `reason`, `needs_funds`. Add funds, then send the refused events again with the same ids.

 

When a pause means nothing in the request was accepted, the status is `429` with `"error": "collection_paused"` and the same fields. Any other error answer names its code in `error`.

 

| Answer | Meaning, and what to do |
| --- | --- |
| `400 invalid_events` | The body is not JSON, holds a field it should not, or is not a list of 1 to 50 events; or an event has a field missing, of the wrong type or outside its rules. Nothing was stored. Fix the request: sent again unchanged, it fails the same way. |
| `400 invalid_timestamp` | A timestamp is more than 5 minutes ahead or more than 90 days back. Nothing was stored. Check your server's clock, and drop events older than 90 days. |
| `400 before_cutover` | A timestamp is earlier than this website's cutover, the point set when its earlier history was imported. Nothing was stored. Send only events from after the cutover. |
| `400 invalid_properties` | A property breaks the rules above. Nothing was stored. Fix or remove the property. |
| `401 missing_server_key` | No `Authorization` header. Send the key. |
| `401 invalid_server_key` | The key is unknown, was replaced or revoked, or its website is removed or has Collect website activity off. Use the website's current key, and check that collection is on. |
| `403 server_only` | The request carried an `Origin` header, as every browser request does. Send from your server only. |
| `404 not_found` | Website analytics is not available. Nothing was stored. |
| `409 site_changed` | The website, its settings or its key changed while the request was handled, or too many of its events are waiting to be stored. Send the same request again shortly with the current key: events already accepted come back as duplicates. |
| `413 payload_too_large` | The body is over 512 KB after gzip is undone. Send fewer events in each request. |
| `429 rate_limited` | Over 600 requests a minute with one key, or 6,000 events a minute for one website. Wait the seconds in `Retry-After`, then send the same request again. |
| `429 collection_paused` | Nothing was accepted: the included events are used up and the balance cannot cover more. Add funds, then send the refused events again. |
| `5xx`, a timeout or no answer | The request may or may not have been stored. Send the same request again, waiting longer each time. |

documents.section_title: Send events from your own servers
documents.title: Retries and duplicates
documents.content:
### Retries and duplicates

 

`eventId` makes a request safe to send again. Ravensight stores an event once for each website and id: the same id with the same content is answered as a duplicate, stored once and charged once. The same id with different content is counted in `conflicts` and not stored. So give each event its own id when it happens, keep the id and everything else about the event for every retry, and set the timestamp when the event happens, never when you send it.

 

Retry when there was no answer (a network error or a timeout), a `5xx`, a `429 rate_limited` or a `409 site_changed`: wait, send the same events again, and wait longer each time. Never retry any other `4xx` unchanged, because it fails the same way again. After a timeout, resend the whole batch: the events that did get stored come back as duplicates, and they are free. Events refused by a pause can wait and be sent again once you add funds.

 

An id from your own records works too, as long as it names one event, such as `payment-8812-confirmed`. That lets an event that must never be lost, such as a payment, be written to your own database with the payment and sent from there until it is accepted.

documents.section_title: Send events from your own servers
documents.title: Example for Node

documents.section_title: Send events from your own servers
documents.title: Usage and billing
documents.content:
### Usage and billing

 

Each accepted server event is one event on your studio's event meter, the same as a page view or custom event from the website snippet. It draws the 1,000,000 included events a month first, then your prepaid balance at the usual [events rate](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/limits/#rates). Server events have no price of their own. Duplicates, conflicts, refused requests and anything sent while collection is paused are free.

 

When the included events are used up and the balance cannot cover more, collection pauses before anything is stored: answers say `paused`, or `429 collection_paused`, until you add funds.

 

Each event is stored with its name, its time, its actor's hashed id and its properties. No IP address, user agent, page, referrer, campaign, country, device or browser is stored for a server event, and never the actor id you sent. Server events are kept for 90 days. Removing the website deletes them.

documents.section_title: Send events from your own servers
documents.title: Where the events show
documents.content:
### Where the events show

 

Server events have one report of their own, for up to 90 days at a time. It lists each event name with its count, how many different actors sent it, and when it was first and last seen. Choose an event for its daily counts and actors, and one of its properties for that property's 20 most frequent values. It holds totals only, never an actor id or a single event. Read it in two places:

 

- In the dashboard, the Server events tab of the website's analytics: Live data > Game website for a title, or View full website analytics on the Company website card for your company.
 
- Over MCP, [`get_server_events`](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/mcp/#get-server-events), with `site:read`, at the price of any MCP call.

 

Server events never appear in any other website report: visitors, page views, sessions, bounce rate, pages, sources, audience, Events, goals, funnels, retention, heatmaps or realtime, in the dashboard or over MCP. So a goal or a funnel cannot use a server event, and your traffic numbers stay what your visitors did. There is no link between a website visitor and an account on your server.

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.content:
2. Public builds

 

## Public builds and open-source games

 

A free demo, a web build anyone can open, or a game whose source is public all ship the key in a place anyone can read. A public key (`gt_pub_`) is made for that case: it can only send the events you list, at the rates you set, into one environment, and you can pause or revoke it without shipping a new build.

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: The trust model
documents.content:
### The trust model

 

- **A shipped identifier is public.** Anything inside a build, a page or a download can be read by whoever has it. A Ravensight ingest key is a key to write events, never to read them: no ingest key can read your analytics, your settings beyond its own game's tracking switch, name and environment, or your account.
 
- **A key injected at build time is not a secret.** Injecting it from CI keeps it out of your repository, which is what stops a fork from reporting into your account. It does not hide it from anyone who downloads the build.
 
- **CORS is not a gate.** The ingest endpoints answer every web origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. That is what lets a browser game on any host send events; it decides nothing about who may send them.
 
- **No token proves where an event came from.** Nothing a client sends can prove which build, which site or which fork sent it. What bounds someone who copies your key is the event allowlist and the rest of the key's policy, the rate limits, the optional ceiling and your ability to pause or revoke it.

 

| Control | What it stops | What it does not stop |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Event allowlist | Every event name you did not list. An empty list refuses every event. | Fake events that use a listed name with plausible values. |
| Payload rules | Large, deep, wide or malformed payloads, and reserved `rs_` keys Ravensight does not read. | Small, well formed payloads with invented values. |
| Rate limits | A flood from one key, one session or one device id. | A slow, patient sender who stays under every limit, or one that makes many device ids. The per-device limits apply only when the client sends a device id. |
| Monthly ceiling (optional) | Accepted events on that key past the number you set, for the rest of the month. | Spending on your other games, keys, MCP calls or AI work. It is not a cap on your bill. |
| Origin hint | With enforcement on, a browser page on a site you did not list. Browsers set `Origin` and a page cannot change it. | A native build, a script or a bot, which can send any `Origin` header or none. |
| Version list | Sessions that declare a game version you did not list, or none. | A client that declares a listed version string. The version is whatever the client says. |
| Pause and revoke | Every new session and every event on the key, at once, including the key's live sessions. | Nothing on another key or on your live key. |

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: The public key
documents.content:
### The public key

 

Create one in **Settings > Projects**, on the game card for the environment it should report into, beside the detection settings. A demo usually gets its own environment, so its traffic never mixes with a released game's. The full key is shown once; after that the dashboard shows its prefix and your label. A game can have at most two live public keys; a paused key still holds its place, and a revoked or expired one gives it back.

 

A public key can call:

 

- `POST /api/v1/session`, for an ordinary player session.
 
- `GET /api/v1/settings`, for its own game's tracking switch and name, with `key.kind` set to `public` and `key.label` to your label.
 
- With the session token it gets: `POST /api/v1/track` and `POST /api/v1/track/batch`; `POST /api/v1/feedback` only when the policy sets `allow_feedback`, and Player Reports only when it sets `allow_reports`.

 

It is refused everywhere else. The agent suggestions feed, the doctor's report and ping read-back, a doctor session (`"platform": "doctor"`), a playtest run and the legacy `/api/track` answer `403 public_key_forbidden`. Every dashboard, billing, organization and MCP path answers `401`, because an ingest key is not a credential there. Like every ingest key, it never reads another game's settings: the game comes from the key, never from the request.

 

The dashboard manages keys through the signed-in API, under `/api/v1/games/:gameId/public-keys`. `GET` lists every key of the game, revoked ones included, as `{ publicKeys, maxLive }`; each key carries its policy, this month's `accepted`, `ceiling`, `remaining` and what the ceiling's events would cost, and its `signals`. `POST` creates one and answers `201 { publicKey, key }`, the only time the full key is returned, or `409 public_key_limit` at two live keys. `PUT .../:keyId/policy` changes only the fields you send (`400 invalid_policy` names the field), and `POST .../:keyId/pause`, `.../unpause` and `.../revoke` answer `{ publicKey }`. `GET .../suggested-events` lists `game_started` and `game_exited`, which every SDK sends on its own, then the game's most frequent event names of the last 30 days, 50 names in all, which is what prefills a new key's allowlist. `GET .../suggested-policy` suggests a policy from the last 7 days of the game's real events and answers `{ policy, basis }`: `allowed_events` (the two SDK events, then the names it saw, most frequent first, at most 100), `max_properties` (the most seen plus 25 percent, at least the default), `max_event_bytes` (the 99th percentile times 1.5, rounded up to 256), `max_depth`, `max_string_length`, and the two per-minute rates (twice the busiest minute seen), each kept inside the allowed values, with the figures behind them in `basis`. It saves nothing, and a game with no recent events gets the defaults. Creating and revoking need the role that may rotate the game's key; editing, pausing and unpausing need the role that may change the game's settings.

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: The policy
documents.content:
### The policy

 

Each public key carries its own policy, stored on the key when it is created, so a later change to a default never changes a key that already shipped. The one exception is `capture_errors`, which arrived later and is on for every key unless you turn it off. Edit it on the key's card. The limits every key already has still apply on top of it, so a policy can only make a key stricter than a live key.

 

| Field | Default | What it does | Allowed values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `allowed_events` | empty | Event names the key may send. Empty refuses every event; the dashboard prefills the list from the game's recent names. | Up to 100 names. A name is any name live ingest accepts: 1 to 200 characters, no surrounding spaces, no control characters. Names starting `ravensight_` or `rs_` are reserved and refused. |
| `max_batch` | 20 | Events in one `/track/batch` call. | 1 to 50 |
| `max_event_bytes` | 2,048 | One event's data, serialized. | 256 to 8,192 |
| `max_properties` | 40 | Keys in one event's data, counted at every level. | 1 to 50 |
| `max_depth` | 2 | How deeply objects and lists may nest. Each object or list adds a level. | 1 to 4 |
| `max_string_length` | 256 | Characters in one string value or key. | 1 to 1,024 |
| Finite numbers | always | A number must be finite. | Always on |
| `max_past_seconds` | 2,592,000 (30 days) | How old an event's timestamp may be. A game that saves its queue offline sends late events, so keep this at days. A key created before November 2026 keeps the 86,400 it was created with until you change it. | 60 to 7,689,600 (89 days) |
| `sessions_per_minute` | 30 | New sessions on this key. | 1 to 60 |
| `events_per_minute` | 300 | Events on this key. | 1 to 600 |
| `events_per_session_per_minute` | 60 | Events from one session. | 1 to 600 |
| `events_per_device_per_minute` | 120 | Events from one device id, when the client sends one. | 1 to 600 |
| `sessions_per_device_per_hour` | 12 | New sessions for one device id, when the client sends one. | 1 to 120 |
| `session_ttl_seconds` | 3,600 | How long a session token from this key lives. A key with an expiry date never mints a session that outlives it: the session lives the shorter of the two. | 300 to 86,400 (24 hours) |
| `monthly_event_ceiling` | none | Optional and off by default. Accepted events on this key in a calendar month (UTC). The dashboard suggests 250,000 when you turn it on. | None, or 1,000 to 500,000,000 |
| `dedupe_window_seconds` | 86,400 (24 hours) | How long, at least, an `rs_event_id` is remembered. 0 turns it off. A key created before November 2026 keeps the 600 it was created with until you change it. | 0 to 604,800 (7 days) |
| `allowed_origins` | empty | Web origins you expect, such as `https://your-studio.example`. | Up to 20, each `scheme://host[:port]` in lower case with no path, at most 200 characters |
| `enforce_origin` | false | Off: an unlisted origin is counted and shown as a signal. On: a session from an unlisted origin is refused. | Needs at least one origin on the list |
| `require_origin` | false | On: a session with no `Origin` header is refused too. Native builds send none, so turn it on only for a key used by web builds alone. | Needs `enforce_origin` |
| `allowed_versions` | empty | Game versions a session may declare. Empty accepts any; once set, a session with no version is refused too. | Up to 50, each 1 to 64 characters |
| `allow_feedback` | false | Allow player feedback on this key. | true or false |
| `allow_reports` | false | Allow Player Reports on this key. | true or false |
| `capture_errors` | true | Error events (`rs_kind: "error"` with a severity of warning, error or critical, or none) pass the event allowlist under any name, and may carry a 200 character message, a 2,000 character stack and a 1,500 character log trail, even where the key's own limits are smaller. The event may grow past `max_event_bytes` by the size of its message, stack and trail only, up to 6,144 bytes. A session may send 10 a minute that need this room. The rest, and any error event larger than its room, are dropped, counted as `error_capture_limited`, and never stored or charged. A key with an empty event allowlist stays shut to error events too. On for keys created before this field existed. | true or false; false holds error events to the key's own limits |
| `require_steam_ticket` | false | Require Steam verification before opening a session. | true or false; needs a Steamworks connection and app id |
| `steam_app_id` | null | The Steam app whose tickets are accepted. | Positive decimal app id, or null when the requirement is off |

 

Numbers are whole numbers. A change outside these values, an unknown field or a wrong type answers `400 invalid_policy` with the `field` it refused. A batch that breaks a payload rule answers `400` with the error and the `index` of the first event that broke it, so every SDK's batch splitting isolates and drops that event and keeps the rest. A batch longer than `max_batch` is refused whole, with no index. The codes are in [the HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/http-api/).

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: Rate limits, in layers
documents.content:
### Rate limits, in layers

 

A request on a public key passes every layer, and the first one that is full answers `429 rate_limited` with a `Retry-After` header. The layers run narrowest first: on `/track` the session, then the device id, then the key, then the game; on `/session` the device id, then the key, then the game. A request one layer refuses has spent only the narrower layers, so one noisy session or device cannot use up the key's or the game's minute.

 

- **Per key:** `sessions_per_minute` and `events_per_minute`.
 
- **Per session:** `events_per_session_per_minute`.
 
- **Per device id:** `events_per_device_per_minute` and `sessions_per_device_per_hour`, only when the client sends a device id. The id is the client's own choice, so these bound a buggy or honest client; the key's limits and the ceiling bound one that invents ids. A public `/session` refuses a device id over 256 characters with `400 invalid_device_id`.
 
- **Per game:** 60 sessions and 600 events a minute, shared with every other key on the game.
 
- **Per IP address:** 100 requests a minute. Players who share one address, such as a LAN party, a school, a venue's network or a mobile carrier, share this budget, so a busy room can see `429` sooner than one player would.

 

A rate limited request counts once per window on the key's usage, not once per retry. Each limit is counted on the API server that answers the request; see [Usage, billing and limits](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/limits/).

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: Timestamps, duplicates and retries
documents.content:
### Timestamps, duplicates and retries

 

An event whose timestamp is older than `max_past_seconds` is dropped the way a live key drops one older than 90 days: it is not stored or charged, the call still answers `202`, and `accepted` is lower than the number you sent.

 

Give every event a unique `rs_event_id` string in its data and a resend is never stored twice. For at least `dedupe_window_seconds` (it can run a little longer, never shorter), an id the same device already sent on this game is skipped, even under a new session: it is not stored, not counted and not charged, and the answer counts it in `duplicates` instead of `accepted`. An id is 1 to 64 letters, digits, `_` or `-`; anything else answers `400 invalid_event_id`. The game's live key dedupes the same way, with a 24 hour window, for events that carry an id. A resend later than the window can be stored twice; the Data quality card counts those as the same event stored twice. A refused or failed request gives its ids back, so the resend is accepted. The public-build SDK releases add the id for you; see [SDK behavior](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/#public-sdk-behavior).

 

| Answer | What the client does |
| --- | --- |
| `202` | Done. Remove the events from the queue, including any counted as duplicates. |
| `400` | Drop the event at `index` and never retry it. Send the rest of the batch again. A `batch_too_large` answer has no index: split the batch. |
| `401` | Authenticate again: open a new session, then send. `public_key_inactive` means the key that opened the session was paused, revoked or expired, and the new session meets its real state. A `401` on `/session` itself means the key is unknown or revoked, so stop. |
| `403` | Stop for this run. The key is paused or expired, its policy refused this origin, a missing origin, this version or this endpoint, or tracking is off for the game. |
| `429` | Wait for `Retry-After`, then resend the same events with the same `rs_event_id` values. |
| `5xx` | Back off, then resend the same events with the same ids. |

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: Rotation, pause and revocation
documents.content:
### Rotation, pause and revocation

 

A game can have two live public keys, so you can rotate without a gap: create the second key, ship builds with it, and revoke the first once the old builds no longer matter. Public keys are revoke only: a revoked key never comes back, and revoking one ends its live sessions at once: their next request answers `401`. Rotating the game's live key leaves public keys and their sessions alone.

 

**Pause** is the reversible stop. A paused key answers `403 key_paused` on every new session and its live sessions end; unpause it and the same builds report again. A key can also carry an optional expiry date, after which it answers `403 key_expired`; no session it mints outlives that date. A change made in the dashboard can take up to a minute to reach every server. Above every key, the game's own kill switch still stops every session with `403 tracking_disabled`.

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: What it costs
documents.content:
### What it costs

 

- **Enabling it is free.** Creating, pausing and revoking keys costs nothing.
 
- **Accepted events are ordinary events.** They draw the account's included monthly allowance first. Past it, each started block of 100,000 events is bought from your prepaid balance at 5 cents. A block that is only partly used is still paid for.
 
- **An empty balance stops ingestion.** When the next block cannot be bought, the account's ingestion answers `429 quota_exceeded` with `reason: "needs_funds"` on every key, live and public, and nothing is charged for the refused events. The key's card and the Implementation card say "Add funds to keep accepting events."
 
- **The ceiling is optional, and off by default.** Without one, the card reads "No ceiling, buys blocks while funded". Turn it on and the dashboard suggests 250,000; the key then "stops accepting at this many events for the month even when funds remain", answering `429 public_key_ceiling`. A batch that would cross it is refused whole. The card prices it in the same blocks, for example "A ceiling of 250,000 events is 3 blocks of 100,000, $0.15 at the current block price, for this key's events past the included allowance." It limits one key; your other keys, your live key and MCP calls draw the same balance, so it is not a cap on your bill.
 
- **Refused traffic is free.** Rejected, invalid, duplicate, rate limited, over the ceiling and origin refused events are never charged.
 
- **Usage emails are information.** The game's owner gets one email at 80 percent of a key's ceiling and one at 100 percent, or when a batch would cross it. They do not stop anything themselves, and each lists every way a public key stops: its ceiling, an empty balance, a pause, a revoke, its expiry, and its rate limits for the moment they are exceeded.
 
- **The billing page shows the share.** It says how many of the month's player events came through public keys, and from how many keys. Those events are already inside the player events figure, never added on top.

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: Forks and source releases
documents.content:
### Forks and source releases

 

Never commit the key. Keep it in your CI's secret store and inject it when you build a release, so the repository, the source archive and a fork's builds have none. A fork's own CI has no access to your secrets, so its builds come out keyless, and a keyless build cannot open a session, so it sends nothing. The public-build SDK releases start inert without a key, so the game still runs. If a key does reach a public repository, pause it, create a second key, and revoke the first once your builds use the new one.

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: Through your own server
documents.content:
### Through your own server

 

If your game already has accounts, keep the live ingest key on your server. After authenticating the player, your server can open `POST /api/v1/session` with `X-API-Key`, using a device or player identifier it has verified. Return only that player's session token to the client over HTTPS. The client can then send events with `X-Session-Token`; it never needs your live key. Renew an expired session through the same authenticated route. Rate limit that route and never accept an arbitrary player id from the browser.

 

This is an HTTP integration pattern. The SDKs do not all provide a method to adopt a server-minted token. Use the [HTTP API](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/http-api/) for that client, or keep tracking on your server. A relay can be a temporary bridge for an existing client, but it must authenticate players, validate events and apply limits. An open relay simply moves the same abuse problem to your server. For games without accounts, use a public key with an allowlist and limits instead.

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: Require a Steam ticket
documents.content:
### Require a Steam ticket
