For a Steam build, connect Steamworks in your studio with a [Publisher Web API key](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/connections/), then enable `require_steam_ticket` on its public key and set `steam_app_id` to your app's decimal id. The flag defaults to false and the app id to null. Turning it on without a Steamworks connection is refused with `400 steam_connection_missing`. This setting applies to new sessions, so use a separate key for builds distributed elsewhere.

 

Your Steam integration obtains a hex ticket with `GetAuthTicketForWebApi("ravensight")` and sends it as `steamTicket` in the session request. Ravensight checks it with Steam using your Steamworks connection's Publisher Web API key, or its first key when it has none, which Steam may refuse. The SDKs do not currently obtain or attach this ticket automatically: wire it into your session transport before enabling the requirement. See [Steam's ticket verification API](https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/webapi/ISteamUserAuth).

 

A missing ticket answers `403 steam_ticket_required`; a refused ticket answers `403 steam_ticket_invalid`. An unusable connection, or a key Steam does not allow to check tickets, answers `403 steam_connection_missing` with one fixed message saying the connection needs a working Publisher Web API key, so a player never learns which keys you hold. Your Steamworks connection in **Settings > Connections** says why. If Steam cannot be reached, the answer is `503 steam_unavailable` with `Retry-After: 30`. None opens a session or charges for verification. Successful checks are cached for ten minutes per key and app. A joined session can reuse its parent's verification only for the same Steam app. Sessions store a keyed hash of the Steam id and the verified app id, never the raw Steam id. A valid ticket verifies access to the app; it does not prove that subsequent client event values are truthful.

 

If you enable Steam verification or use your own account identifier, review your game's privacy disclosures for that configuration. The default random-device-id guidance below does not describe account-linked sessions; hashing a Steam id does not make it an anonymous identifier.

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: SDK behavior in public builds
documents.content:
### SDK behavior in public builds

 

The SDK versions listed under [platform support](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/platform-support/) support keyless builds that send nothing, an optional opt-in consent mode, a distribution label, and event ids that remain stable on retries. Include `game_started` and `game_exited` in your allowlist. Option names and supported transports vary by SDK; follow the [SDK comparison and linked repositories](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/love-sdk/#sdk-compare). The doctor can warn about a live key in source or a shipped bundle; a scan that skips an unreadable file is not proof that no key exists. Keep public keys bounded and live keys on your own server when possible.

documents.section_title: Public builds and open-source games
documents.title: What the server keeps, and what it cannot tell
documents.content:
### What the server keeps, and what it cannot tell

 

Per key and month, Ravensight keeps the number of accepted events, counts of each refusal reason, and short, bounded lists of the origins that opened sessions and the most frequent event names that were refused for not being on the allowlist. It never stores a raw IP address: for [traffic sources](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/traffic/) it keeps a keyed hash and a masked form of each connecting address for 30 days, or for as long as you keep that address blocked. A session records the `distribution` the client declared, and each of its events carries it as a `distribution` property unless the event sends its own. It also records the player's country and the device fields the SDK sent; see [country and device](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/platform-support/#country-device).

 

The honest limit: a native build, a script or a bot can send any `Origin`, any version string and any `distribution`. Treat all three as hints that sort honest traffic, never as proof.

documents.section_title: Error capture
documents.title: Error capture
documents.content:
Error capture

 

## Error capture

 

An SDK with error capture reports what goes wrong in a running game on its own: uncaught errors, failed requests, console errors and clicks that did nothing. Each one is an ordinary [typed error event](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events), scrubbed, grouped by fingerprint and counted on the event meter like any other event.

documents.section_title: Error capture
documents.title: The event
documents.content:
### The event

 

A captured error is an event named `error` by default (any name an allowlist could hold works) with `rs_kind: "error"` and these top-level keys. Only the top level is read.

 

| Key | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `rs_severity` | `debug`, `info`, `warning`, `error` or `critical` |
| `rs_message` | Required. Stored up to 200 characters, scrubbed. |
| `rs_stack` | Optional. Stored up to 2,000 characters, scrubbed. |
| `rs_source` | Where it came from: `manual` (or absent) for an error your code reports, or `uncaught`, `unhandled_rejection`, `request`, `console`, `log`, `dead_click` or `crash` for automatic capture. Any other value breaks the contract. |
| `rs_error_type` | Optional. The error's class or type, such as `TypeError`. Stored up to 100 characters. |
| `rs_trail` | Optional, one string. Up to 20 log lines before the error, oldest first, joined by a line break, stored up to 1,500 characters, scrubbed. Kept only while the game's trail switch is on. |
| `rs_fp` | Written by the server: the error's fingerprint, `v1:` and 16 hex characters. One your game sends is removed. |

 

A failed request's message is the method, the host, the path with its identifiers replaced by `:id`, and the status or `network`, for example `POST api.example.com/v1/kickoff/:id 500`. It never carries a query string, a fragment, a header or a body. A dead click's message is the control's role and name, such as `Dead click: button Kick Off`.

documents.section_title: Error capture
documents.title: What is removed before it is stored
documents.content:
### What is removed before it is stored

 

The SDK scrubs the message, stack and trail on the device, and the server scrubs them again before storing them. Error text is scrubbed once more whenever it is shown or returned (the Errors view, `get_health`, `list_error_issues` and `get_error_issue`), so errors stored under an older rule are covered too.

 

- Email addresses become `[email]`.
 
- Bearer tokens, token-shaped strings, Ravensight keys (`gt_`) and long random strings that contain a digit become `[token]`. A file path keeps its shape.
 
- IPv4 and IPv6 addresses become `[ip]`.
 
- A home folder (`/Users/name`, `/home/name`, `C:\Users\name`, `C:\Documents and Settings\name`, either slash) becomes `~`. The name is the whole folder, spaces included, so `C:\Users\Jo Ann\game` becomes `~\game`.
 
- A web address loses its query, its fragment and any user name and password.

documents.section_title: Error capture
documents.title: How errors are grouped
documents.content:
### How errors are grouped

 

The fingerprint is built from the source, the error type, the message with numbers, ids, quoted text and web addresses replaced, and the file of the first frame in the stack that is your game's code (frames from the engine, the browser and the Ravensight SDK are skipped, as are line numbers and build hashes). On a native build the function name counts as well; on the web it does not, because shipped web code is usually minified. Two errors that differ only in an id or a number are one group on purpose.

documents.section_title: Error capture
documents.title: Resolving and regressions
documents.content:
### Resolving and regressions

 

Resolve an issue with the build the fix shipped in, **Fixed in build** in the Errors view (`build` on `POST /api/v1/games/:gameId/errors/:id/status`). The issue opens again, marked Regressed, when it is seen after the resolve on that build or a later one. A build older than the fix is a player who has not updated yet, and never reopens it. Every build seen since the resolve is checked, not only the latest. Builds compare as numbers part by part (`1.10` is later than `1.9`), a leading `v` is ignored, and a pre-release such as `1.3-beta` comes before `1.3`. With no build named, only a build later than the last one the issue was seen in reopens it. A build that is not a number, such as a commit hash, has no order, so any other build reopens it.

documents.section_title: Error capture
documents.title: Owner, priority, notes and the triage log
documents.content:
### Owner, priority, notes and the triage log

 

Each issue can have one owner and a priority. Set either or both with `POST /api/v1/games/:gameId/errors/:id/triage`, sending the `revision` you read plus `assigneeId` (a member of your studio, or `null` to clear it) and `priority` (`none`, `low`, `medium`, `high` or `urgent`). It answers `{ issue }` with the new revision. A request that changes nothing leaves the revision where it was. The refusals are `400 invalid_revision`, `400 nothing_to_change`, `400 invalid_priority`, `400 invalid_assignee` for anyone who is not a member of the studio, and `409 revision_conflict` when someone else changed the issue first.

 

`POST /api/v1/games/:gameId/errors/:id/notes` with `{ text }` (1 to 1,000 characters) adds a note to the issue and answers `201 { entry }`. A note does not move the revision. It is refused with `400 invalid_note`, or `409 history_full` once an issue holds 500 steps.

 

`GET /api/v1/games/:gameId/errors/activity` is the triage log: every step on every issue of the game, newest first, as `{ entries, nextBefore }`. Each entry names the issue, the step, when it happened and who did it. Page with `limit` (1 to 100, 50 by default) and `before`, passing back the `nextBefore` you were given without reading into it. `action` narrows the log to one step: `note`, `open`, `resolved`, `ignored`, `assigned` or `priority`. An unknown step is `400 invalid_action` and a cursor that was not returned by the log is `400 invalid_cursor`. Writing needs a role that can edit the studio; reading needs one that can read the game.

 

A studio you share a game with reads its error issues but not your triage: no resolved or regressed dates, no fixed-in build, no owner, no priority, no notes and no history, and its triage log is empty.

documents.section_title: Error capture
documents.title: What happened around an error
documents.content:
### What happened around an error

 

An issue's details in the Errors view (and `GET /api/v1/games/:gameId/errors/:id`) add three things for your own studio.

 

- **Players who came back.** Of the devices that hit the error, the share that did not start another session within 7 days, beside the same share for devices that played in the same days and did not hit it. Each device is counted from its first time hitting the error, or from its first event for the others. It reads only days at least 7 days old, so every device had the whole 7 days: pick the last 30 days to see it. This is correlation, never cause. A higher share means players who hit this error returned less often, not that the error made them leave. Playtest and doctor sessions are never counted.
 
- **Breadcrumbs.** For each recent example, the last 20 events of the same session before the error: the event name, its level, its kind (one of the typed kinds, or other) and how long before the error it happened. Never a property value.
 
- **The log trail.** The `rs_trail` the device sent with each example, scrubbed again when it is read and cut to 1,500 characters, shown only while the game's trail switch is on. It is text from players' devices and is marked that way.

 

A studio you share a game with gets none of these three. The `get_error_issue` tool returns them as `playersLost`, `breadcrumbs` and `trail`, and `get_health` lists the five biggest open issues and, for each top message, its builds with exact counts, newest build first.

documents.section_title: Error capture
documents.title: The two switches
documents.content:
### The two switches

 

Each game has two switches in its environment card in Settings, also settable with `PATCH /api/v1/games/:gameId` as `errorCaptureEnabled` and `errorTrailEnabled` (owners and admins).

 

| Switch | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capture errors automatically | On | Off: the SDK installs no hooks, and the server drops any error whose `rs_source` is automatic before it is counted, free, as `error_capture_disabled` on the Implementation health card. Errors your code reports with `rs_source: "manual"` or no source always arrive. |
| Send a log trail with each error | Off | On: a captured error carries its last log lines as `rs_trail`. Off: the server removes any `rs_trail` it receives. |

 

The SDKs read both from the session answer (`POST /api/v1/session`) and from `GET /api/v1/settings` as `"errorCapture": { "enabled": true, "trail": false }`. The server applies them as well, so a build that read its settings before you changed them still stops being charged for automatic errors.

documents.section_title: Error capture
documents.title: Limits on the device
documents.content:
### Limits on the device

 

- Nothing is installed without a key, before the player's consent where your game asks for it, or while capture is off.
 
- A session sends at most 30 captured errors, at most 3 of the same error, at most 10 with a trail, and at most 6 a minute. Past those they are dropped on the device, silently.
 
- The hooks pass every error on to whatever handled it before, and never capture the SDK's own requests or log lines.
 
- With a [public key](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/), `capture_errors` lets error events past the allowlist with room for the message, stack and trail.

documents.section_title: Error capture
documents.title: What it costs
documents.content:
### What it costs

 

One captured error is one event on the shared event meter, the same as any other event: it uses the included monthly events first, then the prepaid balance at the ordinary event rate (see [usage, billing and limits](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/limits/)). The trail adds nothing. A dropped error, on the device or on the server, costs nothing. There is no separate rate and no cap of its own; the device limits above are what bound it.

documents.section_title: Error capture
documents.title: Error text and the analyst
documents.content:
### Error text and the analyst

 

Error messages, issue titles, build versions, breadcrumb names and trails are written on players' devices, so Huginn and the Analytics MCP tools receive them marked as player text, a message cut to 200 characters, an issue title to 120 and a version to 100, to be read as evidence and never followed as instructions.

documents.section_title: Readable stack traces
documents.title: Readable stack traces
documents.content:
## Readable stack traces

 

A shipped build reports stacks with minified or obfuscated names. Upload the source maps or symbol files for that build and Ravensight shows each error's stack the way you wrote it: your file, line and function beside every line a file could map. The raw stack your players' devices sent is always shown too, and each mapped line is marked as symbolicated. Stacks are read when you open an error, never when the event arrives, so a file uploaded today also fixes yesterday's errors from that build.

documents.section_title: Readable stack traces
documents.title: File kinds and matching
documents.content:
### File kinds and matching

 

| Kind | File | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sourcemap` | A version 3 JavaScript source map, plain or indexed | Maps a minified frame's line and column to the original file, line, column and name. Name the map after its bundle (`game.min.js.map` for `game.min.js`); a build with one map uses it for every bundle. |
| `android_mapping` | The R8 or ProGuard `mapping.txt` | Retraces class and method names, and the original line where the mapping records line ranges. Where inlining leaves more than one candidate, all are named. |
| `breakpad` | A Breakpad `.sym` text file | Maps `module+0xoffset` frames to the function, and the source file and line from its line records. Name it after the module (`libgame.so.sym`). |
| `dsym` | A dSYM bundle, zipped | Stored and listed so it is ready; it is not read yet. Apple symbolication comes in a later release. |

 

Files are matched to the `game_version` your game reports, so upload them with exactly that build string. Each file is checked when it arrives, and a file that is not the kind it claims is refused before anything is stored or charged.

documents.section_title: Readable stack traces
documents.title: Limits, price and who uploads
documents.content:
### Limits, price and who uploads

 

**Limits:** 50 MB a file, 500 MB and 50 files a build. Ravensight keeps the newest 10 builds of each game (a build's age is its newest upload), and each file for 90 days; the hourly sweep deletes anything past either limit. Deleting the game deletes its files.

 

**Price:** 10,000 weighted events per started megabyte (1,000,000 bytes) a month, on the same event meter as everything else: the included events first, then prepaid balance, which is $0.005 a megabyte-month. Every file rounds up to a whole started megabyte, in every month: two 1 KB files are 2 MB. An upload pays its own month when it arrives. Each later month, the files uploaded before that month and still kept are counted for the game, each rounded up. No month is charged while the game is inactive or its error capture is off, and stacks are shown raw meanwhile; the files still expire on schedule. A part month counts as a whole month and nothing is prorated, as with extended retention. Reading stacks and listing files is free, and deleting a file refunds nothing. A game at every limit is at most 5,490 started megabytes, $27.45 a month.

 

| Stored | Weighted events a month | After included events |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One 2.4 MB source map | 30,000 | $0.015 |
| 10 builds of one 40 MB file | 4,000,000 | $2.00 |
| 10 builds of one 500 MB file | 50,000,000 | $25.00 |

 

**Funding:** uploading needs a funded prepaid balance. With an empty balance an upload is refused with `402 needs_funds`, and nothing is stored or charged. If a later month's payment is refused, the owner is emailed, and the game has 14 days from that notice to add funds; nothing is deleted until the notice has been sent. After that the month is not pursued and its symbol files are deleted, except files uploaded in the current month, which their upload already paid for.

 

**Who:** only the studio owner uploads and deletes, because every stored megabyte is billed each month. Every member who can read errors sees the list with sizes and monthly cost, in the Symbol files section under Errors. A studio a game is shared with never sees its symbol files and reads raw stacks only. Uploads are never available as an MCP tool; `list_symbol_files` reads the list, and `get_error_issue` returns the symbolicated lines.

documents.section_title: Readable stack traces
documents.title: Upload
documents.content:
### Upload

 

Upload from a build script

 

```
curl -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RAVENSIGHT_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/octet-stream" \
  --data-binary @dist/game.min.js.map \
  "https://api.ravensight.io/api/v1/games/<gameId>/symbols?build=1.4.1&kind=sourcemap&name=game.min.js.map&recurringConsent=true"
```

 

The token is the owner's CLI token (`gt_cli_`, from `ravensight-playtest login`) with the `playtest:upload` scope; the dashboard session works too. `recurringConsent=true` authorizes the monthly charge and is required. `name` is 1 to 200 letters, digits, dots, underscores, at signs, plus signs or hyphens.

 

| Status | Error | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 201 |  | Stored. `charged` gives the megabytes and weighted events paid for this month. |
| 200 |  | The same bytes were already stored for this build. `duplicate` is true and nothing was charged. |
| 400 | `invalid_build`, `invalid_kind`, `invalid_name`, `empty_file`, `invalid_symbol_file`, `recurring_consent_required` | Fix the request; nothing was stored or charged. |
| 402 | `needs_funds` | Add prepaid balance; nothing was stored or charged. |
| 403 | `forbidden`, `insufficient_scope` | Not the owner, or the CLI token lacks `playtest:upload`. |
| 429 | `usage_backstop` | The account reached its monthly usage safety limit; nothing was stored or charged. |
| 409 | `symbol_file_exists`, `too_many_files` | Another file has this name and kind in the build (delete it first), or the build holds 50 files. |
| 413 | `file_too_large`, `build_too_large` | Over 50 MB a file or 500 MB a build. |
| 503 | `symbols_unavailable`, `billing_unavailable`, `symbol_storage_unavailable` | Storage or billing is not available. A storage failure during upload is refunded. |

documents.section_title: Readable stack traces
documents.title: List and delete
documents.content:
### List and delete

 

`GET /api/v1/games/{gameId}/symbols` lists builds and files with sizes, the monthly events and the deletion dates. `DELETE /api/v1/games/{gameId}/symbols/{fileId}` deletes one file (owner only). Another studio's game answers `404`.

documents.section_title: From a player screenshot to a report
documents.title: From a player screenshot to a report
documents.content:
## From a player screenshot to a report

 

The player chooses to attach a screenshot in your game. Let them preview it and hide private information before sending. The SDK uploads the selected image through the existing Player Reports API; the server validates it and stores a sanitized copy. Once processing completes, open **Player reports** in the dashboard for the same game and environment. Click the thumbnail or message to see the full screenshot and context. Under **More filters**, choose **Screenshots only** to find image reports.

 

Player-submitted screenshots are separate from **Playtest → job → Screenshots**, which contains AI playtest evidence. A processing receipt means the image was accepted for checking, not that it is already visible in the inbox. Expired images leave the report text available.

documents.section_title: From a player screenshot to a report
documents.title: JavaScript game canvas

documents.section_title: From a player screenshot to a report
documents.title: SDK support
documents.content:
### SDK support

 

All nine SDKs submit a Player Report with a screenshot. Godot adds an optional overlay that captures the game viewport and lets the player highlight and redact before sending, and JavaScript's `captureScreenshot` captures only the game canvas you pass it. The other seven take an image your game already encoded after the player chose to attach it: Unity, Unreal, C++, iOS and Android accept PNG, JPEG or WebP (iOS a `UIImage`, Android a `Bitmap` or bytes), and LÖVE and Odin accept PNG bytes. No SDK captures the desktop, and an image is sent only when you pass one. Use the SDK README for its consent flow. Ordinary text feedback and error events never upload images; do not treat analytics event properties as file uploads.

 

For a direct integration, use the existing session token: `POST /api/v1/reports` with a stable `clientId`, `capturedAt`, message and image size/SHA-256; request `POST /api/v1/reports/:id/upload`; send the returned fields and file as a multipart POST to the presigned storage URL without API credentials; then `POST /api/v1/reports/:id/finalize`. Read `GET /api/v1/reports/:id` until complete or canceled. Retrying uses the same payload, ID and session. Public ingest keys must allow `allow_reports`. Never embed studio credentials in a game.

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.content:
11. Check your integration: the doctor

 

## Check your integration before and after you ship

 

Two layers watch your integration. The dashboard computes implementation health from your game's own live traffic, and a public scanner checks your source tree before you ship. Both feed the same card on your game's Overview page.

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: Live implementation health
documents.content:
### Live implementation health

 

Automatic, no setup. The API already sees what your integration does: requests rejected for size, event names exploding in cardinality, payloads brushing the 8KB ceiling, sessions with no end-of-session marker, and reserved `rs_` keys with values Ravensight does not know. The Implementation health card on Overview summarizes it over the last 7 days and tells you what to change.

 

`no_game_exited` means no session in the window sent `game_exited`, the marker for the end of a session. It is about the missing marker, not lost delivery: the events in those sessions were stored, and session length is measured to the last stored event. The JavaScript SDK sends `game_exited` automatically in a browser; the native SDKs send it from their quit and lifecycle hooks; a scripted runner that kills the app never sends it. The finding is `info` when every session that started also sent events after `game_started`, and a `warning` only when some sessions sent nothing at all after the start, which can mean the queue is not flushed before the app closes.

 

A game with [public keys](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/) gets a `public_keys` block on the card: each live key (paused included; revoked and expired keys are history, not health) with its label, prefix, state, accepted events this month, its ceiling if one is set, what remains under it and what its events would cost in blocks, its refusal counts and its most frequent unlisted names. The key list in Settings shows the same signals. Its findings, each with the id `public_key:<code>:<prefix>`: `needs_funds` (error: the included allowance is used and the balance cannot buy the next block of events, which stops every key in the account; add funds to keep accepting events), `ceiling_reached` (error: the key is at its ceiling or has refused a batch at it) and `ceiling_near` (warning: 80 percent of the ceiling), `unlisted_names` (note: events refused because their names are not on the allowlist, with the most frequent names, so you can add the ones you meant), `rejection_spike` (warning: at least 100 refusals this month and at least 20 percent of what the key was sent), `origin_mismatch` (sessions from origins not on the key's list: a warning while enforcement is off, a note when they were refused), `expiring` (warning: the key expires within 7 days) and `device_concentration` (warning: at least 1,000 events under the key and one device id sending at least half of them). Device concentration reads the key's recent sessions, those opened in the last 24 hours that are still alive, and a session ends at its lifetime (one hour by default), so it sees roughly the last session lifetime of traffic, not a full day.

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: What this data can answer
documents.content:
### What this data can answer

 

Below its findings, the Implementation health card lists four questions and says, from this game's own events, whether the data can answer each one. A question it cannot answer comes with a one-line reason that names what to send.

 

- **Do players come back?** (`retention`) Needs a real event at least 7 days old, so day 7 retention has a cohort old enough to measure.
 
- **Where do players stop progressing?** (`levels_funnel`) Needs events sent with `rs_kind: "level_start"` and an end: `rs_kind: "level_complete"`, a terminal event from the detection profile, or, when deaths are outcomes, an event sent with `rs_kind: "death"`. A death matched only by its name does not count here. Without them, a funnel read from event names alone (`level_started` and `level_completed` on events that carry a place) still answers, with a note that it is inferred and that `rs_kind` makes it exact.
 
- **Which paths do players take between places?** (`journeys`) Needs events that carry a place.
 
- **How do groups of players differ?** (`segments`) Needs events that carry properties of their own, beyond the reserved `rs_` keys and the place keys `level`, `location` and `track`.

 

In the API answer the block is `answerable_questions`: a boolean per question, `reasons`, keyed by each question that is false, and `notes`, keyed by each question answered only by inference. Two warnings sit beside it on the card, with their own title and detail: `uuid_like_place_values`, when a game has at least 20 distinct places in the last 7 days and half or more look like generated ids, which split one place into thousands of rows; and `synthetic_only_traffic`, when every session in the last 7 days was synthetic: Ravensight Playtest personas or a `ravensight-doctor --live` ping, which every report leaves out by default. Its title counts each kind.

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: ravensight doctor
documents.content:
### ravensight doctor

 

A zero-dependency scanner for your project directory. It detects your engine, finds the SDK, and lints the integration statically: event name length and cardinality, oversized inline payloads, missing track calls, and credentials that must never ship inside a game build (an MCP token or a cloud key in your tree is an error; a gt_live ingest key is not one of those, though a build players receive is better served by a [public key](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/), which `--bundle` points out).

 

Run it

 

```
npx ravensight-doctor

# machine readable, with the full inventory
npx ravensight-doctor --json

# your own track wrapper
npx ravensight-doctor --track-fn capture,Analytics.logEvent

# send one test event and confirm it was stored
RAVENSIGHT_INGEST_KEY=gt_live_xxxx \
npx ravensight-doctor --live

# also submit the report to your dashboard
RAVENSIGHT_INGEST_KEY=gt_live_xxxx \
npx ravensight-doctor --report
```

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: What it recognised
documents.content:
### What it recognised

 

Every report lists an inventory: each track call it found with its file, line and literal event name (or none when the name is a variable), the distinct event names with counts, the track functions it looked for, and how many ingest keys it found in the project and under test paths. The pretty report prints a summary and `--json` prints all of it. A track call counts when the name right before `.track(` is exactly `rs`, `ravensight` or `Ravensight`, with any chain before it, so `this.rs.track(` counts and `analytics.track(` does not.

 

If your game tracks through its own wrapper, name it with `--track-fn` (comma separated and repeatable) or in a `ravensight.config.json` in the directory you scan:

 

```
{
  "trackFunctions": [
    "capture",
    "Analytics.logEvent",
    { "name": "track_event", "argIndex": 1 }
  ],
  "ignore": ["vendor/", "*.generated.gd"],
  "gitignore": true
}
```

 

`argIndex` says which argument holds the event name. `ignore` adds `.gitignore` style patterns, as does `--ignore`, and the root `.gitignore` is honoured unless `gitignore` is `false` or you pass `--no-gitignore`. Ingest keys under test and fixture paths are listed but never used for `--report` or `--live`.

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: Status and exit codes
documents.content:
### Status and exit codes

 

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `fail` | At least one error finding. |
| `inconclusive` | The doctor could not check your events: it found track calls but none names its event with a string literal, or it found an ingest key but no track call it recognises. Name your wrapper with `--track-fn` to resolve it. |
| `warn` | Any other warning. |
| `pass` | No errors or warnings. Only a real pass says your integration looks healthy. |

 

Exit code 1 when any error finding exists, so CI can fail the build, and 0 for `pass`, `warn` and `inconclusive`. Add `--strict` to exit 1 on anything but `pass`. An unusable config file exits 2.

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: Three lines of evidence
documents.content:
### Three lines of evidence

 

From 0.4.2 the report prints three evidence lines: **Static** (what the source scan found), **Runtime trace** (what a recorded run sent) and **Live delivery** (the `--live` ping). The top-level status is the static verdict, so a missing live check never turns a clean scan into a failure.

 

A wrapper that adds properties to every payload centrally declares `enriches` in `ravensight.config.json`, so the contract keys it supplies are not reported missing. An undeclared wrapper is reported as `contract_prop_unproven` at `info`, not as an error. Forwarding closures are resolved automatically, and `forwarders` declares the ones the scan cannot follow.

 

When the build injects the key (an `.xcconfig` value or a CI secret), declare `ingestKey: { "source": "build" }` and point the doctor at the built product with `--bundle`, so it checks the key that ships rather than one in source.

 

```
{
  "enriches": ["Analytics.logEvent"],
  "forwarders": ["Telemetry.send"],
  "ingestKey": { "source": "build" }
}
```

 

Check the built bundle

 

```
npx ravensight-doctor --bundle path/to/YourGame.app
```

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: The live check
documents.content:
### The live check

 

`--live` proves the ingest key can deliver an event end to end. It reads the kill switch, opens a session with `"platform": "doctor"`, sends one `ravensight_doctor_ping` whose data carries a random `rs_doctor` value, then reads it back from `GET /api/v1/doctor/ping/:nonce` every 2 seconds, at most 10 times. The server keeps doctor sessions out of your analytics and your event usage and allows them only that one event. A ping that is read back is reported as stored, with the time the server accepted it. One accepted but not read back within 20 seconds is the warning `live_ping_unconfirmed`. A bad key, tracking switched off, or a refused session or event is the error `live_check_failed`, with a note saying which step failed.

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: In CI
documents.content:
### In CI

 

GitHub Actions

 

```
- uses: Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-doctor@v0
  with:
    path: .
    report: true
    api-key: ${'$'}{{ secrets.RAVENSIGHT_INGEST_KEY }}
```

 

A GitLab CI snippet ships in the [ravensight-doctor repo](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-doctor).

documents.section_title: Check your integration before and after you ship
documents.title: The report API
documents.content:
### The report API

 

The doctor submits to `POST /api/v1/doctor` with your `X-API-Key` ingest key: an engine, a summary (pass, warn or fail with counts), and up to 100 findings. An `inconclusive` result is sent as `warn`, and the inventory and live result stay on your machine. One report is kept per game, newest wins, and it appears on the Implementation health card alongside the live signals.

documents.section_title: Identify players who sign in
documents.title: Identify players who sign in
documents.content:
Identify players

 

## Identify players who sign in

 

Without sign-in, every device is its own player: one person on a phone and two browsers counts three times, and the website visits before they signed in count as a fourth. If your game has its own sign-in, call `identify` with a random id for the account after a player signs in and `resetIdentity` when they sign out. Ravensight then links the device to the account, including what it played before signing in.

documents.section_title: Identify players who sign in
documents.title: The calls
documents.content:
### The calls

 

Call them any time after init, even before the first session opens.

 

| SDK | After sign-in | On sign-out |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JavaScript | `rs.identify(accountId)` | `rs.resetIdentity()` |
| Godot | `Ravensight.identify(account_id)` | `Ravensight.reset_identity()` |
| Unity | `Ravensight.Identify(accountId)` | `Ravensight.ResetIdentity()` |
| Unreal | `Identify(AccountId)` on the Ravensight subsystem | `ResetIdentity()` |
| LÖVE | `ravensight.identify(accountId)` | `ravensight.resetIdentity()` |
| iOS | `Ravensight.identify(accountId)` | `Ravensight.resetIdentity()` |
| Android | `Ravensight.identify(accountId)` | `Ravensight.resetIdentity()` |
| C++ | `client.identify(account_id)` | `client.reset_identity()` |
| Odin | `identify(client, account_id)` | `reset_identity(client)` |

 

Pass a random, high-entropy id, such as a random UUID or a random analytics id you make once for each account and store with it. Never pass a sequential database key, an email address, a name or a platform handle: your game's salt reaches every copy of the game, so anyone could hash 1, 2, 3 and onward and match a guessable id, while a random one cannot be guessed. The SDK refuses any value that contains `@`, an empty value, and anything longer than 256 bytes, and sends nothing for it.

 

The identity is kept across launches. Signing in as a different account on the same device starts a fresh device id first, and so does `resetIdentity`, so the next person's play is not credited to the last account.

documents.section_title: Identify players who sign in
documents.title: What is sent
documents.content:
### What is sent

 

The id you pass never leaves the device. Each game has its own random salt, which the SDK receives when a session opens; the SDK sends an HMAC-SHA256 of that id keyed by that salt, once per session, with the session it belongs to. Ravensight stores a player id made from that hash (`px_` and 32 hex characters).

 

This is a pseudonym, not anonymisation: anyone who has your game's salt and can guess an id can work out its hash. That is why the id must be random. The hash still identifies one player across sessions, so it is a pseudonymous identifier: declare it in your game's privacy notice. The same account in two of your games gets two unrelated ids.

 

To find a player's id yourself, take the salt from `GET /api/v1/identify/config` with your game's key, compute the lowercase hex HMAC-SHA256 of the id you passed to `identify` with the salt's 64 characters as the key (as text, not decoded), and keep `px_` plus its first 32 characters.

documents.section_title: Identify players who sign in
documents.title: Verified links
documents.content:
### Verified links

 

Any copy of your game can claim any account, so claims are bounded: one device can claim at most three different accounts a day, and further claims that day are refused free of charge. If your game has a backend that checks sign-ins, it can vouch for one instead: post `{ "accountHash", "sessionToken" }` to `/api/v1/identify/verified` with the game's live key, using the session token the game passes it. A verified link is outside the daily limit, and a later claim never moves it to another account.

documents.section_title: Identify players who sign in
documents.title: Counting players
documents.content:
### Counting players

 

In Settings, open the environment and choose who counts as a player under Count players by:

 

- **Automatic**, the default: one person across devices, with what a device played before signing in, once your game has identified a player; each install until then.
 
- **Device**: each install is a player, always.

 

Every game starts on Automatic, so a game that never identifies anyone keeps counting installs. If your studio chose Device before, that choice stays.

 

Player counts, retention, returning players and the Overview all follow the choice. Experiments stay assigned by device. Daily totals already stored keep the count they were made with.

documents.section_title: Identify players who sign in
documents.title: Price and limits
documents.content:
### Price and limits

 

Each accepted identify is one event on your usage, drawn from the included monthly events first and then your prepaid balance. That is one event for each session of a player who is signed in. Repeating an identify in the same session, and every refused call, is free. With an empty balance the call is refused with `needs_funds`; the game keeps playing and the SDK tries again at the next session.

documents.section_title: Identify players who sign in
documents.title: Deleting a player
documents.content:
### Deleting a player

 

An owner or admin can delete an identified player with `DELETE /api/v1/games/<gameId>/identified-players/<playerId>`. Its links go at once, and its events are erased in the background: everything sent after it was identified, plus the earlier history of any device your backend verified for it. The earlier history of a device that only the game claimed stays, unlinked, because any copy of a game can claim any device. For questions, write to [support@realityse.com](mailto:support@realityse.com).

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: What each page is for
documents.content:
15. Reading your data: the dashboard

 

## What each page is for

 

The sidebar is grouped by what you are doing rather than by which database the answer comes from. The order below is the order the sidebar puts them in.

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: Build
documents.content:
### Build

 

Project-scoped: these read the title, not one of its builds.

 

- **Brainstorm.** A board of cards beside a partner that has read your studio's own findings, patterns, touchpoints and sales. See [Brainstorm](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/brainstorm/).
 
- **Design.** Your design documents, and a chat that has read your studio's findings before it proposes an edit. See [Design studio](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/design-studio/).
 
- **Code scan.** What your code reports against what your telemetry actually receives. See [Source scan](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/code-scan/).
 
- **Playtest.** Jobs, briefs, findings and reports from AI personas playing your build. See [Playtest](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/).

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: Live data
documents.content:
### Live data

 

Environment-scoped: every number here comes from the events one build sent. Overview, Player insights, Events and Level heatmaps each carry a **Real players** select, because persona sessions are real rows in the same store and are excluded by default.

 

- **Overview.** Daily active players, top events, lifetime totals, retention, the level funnel and the implementation health card. Pick 7 or 14 days and a By hour chart shows active players for each hour (UTC), with no point for an hour that had no events; hours need a window of at most 14 days. Results are cached per scope and range, so a repeat visit does not re-run the warehouse queries; a missing or expired snapshot still fetches fresh.
 
- **Player insights.** A triage board of the sessions the backend flagged, with the plain-language signals behind each call. See [how the detections read your events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#detection-rules). A [campaign link's player count](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/campaign-links/#campaign-links-player-insights) opens it narrowed to the players who arrived by that link. A spread card shows how session length, events per session, sessions per player or playtime per player is distributed: the mean, median, 90th percentile, smallest and largest, and a histogram of 5 to 50 buckets.
 
- **Events.** Raw events newest first, filterable by name and paged, with expandable payload rows.
 
- **Funnels.** An ordered sequence of two to eight event names: who reached each step, how many were lost against the step before, and the average and median gap into each one. Each conversion shows the count behind it and a 95% range, and a funnel with fewer than 30 at step one is marked as a small sample, so a dozen players never read as a precise percentage. Count players or sessions, and filter by an event property: either only the step events that carry it, or whole sessions that touched it, which is what you want when only one step sends the property.
 
- **Retention.** How many players come back, by the day (or week) they first played. Pick up to nine days from day 0 to day 90 and see a curve and a cohort table, each cell with its rate and its count. Classic counts a player who came back on that exact day; rolling counts one who came back on that day or any later one. A start event makes a player's first day their first occurrence of it, and a return event counts only it as coming back; either is an event name, or `kind:purchase` (and the like) for a typed kind: a bare `purchase` is your own event of that name. A typed event stored with `rs_invalid` is never counted. A day a cohort has not lived through yet reads not yet, never zero. Turn on cumulative figures for each cohort's sessions, playtime and revenue per currency. Daily, weekly and monthly active players and stickiness (daily over monthly) sit above. The Overview keeps its day 1 and day 7 tiles and links here. Split it by the build, platform, country, device model, OS version or GPU players started on, or the first value they sent of a property: the five biggest values and the rest, each with its count and a 95% range, because a retention figure for a dozen players is a wide range.
 
- **Level heatmaps.** Where players die or quit in a level, or where any event you name happens: a grid of counts from the positions your events carry. Send `rs_x` and `rs_y` as numbers in your game's own units; the [JavaScript SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/javascript-sdk/)'s `trackAt` and the [Godot SDK](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/godot-sdk/)'s `track_event_at` set them for you, for example `Ravensight.track_event_at("player_died", player.position, {"level": "room_4", "rs_kind": "death"})`. Plain `x` and `y` still work, and you can name other properties instead. A quit is where a session stopped: its last position, in a level it did not complete afterwards, once the session has been quiet for ten minutes. Each spot lists its events and its players, because one player dying twenty times is a different finding from twenty players dying once, and the page says how many deaths or events had no position. Positions add no events: they ride on events you already send. Include AI personas with the sessions control at the top of the page to see where your playtests died and quit. You can pick an image of your level to draw the map over; it stays in your browser and is never uploaded, and you give it the coordinates its corners stand for. The map assumes y grows downward, as in Godot 2D.
 
- **Why it moved.** How much a number changed between two equal windows, whether a change that size could be chance, and where it sits: by platform, build, level, new or returning and your top properties. Open it from an anomaly on Alerts and it compares that day with the same weekday a week earlier. It says where a change sits, not why; the link at the top asks Huginn, at its normal price. It covers players, new players, sessions, average session, events, errors, errors per session and progression failures. Revenue is not split here, because money stays per currency.
 
- **Builds.** Did your patch help: two values of `game_version` side by side. Day 1 and day 7 retention follow the players who started on each build, and a return on any build counts. Players who hit an error, median session and frame rate read what happened on the build, and you can name a funnel to run on each. Every number shows what it rests on and a 95% range. A reading needs 10 on each side and says "not enough data" below that; under 30 a number is marked as a small sample. With several measures on one page one can look clear by chance alone, so confirm a surprise before acting on it.
 
- **Monetization.** What players spent, from purchase events (`rs_kind: "purchase"`): paying conversion, payers, first purchases and the time to a first purchase, then one currency at a time its revenue, transactions, revenue per paying player and per daily active player, a daily chart, a histogram of revenue per paying player and the top items. Amounts stay in their own currency and are never converted or added across currencies; a purchase stored with `rs_invalid` is never counted. Below them, ads and total revenue: ads shown, clicked and rewarded, ads per session, purchases plus `ad` revenue per currency, revenue per player and per daily player, and ads by placement, network or format. Ad revenue keeps its fractions of a cent.
 
- **Acquisition.** Where players came from and what each campaign returned. Installs come from [`attribution` events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events); revenue is what those players spent in the window, purchases and ads; spend is what you import from a daily CSV export (a date, a campaign and the amount, with its currency; importing the same file again updates the same rows). Revenue is credited to the campaign on the player's latest event. Return on spend is revenue over spend in one currency, and a campaign with no spend imported says so rather than showing zero. Players whose attribution named no campaign count as installs, but their revenue is not measured. Spend, return on spend and this page are for your own studio only: a studio you share a game with can read the campaign columns and value per player by campaign through its analytics, never your spend. A forecast of value per player, by day 30 to 365 with a likely range, is fitted on what players have spent so far and is labelled as a forecast, because events are kept 90 days and later days are an extrapolation.
 
- **Campaign links.** Make a tracked link to your store page or any https address, share it, and count the people who follow it, by source, campaign, link, device and day. It needs no code in your game. A click is a referral click, never a conversion. See [campaign links](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/campaign-links/).
 
- **Progression.** How players move through your own hierarchy, from `progression` events (`rs_p1`, `rs_p2`, `rs_p3` name a world, a level and a stage). Start at the top level and open a row to look one level deeper, with attempts, completes, fails, players, the win rate (completes over completes plus fails), the median time from a session's first start to its first completion and the median `rs_score`. A place that only has fails still appears in the Overview level funnel, with a fails count. A progression event stored with `rs_invalid` is never counted.
 
- **Economy.** The virtual currencies your game creates and removes, from `resource` events (`rs_resource` names the currency, `rs_flow` is `source` or `sink`, `rs_amount` is how much). Every resource lists what was earned and spent, the net, the players who earned and the players who spent. Pick one to see a daily earned, spent and net chart and the items that drained or filled it most. Amounts are the game's own units, not money, and a resource event stored with `rs_invalid` is never counted.
 
- **Health.** The errors your game reports and how it performs. Send `error` events (`rs_severity` is `debug`, `info`, `warning`, `error` or `critical`, and `rs_message` is cut to 200 characters) and `health` events (`rs_fps_median`, `rs_fps_p10`, `rs_memory_mb` and `rs_boot_ms`, each optional). You see the errors per affected player, a daily chart per severity, the most frequent messages (open a row for the whole message) and the builds that raise them against their sessions. Performance is one sample per session, the latest it sent, grouped by platform and build with the median and slowest-tenth frame rate, memory and boot time, plus sessions per frame rate bucket. The Hardware card groups the same samples, and the share of sessions that raised an error, by device model, OS version or GPU (see [country and device](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/platform-support/#country-device)), and suggests a minimum spec: the groups whose median is under 30 frames per second or where more than 5% of sessions hit an error, judged only on groups with 20 or more sessions that sent a health sample, and for OS versions the lowest version per platform from which every version meets that target. An event stored with `rs_invalid` is never counted. The Data quality card below shows how late events arrive (an hour or more; a game that queues offline is late by design), duplicates dropped at ingest and repeats stored past it, what changed in event names and top-level keys between your two most recently seen builds, which SDKs sent in the last 24 hours and what ingest refused this month.
 
- **Journeys.** The level-to-level graph, where players stop, churn-heavy transitions, loops and estimated common paths. Only on deployments with journey graphs configured.
 
- **Player Reports.** The inbox for what players sent from inside the game. See [Player Reports](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/godot-sdk/#player-reports). A game without the report overlay sees its free-form feedback here instead, summarized by sentiment and theme and searchable by meaning.

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: Understand
documents.content:
### Understand

 

- **Studio Intelligence.** An investigation that ties a question to its evidence to a decision. See [Studio Intelligence](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/studio-intelligence/).
 
- **Huginn (AI analyst).** Ask in plain English; Huginn picks its own read-only tools and answers with the numbers it used. Conversations are listable, resumable, renameable and deletable. See [Huginn, the AI analyst](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/analyst/).
 
- **Muninn (studio memory).** What your studio has learned: one game's facts and the patterns that cite it, or under All games, every game's. See [Muninn, studio memory](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/studio-context/).

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: Studio
documents.content:
### Studio

 

- **Marketing.** What you did outside the game and the lift the platform measured afterwards. See [Marketing memory](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/marketing-memory/).
 
- **Sales.** Its own page directly below Marketing in the Studio navigation. Record what each title earned, filter the ledger, compare totals by currency, explore a 90 day launch curve, and import store exports. See the [Sales ledger](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/sales-ledger/).

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: In the footer
documents.content:
### In the footer

 

Settings sits below the groups rather than inside them, because it is global to the account rather than to the selected game. Its tabs are Usage and billing and Payment history (both owner only), Projects, Team, Huginn, MCP access, Playtest CLI and Appearance. Settings also links to the audit log, who did what in the org, for owners and admins. The usage meter beside it, titled Events, shows this month's total against the included events on one bar, split into the share your games' player events and reports sent and the share MCP calls count as, with a line under the bar for each. For the owner, a prepaid balance extends the figure to an estimate: the included events plus what the balance covers at the event rate, though the balance is shared with AI units, playtests and scans. The bar turns amber at 80 percent, and hovering the meter gives the totals and the overage so far.

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: How the built-in detections read your events
documents.content:
### How the built-in detections read your events

 

The level funnel, journeys, and the player flags are computed from your event names and the place fields, with no configuration. Name your events accordingly and they light up.

 

- **Deaths** are events whose name contains `died`, `destroyed`, or `killed` (lowercase substring match, so `player_died` and `ship_destroyed` both count).
 
- **Level starts** are names containing `start`, `begin`, or `enter`; **completions** contain `complet`, `finish`, `win`, or `clear`.
 
- **An explicit `rs_kind` comes first.** Set `rs_kind` in the event data to `level_start`, `level_complete`, `death`, or `none` and the level funnel, per-level deaths, journeys and the death count read it before the name. `none` opts an event out, so `checkout_started` with `rs_kind: "none"` is not a level start. An unknown value falls through to the name match. The five [typed kinds](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events) are known values too, so a `purchase` is never read as a level by its name, and a `progression` event is read by its `rs_status`. Keys that start with `rs_` are reserved for Ravensight. The rage quit rules below read it too.
 
- **`level`, `location` and `track` fold into one place.** The first non-empty one wins, in that order. The funnel, per-level deaths, and journeys only see events that have a place. It is any string that names a place or mode in your game: a level id, an encounter, a scene name. An event with a place that is not a level start, completion or death is navigation only: it stays out of the funnel and is counted as `place_without_kind` on the Implementation health card, unless it sends `rs_kind: "none"`.
 
- **Rage quit likely** flags a session with 3 or more deaths in its last 5 events, 3 or more deaths at the same level, or a final death followed by more than 10 minutes of silence inside the queried window. A death here is an event sent with `rs_kind: "death"`, whatever its name, so a `run_ended` event with `rs_kind: "death"` counts. Without a known `rs_kind`, the first two read `died`/`destroyed` names and the last reads a name containing `died`; `rs_kind: "none"` is never a death.
 
- **Potentially stuck** flags a session that repeats one event 10 or more times at the same level while the whole session has fewer than 20 events. The same event at a new level each time is movement, not stuck. Events with no place are grouped together, so ten repeats of a placeless event in a short session count; send a place or accept it.
 
- **Highly engaged** flags a session with at least 20 events at more than 2 events per minute and fewer than 5 deaths.

 

Every flag comes back with the plain-language indicators that triggered it, so you can always see why a session was tagged.

documents.title: Worked examples

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: The detection profile
documents.content:
### The detection profile

 

The rules above assume dying is failing and a level ends in a completion. Some games are built the other way round, so each game has a detection profile, set on the game's card under **Settings > Projects** by an owner or an admin and saved through a confirmation. It has three settings:

 

- **A death is a failure or an outcome.** Failure is the default. Choose outcome when dying is how a run normally ends, as in a roguelike: a death then counts as an intended end of the run, a completion in the level funnel, and never as a death, a rage quit signal or a reason a session is not engaged.
 
- **Rage quit detection on or off.** Off, the flag is not computed at all and each session row answers `rageQuitLikely: null` rather than false, so the dashboard says detection is off instead of showing zero. Every rage rule reads deaths, so deaths as outcomes also stop rage quit being inferred.
 
- **Terminal events.** Up to 20 event names, 1 to 200 characters each, that end a run on purpose, such as `run_summary` or `credits_shown`. They count as completions, never as starts or deaths, and never as the action the stuck rule looks for.

 

Every flag is inferred, and the answers say so. The session list (and the MCP tool `query_players`) carries `inferred: true` and `sample_sessions`, the number of sessions the flags were inferred from, and the overview carries `detection: { profile, sample_sessions }`. The dashboard labels a flag or a count with its sample, and a count of zero reads "No flags inferred from N sessions", never as players being fine. The profile is also readable and writable at `GET` and `PUT /api/v1/games/:gameId/settings/detection`, where the `PUT` body is any subset of `death_kind`, `rage_quit` and `terminal_events`.

documents.section_title: What each page is for
documents.title: Typed events: purchases, resources, progression, errors, health, ads and attribution
documents.content:
### Typed events: purchases, resources, progression, errors, health, ads and attribution

 

Seven more `rs_kind` values give an event a fixed meaning: `purchase`, `resource`, `progression`, `error`, `health`, `ad` and `attribution`. Each one has a small contract of reserved `rs_` keys, sent at the top level of the event data next to your own properties. Any other key you send is stored as usual.

 

| rs_kind | Required keys | Optional keys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `purchase` | `rs_amount` (whole minor units: an integer or a string of up to 15 digits), `rs_currency` (three-letter ISO 4217 code), `rs_item_type` and `rs_item_id` (1 to 100 characters) | `rs_cart` (up to 100 characters), `rs_transaction_id` (up to 128) |
| `resource` | `rs_flow` (`source` or `sink`), `rs_resource` (1 to 64 characters), `rs_amount` (a plain number of zero or more) | `rs_item_type` and `rs_item_id` (1 to 100 characters each when sent; the economy page shows a missing one as no item) |
| `progression` | `rs_status` (`start`, `complete` or `fail`), `rs_p1` (1 to 100 characters) | `rs_p2`, `rs_p3` (`rs_p3` needs `rs_p2`), `rs_score` (a number) |
| `error` | `rs_severity` (`debug`, `info`, `warning`, `error` or `critical`), `rs_message` (stored up to 200 characters) | `rs_stack` (stored up to 2,000 characters), `rs_source`, `rs_error_type` (up to 100 characters), `rs_trail` (stored up to 1,500 characters); see [error capture](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/error-capture/) |
| `health` | At least one of `rs_fps_median`, `rs_fps_p10`, `rs_memory_mb`, `rs_boot_ms`, each a number of zero or more | The other three |
| `ad` | `rs_ad_network` (1 to 64 characters), `rs_ad_format` (`banner`, `interstitial`, `rewarded`, `native`, `app_open` or `other`), `rs_ad_result` (`shown`, `clicked`, `failed` or `rewarded`) | `rs_ad_placement` (1 to 100 characters), `rs_revenue_micros` (a string of up to 18 digits) with `rs_currency` (three-letter ISO 4217 code, required with revenue) |
| `attribution` | `rs_attr_source` (1 to 64 characters, for example `utm` or `organic`) | `rs_attr_network` (up to 100 characters), `rs_campaign`, `rs_adset` and `rs_creative` (up to 200 characters each), `rs_touch_time` (epoch milliseconds) |

 

- **Money is whole minor units.** A purchase of 4.99 US dollars is `"rs_amount": 499, "rs_currency": "USD"`; 500 yen is `500` with `JPY`. A decimal such as `4.99` breaks the contract rather than being rounded. The currency is stored upper-cased, and totals are never added across currencies. A repeated transaction id is counted once: resending a purchase with the same `rs_transaction_id` from the same device is one purchase in every report, while a purchase with no transaction id always counts on its own. Do not send a purchase when a store restores one the player already owns, only for a new transaction.
 
- **Ad revenue is whole micros.** One ad impression is often worth a fraction of a cent, so ad revenue has its own key: `rs_revenue_micros` is millionths of one unit of `rs_currency`, sent as a string of digits. 0.0015 US dollars is `"rs_revenue_micros": "1500", "rs_currency": "USD"`. A decimal such as `0.0015` breaks the contract. Send revenue on the `shown` event, the paid impression, and send `clicked`, `rewarded` and `failed` without it: revenue on any other result breaks the contract.
 
- **Attribution is recorded once per device.** Send one `attribution` event when a player first installs or lands. The first one for a device is kept, and every later event from that device carries its `campaign`, `adset` and `creative`, so revenue can be credited to the campaign that brought the player. A browser game can read its landing page's UTM parameters and send them this way.
 
- **Resource amounts are plain numbers**, not money: `12.5` gold is fine. `rs_flow` says which way it moved, so the amount is never negative: spending 5 gold is `"rs_flow": "sink", "rs_amount": 5`. A negative amount breaks the contract and is left out of the economy report.
 
- **Progression feeds the level funnel.** A `start` counts as a level start, a `complete` as a completion, and a `fail` in the funnel's `fails` column. An event with no `level`, `location` or `track` is placed at its nodes joined with `/`, so `rs_p1: "world_1", rs_p2: "stage_2"` is the place `world_1/stage_2`.
 
- **Send health once per session**, as a summary near its end, rather than once per frame or per minute.
 
- **Accepted and flagged, never refused.** An event that breaks its contract is still stored and still answers 202. The server adds `rs_invalid` with the broken rule (for example `purchase_amount`), every typed report leaves the event out (a flagged `progression` event is not a start, completion or fail in the level funnel), and it is counted as `typed_event_invalid` on the Implementation health card. The 202 body then carries `invalid`, the number of such events in the request; when there are none the body is exactly `{ "accepted": n }`. The 8 KB data limit is measured on what you send, before `rs_invalid` is added. Only the server writes `rs_invalid`: one your game sends is dropped from the stored event and counted as `rs_key_unknown`.

documents.section_title: Explore your own questions
documents.title: Explore your own questions
documents.content:
## Explore your own questions

 

Explore groups events, players, sessions, events per player or session, and numeric property sums or averages by UTC day or hour, event name, platform, build, level, country, device model, OS version, GPU or a property. Grouping by country or a device field keeps the 50 biggest values for the whole window and says how many there were. Add a second grouping and up to 20 event names. Hourly queries cover at most 14 days. A second grouping keeps its eight biggest values for the whole window, and the answer says how many there were. Results are capped at 1,000 rows; the page and CSV explicitly mark truncation. Missing numeric values remain empty. Narrow your query before interpreting a partial result.

 

Enter event names to also see a feature engagement matrix. Breadth is the fraction of all active players in the selected window who used that event. Frequency is the mean event count among those players; per-active-player frequency includes everyone in the window. This is descriptive usage data, not evidence of causation.

 

Dashboard reads are included. CSV download uses the applied query and is capped at 256 KB, with spreadsheet formula escaping and a truncation note. The game-scoped API endpoints are `/analytics/explore`, `/analytics/explore.csv` and `/analytics/engagement`. HTTP queries also accept up to five `prop.key=value` filters and exact `platform`, `gameVersion`, `country`, `deviceModel`, `osVersion` and `gpu` filters.

 

Overview and Monetization show players, sessions, paying players and payer conversion by country, device model, OS version or GPU, from `/analytics/dimensions/{dimension}` (20 values by default, 50 at most, the rest as other). Player segments can name a country code and any of the three device fields, and every read that takes a segment honours them. Experiments and config rules still target platform and build only, because the rest is not known when an SDK fetches its config.

 

MCP `explore` and `get_engagement_matrix`, and REST `/api/v1/data/games/{gameId}/explore` and `/engagement`, use the standard programmatic rate and existing token scope. Group a property with `groupBy=prop:difficulty`; property sum and mean require `propKey`. These tools, along with realtime and anomaly reads, are available through MCP and REST rather than the hosted analyst toolset to preserve its request budget. AI playtest events remain excluded unless explicitly included.

documents.section_title: Save views and build dashboards
documents.title: Save views and build dashboards
documents.content:
## Save views and build dashboards

 

Use Save as view on analytics pages to keep query settings, then add the view in Dashboards. Members can create their own views and layouts. A studio holds up to 200 saved views and 50 dashboards, with at most 24 widgets per dashboard. Explore and Funnels save the query behind the displayed result, so unapplied form edits do not change it. Explore saves its selected relative range, which moves forward with time. Absolute Explore ranges supplied through the website API preserve a fixed window.

 

Start empty or from Overview, Monetization and Health presets. A game dashboard accepts views for that game. Portfolio dashboards use the existing studio metrics, monetization, funnel and property-breakdown endpoints; unsupported portfolio view types are refused. Those studio readers retain their existing game limits and aggregation semantics. Widgets do not introduce a new query engine or price.

 

Move widgets with labelled buttons or focus a widget and use arrow keys. Full width and Half width reflow the layout. Save changes explicitly; phone layouts use one column. Tables show up to 100 scalar values per widget and say when capped. Saved queries retain the original endpoint's data limits and units.

 

Dashboards start private to their creator. Only owners and admins can share them with the studio. Other members can read a shared dashboard or duplicate it, but cannot edit it. Saved views are studio-readable and creator-editable. A referenced view cannot be removed or change its game or kind until removed from dashboards; duplicate it instead. Deleting a game removes its saved views and dashboards.

 

MCP `list_views`, `list_dashboards` and `get_dashboard` read saved definitions at the standard programmatic rate. These reads do not execute widgets or change sharing. Dashboard writes stay in the authenticated website API.

documents.section_title: Saved player segments
documents.title: Saved player segments
documents.content:
## Saved player segments

 

Choose Player segment on supported analytics pages to reuse a named group of players. Members, admins and owners can create and edit up to 100 segments per game. Viewers and recipients of shared games can read them. Rules match platform, build, a level prefix, up to five exact event-property values, and up to five behaviour rules.

 

**Behaviour rules** select players by what they have done, read from their retained history up to the end of the query window: total spend in minor units of one named currency (never converted), total playtime in seconds, number of sessions, or whole days since last seen, each as at least or at most a whole number. Ad revenue rules are listed but refused until ad revenue data is available. For remote config and experiments, membership is worked out once an hour for each behavioural segment a config rule or a running experiment uses, so the config fetch never waits on the event store. A segment with more than 100,000 matching players is not used at fetch time and says so; split it with another rule. A game can use up to 20 behavioural segments in remote config and experiments; more are listed as over the limit and match nobody at fetch time.

 

**Device IDs are not secret.** A config fetch trusts the device ID the game sends, so anyone with the build's key and another player's device ID can read that player's values, and from them which segments the player matched. Do not target a sensitive behavioural segment, such as high spenders, with a value whose presence reveals the targeting.

 

All rules must match the same event during the query window. Analytics then reads the matching players, retaining their full history for session lengths, first-seen retention cohorts and purchase deduplication. Activity uses its own trailing 30-day window. Synthetic-player settings still apply. Property comparisons use stored text and are case-sensitive.

 

Segments apply to Overview, metrics, Players, levels, retention and activity, Monetization, Economy, Health, Builds, Why it moved, Progression, Distribution, funnels, property breakdowns, Explore and engagement. Long-range rollups, activity-history charts, session timelines, studio portfolio queries, realtime and SQL do not apply saved segments. Player Insights labels its whole-game history separately.

 

Website analytics requests accept `segment`. Supported MCP and REST analytics reads accept `segment_id`; MCP `list_segments` lists definitions at the usual programmatic rate. Explicit platform, build, level-prefix and property values replace the corresponding saved rule while preserving other rules. A segment from another game is refused. The hosted analyst does not advertise segment selection.

 

Saved views keep the segment ID, so editing its rules changes future results. Remove references from saved views before deleting a segment. Deleting a game removes its segments. Segment definitions contain no keys or player credentials.

documents.section_title: Event catalogue, test devices and purging
documents.title: Event catalogue, test devices and purging
documents.content:
## Event catalogue, test devices and purging

 

**Event catalogue.** The Event catalogue page lists every event name the game sent in a window (30 days by default, up to 400): how many times, from how many devices, when it was first and last seen, and its ten most common top-level property keys. Up to 500 names, busiest first. Real players only by default; the synthetic switch works as it does everywhere. MCP `get_event_catalogue` reads the same list at the normal programmatic rate.

 

**Test devices.** Owners and admins can mark up to 200 device IDs per game as test devices, with a label. Analytics pages leave them out by default, the way playtest sessions are left out. The Event catalogue page has a switch to count them, website analytics requests accept `test_devices=include`, and MCP analytics reads always leave them out. Bulk export, SQL, realtime and long-range history are not filtered.

 

**Purge an event name.** The owner can delete every stored event with one name for this game. The delete runs in the background, one purge per game at a time, and is recorded in the audit log. It cannot be undone, and daily and monthly totals already written keep their counts. Another game's events are never touched.

 

**Keep an event shorter.** The owner can keep one event name for fewer days than the game's retention (1 day up to one day less than the game's). Once a day, rows of that name older than its days are deleted. A game can have 50 such rules. Both actions are free.

documents.section_title: See recent activity as it arrives
documents.title: See recent activity as it arrives
documents.content:
## See recent activity as it arrives

 

Realtime shows the last 24 hours by UTC hour: players, sessions, events, typed errors and revenue in each currency's minor units. Purchases use the same transaction deduplication as other analytics. New and returning player classification uses the device registry and at most 50,000 device-hour pairs; the dashboard marks truncated classification. Activity totals remain complete.

 

Overview and SDK inventory refresh once a minute. Live events refresh every five seconds while the page is visible. Filter by event pattern (`*` matches any text), exact build or a device prefix of at least four characters. Literal underscores and percent signs stay literal. Show up to 200 recent events or inspect their raw JSON. AI playtest events are excluded by default.

 

SDK inventory groups real sessions created in the last 24 hours by platform and SDK. Session creation accepts an optional `sdk` value such as `godot/0.3.1`; invalid values are ignored and older clients appear as unknown. The SDK name uses lowercase letters, digits or hyphens and the version uses letters, digits, periods, plus signs or hyphens, each at most 32 characters.

 

MCP `get_realtime` and REST `GET /api/v1/data/games/{gameId}/realtime` read the hourly view at the standard programmatic rate. The live tail stays dashboard-only to avoid unattended polling costs. Existing token scope and shared-game rules apply.

documents.section_title: Monitor unusual changes
documents.title: Monitor unusual changes
documents.content:
## Monitor unusual changes

 

Owners and admins can create up to ten enabled monitors per game in Alerts. Choose players, new players, sessions, median session length, errors per user, purchases, resource flow or progression failures. Money metrics use one currency, and resource monitors use one named resource and direction. An optional property scope narrows the data.

 

After the daily rollup, monitoring compares yesterday with 28 trailing days. At least 14 observed history days are required. The rule removes weekday offsets, uses a median and median absolute deviation with a minimum spread, and compares against your selected confidence threshold. These are statistical heuristics, not guarantees of a problem. Missing observations are not treated as zero.

 

Monitoring pauses after 90 days or when history is insufficient. Use Keep monitoring to renew. Selected current studio members receive email, or the owner if no recipients are selected. Duplicate job runs do not send duplicate alerts. The anomaly log expires after 180 days. Shared games cannot be monitored by the receiving studio.

 

Detection does not call AI. Ask Huginn only prefills a question; sending it uses the normal analyst price. MCP `list_anomalies` and REST `/api/v1/data/games/{gameId}/anomalies` use standard metered reads. Scoped new-player monitoring is limited to 50,000 registered devices.

documents.section_title: Schedule studio reports
documents.title: Schedule studio reports
documents.content:
## Schedule studio reports

 

Owners and admins can create up to 20 schedules in Settings, Reports. Choose daily, weekly or monthly delivery, a UTC hour, one owned game or the studio, and an overview, monetization or health template. Select current studio members as subscribers. Monthly reports send on the first; weekly reports use your selected weekday. Each report covers the preceding complete UTC period and compares it with the period before that.

 

Reports are deterministic and make no AI call. Studio reports include at most the 12 newest owned games and show when capped. Totals sum across games without deduplicating people. Overview active player-days sum daily active players, not distinct people over the period; missing rollups contribute no counts. Currency totals remain separate, and revenue stays in minor units. Shared games cannot be scheduled by recipients.
