CSV attachments are optional and capped at 256 KB with a visible truncation note. Test reports go only to the requesting user, with at most five test sends per schedule per UTC day. Duplicate scheduler ticks cannot resend a claimed period; failures appear on the schedule and do not automatically retry that period. MCP `list_report_schedules` reads configuration and status at the standard programmatic rate without sending mail.

documents.section_title: Experiments and measured outcomes
documents.title: Experiments and measured outcomes
documents.content:
## Experiments and measured outcomes

 

Owners and admins can create a draft with a hypothesis, a fixed key, two to eight named variants and whole-number weights totaling 100%. The first variant is the baseline. Choose one primary outcome and optionally target a segment by platform, build or behaviour. A game can keep 100 experiments and run ten at a time. Members and viewers can read; incoming shared-game access does not include experiments.

documents.section_title: Experiments and measured outcomes
documents.title: Targeting and sample size
documents.content:
### Targeting and sample size

 

A targeted experiment keeps a device once it has matched. Its first assignment is recorded, and a device that later leaves the target segment (a new build, a lower spend) stays in its arm until the experiment stops. Stopping ends every recorded assignment. Choose **Include new builds** on a build-targeted draft to also enrol devices on builds first seen after the start: the builds already seen are listed at the start, so the experiment needs the event store then, and a game with more than 1,000 builds must target one build.

 

Set an optional **target sample size**, 10 to 10,000,000 exposed players per variant. The draft form estimates one for a yes or no outcome: about 16 × p × (1 − p) ÷ d² players per variant to detect a change of d from a baseline rate p, at 80% power and 5% significance. The creator and the studio owner get one email when every variant reaches the target, and one when the experiment stops. Neither email concludes or promotes anything.

documents.section_title: Experiments and measured outcomes
documents.title: Config rules and assignment
documents.content:
### Config rules and assignment

 

Add experiment-variant rules to Remote config before starting. On a config fetch, running experiments assign a variant using the SHA-256 hash of `experimentKey + ':' + deviceId`, reduced modulo 10,000 and compared with cumulative weights. The result is deterministic for the same key, device and weights; changing weights would change assignments, so started experiments keep their allocation, targeting and outcome fixed. Start a new experiment key for a new test. Device IDs are the unit of assignment, not verified people.

 

Attach `rs_exp_<experiment_key>` to gameplay events with the assigned variant name. From Godot 0.5.0, JavaScript 0.7.0, LÖVE 0.7.0, Unity 0.5.0, Unreal 0.5.0, C++ 0.5.0, Odin 0.6.0, iOS 0.6.0 and Android 0.5.0, every SDK does this for you: the first typed config read sends one `rs_exposure` event and tags the events after it (per session, or per run in C++, iOS and Android), a fetch alone tags nothing, and a well-formed `rs_exp_<key>` your game sets itself is left alone. On an older SDK, tag events yourself. Variant names start with a lowercase letter and use lowercase letters, digits, underscores or hyphens, up to 40 characters. Malformed exposure labels are removed and counted as reserved-key warnings; the rest of the event stays usable. A config fetch alone is not a measured exposure. Exposure tags add no extra event charge.

 

Stopping removes assignments from future fetches; cached clients keep their last values until they refresh. Results remain readable. Concluding can name a winner without promotion, or explicitly promote the winner's bound values to config defaults. The review shows before-and-after defaults and sends the reviewed config version. A concurrent change refuses promotion so you can review again. Existing segment rules still take precedence where applicable.

documents.section_title: Experiments and measured outcomes
documents.title: Results and comparisons
documents.content:
### Results and comparisons

 

Results include real-player events after the first recorded exposure and within the experiment's start/stop window. Players tagged with more than one variant are excluded. Purchases retain historical transaction deduplication and remain in one selected currency. Retention uses complete UTC days after exposure; immature cohorts are excluded. New-player share uses the first-seen registry and excludes players not yet recorded there. Synthetic playtests never enter experiment results.

 

Comparisons use the labelled player-level outcome: sessions, active days, mean session seconds, errors, currency revenue, transaction counts, resource amounts, progression failures, purchasing/new-player shares, funnel conversion or day-1/day-7 return rates. These are not differences in aggregate DAU, pooled session medians or errors per affected player. Daily charts group outcomes by first exposure day. Experiment results are limited to the latest 90 days, even when raw-event storage is extended, with partial windows identified. Reads cap at 50,000 exposed players, five million scanned rows and 15 seconds; they fail visibly rather than silently sampling.

 

Continuous outcomes use a Welch t comparison; binary outcomes use a two-proportion z comparison when successes and failures are sufficiently represented. Results show treatment-minus-baseline differences and 95% intervals, with a caution below 100 measured players per arm. Sparse or constant samples do not receive fabricated precision. Intervals are unadjusted for repeated looks and multiple variants, and changes to other game settings can affect the comparison. The system never selects or promotes a winner automatically. Methods: [NIST two-sample comparisons](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda353.htm) and [difference of proportions](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/software/dataplot/refman1/auxillar/diffprop.htm).

documents.section_title: Experiments and measured outcomes
documents.title: Over MCP
documents.content:
### Over MCP

 

MCP `list_experiments` reads definitions and `get_experiment_results` reads outcomes. REST `GET /api/v1/data/games/{gameId}/experiment-results?experiment_key=...` uses the same scoped programmatic token and standard metered rate. These reads do not mutate lifecycle state or config. They are not added to the hosted analyst's prompt. Experiment results and configuration changes do not automatically become studio-memory findings or investigation evidence.

documents.section_title: Remote configuration
documents.title: Remote configuration
documents.content:
## Remote configuration

 

Use Remote config to draft up to 50 typed keys for the selected game environment. Owners and admins can review the before-and-after diff and publish. Members and viewers can read configuration; incoming shared games cannot. An outdated version is refused so another editor's changes are preserved.

 

Keys start with a lowercase letter and use lowercase letters, digits and underscores, up to 64 characters. Values are strings, finite numbers, booleans or JSON, with an 8 KB limit per value and 20 nesting levels. Types are checked without implicit conversion: the string `"false"` is not a boolean. Each key can have up to 20 ordered rules; the first matching platform, build or behavioural segment supplies its value. Event properties and levels are unknown during a config fetch, so segments using them cannot be config rules.

 

Fetch `GET /api/v1/ingest/config?deviceId=...&platform=...&gameVersion=...` with the build's `X-API-Key`. Device IDs are required and limited to 256 characters; platform and build are optional and limited to 128. Game and environment come from the key, never a query parameter. The result contains `values`, `experiments` and `etag`. Cache the document and send its ETag in `If-None-Match` on the next fetch. A matching response returns 304 with no body. Use local defaults or the last cache if a fetch fails.

 

One successful non-cached config fetch counts as one event on the existing shared meter. A 304 is free. Config fetches have a separate usage line and do not create player analytics events. Ingest game/key/device limits and public-key origin, allowed-build and revocation checks apply. Config fetches additionally allow 30 requests per device per game per minute. Disabled games refuse fetches. Config values are public to anyone holding the build's ingest key; use them for game settings, never credentials or server secrets.

 

Editing a referenced platform/build segment rebuilds the snapshot and advances the configuration version. A referenced segment cannot be removed or changed to property/level rules. Audit history lists key names and versions, excluding values. Disabled or deleted keys disappear on the next successful fetch, so clients should use their local defaults for missing keys.

 

**Scheduled values.** Owners and admins can schedule a value for one published key: a start time, an optional end time up to 90 days later, and a note. The fetch compares the times with its own clock, so a schedule takes effect to the second. While active it replaces the key's rules and default for every player, and when two overlap the later start wins. A game can have 50 upcoming or active schedules, each up to 400 days ahead. Cancel one at any time; creating and cancelling are in the audit log. Schedules cost nothing extra: a cached client keeps its free 304 until a schedule actually changes a value it receives.

 

**Staged rollouts.** Roll a new default out to a rising share of devices, such as 10%, 50% then 100%, with 1 to 168 hours per stage. A device's place is a stable hash, so a device inside 10% stays inside at 50%. Segment and experiment rules still apply first. Every quarter hour Ravensight halts the rollout if one of the game's monitors for errors, progression failures, sessions, active players or session length has moved the wrong way since it started, or if errors per player inside the rollout during the stage exceed players outside it over the same window by more than your limit (10% to 500%), with at least 50 players inside. The comparison never treats fewer than 0.02 errors per player as the baseline, so one early error does not stop a rollout. At 100% the comparison is with the same length of time just before the stage. A publish that changes the key's default or removes the key cancels its rollout, and completion never overwrites a default someone published meanwhile. Halting returns every player to the previous value and records why. After the last stage the value becomes the key's default. A game can run five rollouts at once, one per key.

 

MCP `list_config_schedules` reads schedules and rollouts, with their status and why a halted rollout stopped. It creates and cancels nothing.

 

MCP `list_remote_config` reads names, types, enabled flags, versions and rule counts at the normal programmatic rate. It does not return values or publish changes. Configuration writes use the authenticated website API. All nine SDKs include typed config access, scoped ETag caching and explicit experiment exposure labels. Running experiments add deterministic assignments and matching variant rules to the same response.

documents.section_title: Campaign links
documents.title: Campaign links
documents.content:
Campaign links

 

## Campaign links

 

Make a short link for each place you share your game, and see how many people followed it. It works for any game with a page to send people to, and nothing has to be added to the game itself. It is in beta.

documents.section_title: Campaign links
documents.title: Make and share a link
documents.content:
### Make and share a link

 

1. Open **Campaign links** in the Live data group of the dashboard.
 
1. Paste the address people should land on, for example your store page. It must start with `https://`.
 
1. Choose the traffic source, such as a video, a newsletter or a community post, or type your own. Pick an existing campaign or name a new one. A medium and a label are optional and help you tell links apart.
 
1. Create the link and press **Copy link**. The link looks like `https://go.ravensight.io/k7Qm2xR`. Share it where you chose.

 

A link can be disabled, which stops it redirecting and can be undone, or deleted, which cannot be undone. A game can hold up to 200 campaigns, and a campaign up to 500 links. The destination is checked when you create or edit the link: it must be an `https://` address with a site name, no username or password, no custom port, no numeric address, nothing on a private network, nothing with look-alike characters in the site name, and nothing that points at another campaign link. It can be up to 2,048 characters. The link redirects to the address you saved, plus the tags below when they apply, whatever is added after it in the shared link.

documents.section_title: Campaign links
documents.title: Tags added to the address
documents.content:
### Tags added to the address

 

For two kinds of destination the redirect adds a few tags to the address, built only from what you saved on the link. A tag the address already carries is never replaced, and the rest of the address is kept as you saved it. Each link's details row shows the tags, the address visitors land on and an **Add tags** switch. Tags are on by default; turned off, visitors land on the address exactly as saved.

 

- **A Steam store page** (`store.steampowered.com`) gets `utm_source` (the link's source), `utm_medium` (its medium, when it has one) and `utm_campaign` (the campaign name in lower case, words joined by dashes). Steam reports wishlists for these tags in Steamworks, under UTM analytics, so you can see visits and wishlists per link there. Ravensight does not import that report.
 
- **Your own web page**, your site or a web build you host, gets `rs_link`, the link's id. Every Ravensight SDK reads it and counts the player: a web build from the page address on its own, and an app or a native build when your link handling passes it on. See below.
 
- An App Store, Google Play, Epic, Discord, Kickstarter or itch.io address, and a Steam address that is not the store page, gets nothing. An itch.io browser game plays in a frame that itch.io serves from its own address, which would never see the tag.

documents.section_title: Campaign links
documents.title: Players who arrived by a link
documents.content:
### Players who arrived by a link

 

When a Ravensight SDK learns the link a player arrived by, it sends the link's id with the first session it opens, once. Ravensight keeps it only when it names a link of the same game, and adds it to that session's events. The Clicks tab then shows **Players who arrived** (different devices) and **Sessions from links** in the window, and the same split by link; each web link's details row shows its own. Playtest and doctor sessions never count. The link id is one you created, not personal data, and it goes under the same consent as everything else: with opt in, only after the player's yes, and never for a player who opted out. Nothing about it is stored on the device. An itch.io link counts clicks and no players, because it gets no tag.

 

- **A web build** (the JavaScript SDK on your page, a Godot web export, Unity WebGL or a LÖVE web build) reads `rs_link` from the page address once, when it starts. There is nothing to call, and the address is left as it is.
 
- **An app or a native build** cannot see a web address, so your game passes the id on. Point the link at your own `https` page that opens the app (a universal link or App Link), or read it from an install referrer you already handle, take `rs_link` from that address, and call the SDK's campaign link setter below. It returns false, and changes nothing, for anything that is not a link id (24 characters, `0` to `9` and `a` to `f`). Call it before the SDK opens its first session; a later call goes with the next session it opens.

 

| SDK | Call | From version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [JavaScript](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/javascript-sdk/) | `rs.setCampaignLink(id)` | 0.12.0 |
| [Godot](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/godot-sdk/) | `Ravensight.set_campaign_link(id)` | 0.7.0 |
| [Unity](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-unity) | `Ravensight.SetCampaignLink(id)` | 0.6.0 |
| [Unreal Engine](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-unreal) | `URavensightSubsystem::SetCampaignLink(LinkId)` | 0.6.0 |
| [LÖVE](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/love-sdk/) | `ravensight.setCampaignLink(id)` | 0.8.0 |
| [iOS](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/ios-sdk/) | `Ravensight.setCampaignLink(id)` | 0.7.0 |
| [Android](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-android) | `Ravensight.setCampaignLink(id)` | 0.6.0 |
| [C++](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-cpp) | `client.set_campaign_link(id)` | 0.6.0 |
| [Odin](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-odin) | `rs.set_campaign_link(client, id)` | 0.7.0 |

 

The JavaScript SDK has read the page address since 0.8.0. In a LÖVE web build the page's JavaScript SDK opens the session and reads it, so the LÖVE call is for desktop builds. The C++ and Odin SDKs have no supported web build, so a C++ or Odin game always uses the call.

documents.section_title: Campaign links
documents.title: Open a link's players
documents.content:
### Open a link's players

 

A link's player count, in its details row and in **Players by link** on the Clicks tab, opens [Player insights](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/) narrowed to the players who arrived by that link, over the same days. The list holds every session those players played in those days, not only the first, so you can see what they did after arriving. A chip above the sessions names the link and the days; remove it to see every player again. The filter is part of the page address, so a reload or a shared address keeps it, and it names the game, so it opens the right one. Switching game yourself drops it, because a link belongs to one game.

documents.section_title: Campaign links
documents.title: Lift estimate per campaign
documents.content:
### Lift estimate per campaign

 

Each campaign is also a [Marketing](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/marketing-memory/) touchpoint, made when the campaign is made (or, for a campaign older than this, the first time its estimate is shown) and dated by its first link. Its name, kind, channel and date follow the campaign, so they change in Campaign links; notes, spend, tags and the game stay yours to edit in Marketing, and it cannot be deleted there. Choose a campaign on the Clicks tab to see its estimate: the new players in the 72 hours from the first link against the 7 days before, measured overnight like every touchpoint, and, where a Steamworks connection reports wishlists for the game's title, the wishlist adds in the same days the same way. It is an estimate, compared with the days before: anything else you did in those days counts too. Deleting a game keeps the touchpoint in Marketing as an ordinary one you can edit or delete.

documents.section_title: Campaign links
documents.title: What a click does and does not prove
documents.content:
### What a click does and does not prove

 

A click is a referral click: a browser asked for your link and was sent on. It shows that the link was followed. It does not show that the visitor installed, wishlisted or bought anything, that the same person did not click twice, or that the page they reached loaded. The page calls these referral clicks for that reason, and no number on it is a conversion rate.

 

- **Total clicks** is every request for a link that was answered with a redirect.
 
- **Valid clicks** leaves out the ones that look automated: crawlers, link preview fetchers, requests with no browser name, browser prefetches, and a burst of more than 20 requests a minute from one visitor on one link.
 
- **Filtered clicks** is the difference. They are stored so you can see them, and they are not billed.
 
- A request that only checks the link, a `HEAD` request, is answered the same way and is not recorded.
 
- Detection is a heuristic. A bot that looks like a browser counts as valid, and a person on an unusual setup may be filtered.

documents.section_title: Campaign links
documents.title: What is kept

documents.section_title: Campaign links
documents.title: Cost
documents.content:
### Cost

 

One valid click is one event on the shared event meter, the same meter as [game events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/data-api/). Filtered clicks are not billed. A link never stops working because an allowance ran out or a balance is empty: the visitor is still sent on, the click is still counted, and the stats page says how many clicks were not billed. Reading the numbers in the dashboard is not a billed action.

documents.section_title: Campaign links
documents.title: API
documents.content:
### API

 

- `GET` and `POST /api/v1/games/:gameId/campaigns`, `PATCH /api/v1/games/:gameId/campaigns/:id`: list, create and rename campaigns.
 
- `POST /api/v1/games/:gameId/campaigns/:id/links` with `{ destination, source, medium?, label?, tagDestination? }`, then `PATCH` and `DELETE /api/v1/games/:gameId/links/:id`. A refused destination answers `400 invalid_destination` with a `reason` and a plain `message`. A link answers `tags` (`steam`, `players` or null), `tagDestination` (true unless turned off, `400 invalid_tag_destination` for anything but true or false) and `redirectsTo`, the address visitors land on.
 
- `GET /api/v1/games/:gameId/analytics/players?campaignLink=<link id>`, with the usual `from` and `to` in unix seconds: the session list of the players who arrived by that link in the window, every session they played there, and `campaignLink: { id, players }`, how many players that is. Anything but a link id answers `400 invalid_campaign_link`. Over MCP, `query_players` takes the same id as `link_id`.
 
- `GET /api/v1/games/:gameId/campaigns/stats` with optional `from` and `to` as whole days (`2026-11-01`, both included, counted in `tz`, a time zone name such as `Europe/Berlin`, default UTC), `campaignId`, `linkId` and `source`: totals plus the split by day, source, link, campaign, destination type, device and referring site (`byReferrer`, with `(none)` and `(other)`), `totals.players`, `totals.sessions` and `playersByLink`, and with a campaign, `campaignLift`. Left out, the window is the last 30 days ending today; it is at most 90 days. Any other date form answers `400 invalid_range`, and an unknown zone `400 invalid_tz`.

documents.section_title: Campaign links
documents.title: Not yet
documents.content:
### Not yet

 

Custom link domains, importing Steam's UTM report or matching clicks to wishlists or sales one by one, install and purchase attribution, players from a store page link (a store page gets no tag), QR codes and splitting traffic between destinations are not part of this beta.

documents.section_title: Forms and surveys
documents.title: Forms and surveys
documents.content:
Forms

 

## Forms and surveys

 

Collect feedback, survey answers, interest in a beta, or contact details through a hosted page or a form embedded on your website. A form belongs to your company or one project title. Project forms are shared across that title's game environments.

documents.section_title: Forms and surveys
documents.title: Build and publish
documents.content:
### Build and publish

 

Open Forms in company or project scope. Start with a template or build your own. Add up to 20 pages and 100 questions, with up to 50 choices per question. You can ask for text, numbers, ratings, scales, single or multiple choices, a platform or a country. Contact forms can also request a name or email address. Anonymous forms cannot include contact fields; remind respondents to leave identifying details out of free text.

 

Show a question when an earlier answer matches a condition. A page can skip forward to another page or complete the form. If several skip rules match, the first matching rule wins. Randomization changes the order of independent questions or choices while keeping a condition's question before the question that depends on it.

 

For a quiz, set the correct answers and points. Choose whether respondents see a score and correct-answer feedback after an accepted submission. Correct answers are not included in the public form before submission.

 

Set your title, short introduction, completion message, logo, colors, studio contact and privacy notice. Preview uses the same form layout and branching without saving responses or recording views. Publishing creates an immutable version. Later draft changes, including a new logo, reach the public form only when you publish again. A published form keeps its address.

documents.section_title: Forms and surveys
documents.title: Share or embed
documents.content:
### Share or embed

 

Copy the hosted address from Share. For an embed, add the exact website origins allowed to display your form and copy the iframe code. Origins include the scheme and host, such as `https://studio.example`. The embed resizes to fit its content; answer values and receipt tokens are never sent to the parent page.

 

Company forms work even when your company has no games. Add bounded campaign tags to a company form's hosted link to compare sources. Native [campaign links](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/campaign-links/) remain game scoped and can target a form only when the game and form belong to the same project. Form submissions appear as aggregate campaign outcomes, without identifying respondents or joining their answers to gameplay.

documents.section_title: Forms and surveys
documents.title: Read results and export
documents.content:
### Read results and export

 

Results show views, accepted submissions, daily totals, sources and question summaries. All form report dates use UTC. Published versions are reported separately so a renamed or changed question is not silently combined with its previous meaning. Each question shows answered and skipped counts; choice counts and numeric summaries use the responses still retained.

 

Submissions per recorded view divides accepted submissions by recorded views. It is not a unique-person conversion rate and may exceed 100%, because a browser privacy preference can stop view collection while still allowing an intentional response. With no recorded views, the ratio is unavailable.

 

Owners and admins can read individual responses, filter by version or campaign and export up to 10,000 matching responses as CSV. Narrow the date range or filters for a larger set. Members can build forms and read aggregate results, but cannot publish, close, delete, export responses or read contacts. Viewers and people with access only to a shared game cannot access these company or project records.

documents.section_title: Forms and surveys
documents.title: Contact entries and consent choices
documents.content:
### Contact entries and consent choices

 

Contacts are a projection of submitted response fields. An email address, name or consent choice is recorded as entered and is unverified. Two responses using the same email address remain separate. Collecting an address does not create a player account or establish control of that address. Ravensight sends no respondent email, confirmation or campaign broadcast from forms.

 

A checkbox records the wording of that published form version, the choice and the submission time. It does not verify identity or certify consent. You decide the purpose of the collection and whether those choices meet your obligations.

documents.section_title: Forms and surveys
documents.title: Privacy and response receipts
documents.content:
### Privacy and response receipts

 

Each accepted response receives a private receipt link. Its secret stays in the link fragment, and the respondent can download the receipt for safekeeping. Opening the link does not change or disclose the response. The receipt page lets its holder download, withdraw or delete that response through an explicit action. It never gives access to another response submitted with the same email address.

 

There is no email recovery for a lost receipt. A respondent can contact the studio for help. Deleting or withdrawing a response removes its answers and any contact entry derived from it. Previously recorded aggregate collection totals and minimal billing retry records remain; the latter contain no answers or receipt secret.

 

Set automatic deletion to 12 or 24 months, or keep responses until deleted. A minimum-age acknowledgement can be configured from 13 through 99; no birth date or birth year is collected. Forms directed to children are not supported. The studio is responsible for its audience, lawful collection and privacy notice.

documents.section_title: Forms and surveys
documents.title: Collection and limits
documents.content:
### Collection and limits

 

Each accepted response uses one event from the existing shared included event allowance and then available prepaid capacity. Each recorded pageview uses one event. The page reports a view only after it has been open long enough for a person to read it, and the server checks that time against the page's signed token: a faster view is counted as bot traffic and uses no events. Automated submissions, including any that fill the hidden field people never see, are also counted as bot traffic. Results show bot views and bot submissions apart from your real numbers; they store no response and are never billed. The submission total and completion summary are derived from the accepted response and do not add another charge. Retries with the same accepted submission are deduplicated.

 

When both included allowance and available prepaid capacity are exhausted, collection pauses before a new response is stored. Responses are not held for later acceptance. Existing account-owner usage alerts identify affected collection. Invalid, blocked and rejected submissions do not use events. A title's forms refuse addresses on its games' block lists. Company forms have their own list: owners and administrators add an address under Blocked senders on the Forms page, and only a masked form of it is kept. Hosted forms use no cookies or persistent visitor identifier; view collection respects Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control, while intentional submissions remain available.

documents.section_title: Forms and surveys
documents.title: Aggregate agent access
documents.content:
### Aggregate agent access

 

The game analyst can read the current title's aggregates when the caller has permission, without selecting another title or company. The [MCP server](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/mcp/) offers `list_forms` and `get_form_stats` with the `forms:read` permission. These read form status and aggregate results only. No tool exposes individual responses, contact entries, consent assertions, quiz keys or receipt secrets. Supply `project_id` for a project title or omit it for company scope. A project-restricted token cannot use company scope. Every call uses the existing programmatic event meter and its funding and token-budget rules.

documents.section_title: Traffic sources and the block list
documents.title: Traffic sources and the block list
documents.content:
3. Traffic sources and the block list

 

## Traffic sources and the block list

 

See which connecting addresses a game's sessions and events come from, tell a keen player from a bot, and block an address that is abusing a key. It works for every key, live and public.

documents.section_title: Traffic sources and the block list
documents.title: What is kept
documents.content:
### What is kept

 

A raw IP address is never stored. For each game, address and UTC day, Ravensight keeps a keyed hash of the address and a masked form a person can read (an IPv4 address as its /24, like `203.0.113.0/24`, an IPv6 address as its first 48 bits), with that day's sessions, accepted events, refused events, how many devices opened sessions from it (counted up to 50, then shown as 50 or more), and a short, sampled list of its most frequent event names. Device ids are kept only as short digests. These rows are deleted after 30 days; a block keeps the hash and masked form for as long as the block stands. Refused events count only when the address caused them (invalid events, policy refusals, its own session's or device's limits, a block), never when the game is out of funds, at a key's ceiling, switched off or at its game-wide limit. A session also keeps the hash and masked form of the address it was opened from, until the session expires. Playtest and doctor sessions are left out.

documents.section_title: Traffic sources and the block list
documents.title: Shapes
documents.content:
### Shapes

 

Each address's day gets one shape. Events means accepted events; refused events are counted apart.

 

| Shape | When | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `many_devices` | 10 or more devices opened sessions from the address that day. | A warning on the Implementation card, and the day's traffic email to the studio owner (one per game and day, listing up to ten addresses). It may be a bot or a shared network, such as a school or a cafe. |
| `rejections` | At least 50 refused events, and at least 30 percent of everything the address sent. | A warning, listed in the same daily email. |
| `heavy_player` | At least 1,000 events and at least 20 percent of the game's day, from one or two devices. | Information only: a heavy player at a steady pace. No email, no action suggested. |
| `normal` | Everything else. | Nothing. |

documents.section_title: Traffic sources and the block list
documents.title: Blocking an address
documents.content:
### Blocking an address

 

Block an address from its row in the traffic list, or by typing it; a typed address is hashed and masked and never stored. A block carries a reason (`abuse`, `bot`, `testing` or `other`), an optional note of up to 500 characters, and an optional expiry from one hour to 90 days. A blocked address gets `403 ip_blocked` on `POST /api/v1/session`, `/track` and `/track/batch`, before any rate limit or allowance check, so a refused request is free and never billed. Each block counts the requests it refused. A block or an unblock takes effect within 30 seconds on every server. An SDK treats the 403 as a stop, like any other 403.

 

The honest limit: one address can be many people (a school, an office, a mobile carrier), and a determined sender can change addresses. Block what looks like abuse, and pair it with a [public key's](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/) allowlist and limits.

documents.section_title: Traffic sources and the block list
documents.title: API and MCP
documents.content:
### API and MCP

 

- `GET /api/v1/games/:gameId/traffic/sources?day=YYYY-MM-DD`: the day's totals and the 50 busiest addresses by events, each with `ipHash`, `ipDisplay`, counts, sampled `names`, `shape` and `blocked`.
 
- `GET`, `POST` and `DELETE /api/v1/games/:gameId/traffic/blocks`: list, add (`{ ipHash or ip, reason, note?, expiresInSeconds? }`) and remove blocks. Adding or removing one needs a role that may change game settings.
 
- Over [MCP](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/mcp/): `list_traffic_sources`, `list_ip_blocks`, and with a write token `block_ip` and `unblock_ip`. `get_integration_status` carries today's ten busiest addresses and the block list as `traffic`.

documents.section_title: Website analytics
documents.title: Website analytics
documents.content:
Websites

 

## Website analytics

 

See how visitors reach and use your company or project website. Website collection is separate from game telemetry. It does not need a game environment, create player identities or join form contact details to visits.

documents.section_title: Website analytics
documents.title: Company and project scope
documents.content:
### Company and project scope

 

Company home shows your project titles, their environments, existing game activity coverage, company website status and company form totals. It works before you create a game. Open website setup from the Company website card to configure your company website in a dialog. Choose View full website analytics on that card to see its reports.

 

For a game's website, select its project and open Game website under Live data. The website belongs to that title across all its environments. Its domains, tracking key and reports stay separate from your company website and other games.

 

Owners, admins and members can read and configure websites. Shared-game access and the viewer role do not grant access to company or project website records. A project-restricted agent token can read only its allowed projects. With explicit write permission, its website tools can configure only those titles; company scope and studio-wide writes remain unavailable.

documents.section_title: Website analytics
documents.title: Connect a website
documents.content:
### Connect a website

 

1. For your company, open website setup from the Company website card on Company home. For a game, select its project, open Live data > Game website and choose Setup. Enter a website name.
 
1. Add each allowed origin, such as `https://studio.example`. Use exact origins without a path, query or wildcard.
 
1. Choose whether collection waits for your consent control, and whether to enable heatmaps.
 
1. Copy the installation snippet into your website. Use the generated public website key, separate from any game ingest key.
 
1. Check installation status after an accepted event arrives. A copied snippet alone does not count as a verified installation.

 

The website tracker supports client-side navigation and named custom events. Do not put personal information in event names or campaign tags. Browser Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control stop collection. Bots are excluded. Your studio remains responsible for deciding when visitor consent is required and providing the appropriate control and notice.

 

To record what happens on your own servers, such as an account created or a payment confirmed, create a server key in the website's setup and send [server events](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/server-events/) from your backend. They appear only in the website's Server events tab and its MCP tool, never in Events, goals, funnels or any other report, and they do not mark the website as installed. The server key is secret: keep it on your server, never in the snippet.

 

For a private signup or checkout flow, the SDK's outcome-only mode can explicitly report the registered events `signup_form_viewed`, `signup_failed` and `checkout_failed`. It observes no page, form values, account identity or attribution. Failures carry only approved reason categories and, for checkout, an optional monthly or annual plan. These are anonymous observations, not verified signups or purchases. They follow the same consent, privacy and one-event collection rules. Ordinary auth-page tracking remains excluded.

documents.section_title: Website analytics
documents.title: Read reports
documents.content:
### Read reports

 

Overview shows visitors, pageviews, sessions and bounce rate. Pages adds entry and exit counts. Sources separates referring hosts and campaign tags, while Audience groups broad browser, device and country values. Realtime shows the last five minutes of accepted activity. Reports use normalized addresses, not full query strings or fragments.

 

Imported history may lack active time or other engagement measurements. When newer visits have measurements, the overview shows the available values as a measured portion and explains its coverage. Engagement and bounce rates use only sessions with complete engagement evidence. Missing history is never counted as zero; a range with no measurements stays unavailable.

 

Save a goal for a path or named event. Save a funnel with ordered steps and a completion window to see where sessions stop progressing. Campaigns adds aggregate outcomes and marketing timeline entries from the same permitted scope. There is no person-level attribution between website visitors, contacts and gameplay.

 

Explicit private-flow outcomes appear in Events and event goals or funnels. They do not create a homepage visit, a page-list row or a page session. Realtime event counts include them, while its page list shows observed addresses only. Deliberately absent pages are separate from missing imported history.

 

Events your own backend sends with the website's server key have their own Server events tab: each event name with its count, how many different actors sent it and when it was first and last seen, and for one event its daily counts and one property's 20 most frequent values, for up to 90 days. They never appear in Overview, Pages, Sources, Audience, Events, goals, funnels, retention, heatmaps or Realtime. See [where server events show](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/server-events/#server-events-reports).

 

Raw website reports support up to 90 days. Daily heatmaps use UTC; the other reports use the selected reporting time zone. Company home includes all authorized game environments, with an environment filter. Campaign summaries show coverage indicators when they include only a bounded selection of game environments.

documents.section_title: Website analytics
documents.title: Read heatmaps safely
documents.content:
### Read heatmaps safely

 

Heatmaps are off until you enable them. They record coarse percentage cells for clicks and ten scroll-depth buckets, grouped by page and small, medium or large viewport. They do not record a session, capture typed values, collect page text or take screenshots. Form fields and private regions are excluded.

 

Choose a recorded page and viewport to see click density and scroll depth without uploading an image. You may add a reference image to provide visual context. Remove private information before uploading it. The image is available only through authenticated website access; it is not an automatically captured visitor page. You can remove it independently of the aggregate heatmap.

documents.section_title: Website analytics
documents.title: Usage and deletion
documents.content:
### Usage and deletion

 

Each accepted pageview, custom event or server event uses one event from the existing shared included allowance and then available prepaid capacity. One combined heatmap summary uses one event. An engagement summary, the active time on a page sent when the page is hidden or left, also uses one event, at most six per page view. A typical visit therefore uses about two events: for example, 50,000 one-page visits in a day use about 100,000 events, which is 5 cents once the included allowance is used. When a page loads, the website tracker asks for a short-lived page token, and a page view is billed only when it carries a token held for at least a second, the same check a hosted form uses: a page view sent sooner, or with a token from another website, is counted as bot traffic instead. Trackers that do not send the token yet keep working as before. Automated visits from known bots and automation tools use no events: they are counted per day, with no visitor, page or address detail, and shown as Bot traffic on the Overview, apart from your visitor numbers. Stable event identifiers deduplicate uncertain retries. Invalid, blocked and rejected events do not use events.

 

When included allowance and available prepaid capacity are exhausted, new collection pauses before storage. The tracker clears its queue on a funding pause; it does not keep unfunded collection for later. Existing account-owner usage alerts identify affected website and form collection.

 

Raw events expire after 90 days. Daily aggregate heatmaps remain until the website is deleted. Deleting a website retires its collection identity and removes its analytics and reference images. Minimal usage and retired-identity records remain so retries cannot revive the deleted site. A new website receives a new collection identity.

documents.section_title: Website analytics
documents.title: Agent setup and aggregate reports
documents.content:
### Agent setup and aggregate reports

 

The game analyst can read the current title's aggregate website and form results when the caller has the required permission. Its tools cannot switch to a different company or title. The [MCP server](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/mcp/#mcp-sites-forms) exposes scoped setup, installation, verification, goals and funnels with website write permission. `get_site`, `verify_site`, `get_site_report` and `get_server_events` need `site:read`; `get_server_events` reads the website's server events, which no other tool or report includes: names with counts, actors and first and last seen, and for one event its daily counts and a property's 20 most frequent values. Reports include events and permitted property breakdowns, engagement, retention, diagnostics, history coverage and aggregate CSV exports. Use `heatmap_pages` to discover recorded pages and viewports. These tools return configuration and aggregates, never raw visitor records, private reference images or contact entries. MCP calls use the existing programmatic event meter, funding requirement and token budget.

documents.section_title: Huginn, the AI analyst
documents.title: Huginn, the AI analyst
documents.content:
16. Ask your events a question in plain English

 

## Huginn, the AI analyst

 

Huginn, the AI analyst, lives under **Understand > Huginn**. It picks its own read-only tools, runs them against the game you have selected, and answers with the numbers it used. A completed question is one shared AI unit, including every tool call it made on the way.

documents.section_title: Huginn, the AI analyst
documents.title: The tools it reaches for
documents.content:
### The tools it reaches for

 

`get_overview`, `query_players`, `query_levels`, `get_retention`, `get_history`, `get_metrics`, `get_monetization`, `get_ad_revenue`, `get_campaigns`, `get_ltv_forecast`, `get_progression`, `get_economy`, `get_health`, `get_distribution`, `get_level_map`, `get_retention_split`, `get_data_quality`, `explain_metric_change`, `list_builds`, `compare_builds`, `get_funnel`, `get_property_breakdown` and `search_feedback` cover the numbers, what players spent and what players wrote. `get_code_brief` reads the source scan's notes, `list_playtest_jobs`, `list_playtest_findings`, `get_playtest_report` and `get_validation_report` read playtests, `list_feature_specs`, `get_feature_spec` and `get_feature_job` read [Build a feature](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#labs-feature), `list_game_plans` and `get_game_plan` read [Create a game](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#labs-create), and `list_touchpoints` and `get_sales` read marketing memory and the sales ledger, and the `list_pulse_*`, `get_pulse_post` and `search_pulse_comments` tools read [Pulse](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/pulse/). Huginn can call `describe_studio_data` to check what data the studio holds (see [Studio data](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/studio-data/)) before it chooses a tool. On deployments with journey graphs, `get_journeys`, `find_bottlenecks` and `get_top_paths` read those. When nothing else answers, it writes SQL with [run_sql](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/run-sql/). Every tool is read-only, and the game it reads is the one you selected, never an argument the model can change.

documents.section_title: Huginn, the AI analyst
documents.title: Analyst context you write yourself
documents.content:
### Analyst context you write yourself

 

Findings are extracted by a model. Analyst context is the opposite: it is what you write, and the analyst is told to trust it over its own reading of the data. There are two levels, both inserted into the prompt verbatim and ahead of the findings. Game context lives in **Settings > Huginn** and holds up to 2,000 characters of facts about one game. Studio notes hold up to 1,000 characters of facts that are true across every game in the studio. A note like "levels 5 through 7 are an intentional difficulty spike" or "we ship weekly builds on Fridays" heads off a wrong conclusion before the analyst reaches for a tool. Writing either needs a member role or above; reading them needs nothing extra.

documents.section_title: Huginn, the AI analyst
documents.title: The same question across every game
documents.content:
### The same question across every game

 

Four questions can be asked of the whole studio rather than one game: the headline metrics, what players spent, a funnel, and an event property's breakdown. The analyst has them as `compare_metrics`, `compare_monetization`, `compare_funnel` and `compare_property`, and the API exposes them under `/api/v1/studio/analytics/...`. This is how a problem in one game is told apart from a habit of the studio: if the tutorial loses the same share of players in all three of your games, the tutorial design is the finding. Studio totals are sums and conversions are weighted by volume. There is deliberately no studio median, because the median of medians is not the median. Studio revenue is summed per currency and never across two, and there is no studio revenue per paying player.

 

A studio answer covers at most 12 games. When more were eligible the response says so rather than presenting twelve games as the studio: `studio.truncated` is true and `studio.omittedGames` counts the games left out. A property breakdown also carries `studio.other`, the count of events whose value is not in the merged top list.

documents.section_title: Your events, queryable directly
documents.title: Your events, queryable directly
documents.content:
17. AI analyst: run_sql and the events schema

 

## Your events, queryable directly

 

`run_sql` is available both as an MCP tool and to the in-dashboard analyst. It is a real SELECT against your event store, not a canned report.

documents.section_title: Your events, queryable directly
documents.title: events table columns
documents.content:
### events table columns

 

| Column | Type |
| --- | --- |
| `game_id` | String |
| `device_id` | String |
| `session_id` | String |
| `event_name` | String |
| `ts` | DateTime64(3, 'UTC') |
| `level` | String |
| `platform` | String |
| `game_version` | String |
| `country` | String, a two-letter country code, empty when unknown (see [country and device](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/platform-support/#country-device)) |
| `device_model` | String, empty when unknown |
| `os_version` | String, empty when unknown |
| `gpu` | String, empty when unknown |
| `campaign`, `adset`, `creative` | String, where the device was acquired, from its [attribution](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events); empty for a device with none |
| `payload` | String, arbitrary JSON |
| `props` | Map(String, String) of the payload's top-level keys, so `props['difficulty']` reads a property directly. Values are text: cast before comparing numerically. The [typed event](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#typed-events) keys read the same way, so `toUInt64OrNull(props['rs_amount'])` is a purchase's minor units; leave out rows where `mapContains(props, 'rs_invalid')`. |

documents.section_title: Your events, queryable directly
documents.title: Rules
documents.content:
### Rules

 

- **SELECT only.** A single `SELECT` or `WITH ... SELECT` statement. Writes, DDL, and settings changes are rejected before the query runs.
 
- **No comments, extra statements, dollar signs or table functions.** `--`, `/* */`, `#`, and semicolons (beyond one optional trailing one) are all rejected, as is a `$` anywhere in the query and any table-function call such as `FROM name(...)`.
 
- **events only.** The only readable table is `ravensight.events`, plus any CTEs you define in the same query. Other table names, table functions, and cross-database reads are rejected.
 
- **The game filter is automatic.** Every reference to `events` is rewritten to a subquery scoped to your own `game_id` before it runs. Do not write your own `game_id` predicate: you cannot see or query another game's rows regardless.
 
- **Row cap.** Results are capped at 100 rows when usage metering against the prepaid balance is on, and at 200 rows where metering is off, no matter what `LIMIT` you write. The same cap applies to the analyst and to MCP.
 
- **Money has its own tool.** For revenue use `get_monetization`. If you must read purchases here, `props['rs_amount']` is integer minor units of `props['rs_currency']`, so group by currency, leave out rows with `rs_invalid`, and count a repeated `rs_transaction_id` once per device.
 
- **Query and time limits.** Queries are capped at 4,000 characters and run with `readonly=1` at the database level. A metered query gets 3 seconds of execution and reads at most 1,000,000 rows and 64 MB; with metering off the limit is 15 seconds.

documents.section_title: Your events, queryable directly
documents.title: Example
documents.content:
### Example

 

Deaths by level, most first:

 

```
select level, count() as deaths
from events
where event_name = 'player_death'
group by level
order by deaths desc
```

documents.section_title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.content:
14. Check your integration: source scan

 

## The gap between what your game does and what it reports

 

Analytics can only answer questions about events you actually send. The source scan reads your code and your live telemetry together, and tells you where the two disagree.

documents.section_title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.title: How it runs
documents.content:
### How it runs

 

Three front doors, one pipeline. Connect GitHub and a push scans itself (below), or send your source as a zip upload up to 100 MB, or as a JSON body of `{ files: [{ path, text }] }` up to 40 MB, which is what makes it easy to post from CI. A cheap model reads the files in batches and writes short notes on what each one does and what it reports. A stronger model then reads those notes alongside a deterministic gather of the last 30 days of your own events, and writes the findings. Neither stage is given tools.

 

Those notes are kept, and your source is not. A scan builds a standing model of the repository: per file, the path, a hash of its text, and our one-line note about it, plus a repository-level read of the architecture, the modules, and which telemetry the code does and does not send. There is nowhere in it to put your code. The next scan compares hashes against that model and re-reads only what changed, which is both why a rescan is priced at a floor rather than by repo size and why the findings get sharper each time: the model that writes them is looking at the whole repository, not at the diff you happened to send. Because it does read the whole repository, a very large one is quoted at its size tier instead of the floor.

 

Your analyst can read that model too, and so can your own agents over MCP, through `get_code_brief`. That is what lets an answer about a funnel that dies at step three come back with the reason: not that players quit, but that nothing in the code reports the step.

 

Only code is read, and only so much of it: eight source extensions, files up to 100 KB, at most 6,000 files, with dependency and build directories skipped. Binaries are detected and dropped rather than counted. Every run carries a hard token budget, so a repo that turns out larger than it looked stops at the budget and reports what it got rather than spending without limit.

documents.section_title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.title: Scanning on every push
documents.content:
### Scanning on every push

 

Connect GitHub once and a push scans what changed, without anybody uploading anything. Open **Code** in the dashboard and press **Connect GitHub**, which installs the Ravensight app on the account or organization that holds your repositories. You choose which repositories it can see, and you can change that on GitHub at any time. Connecting is an owner action, because a connected repository can spend your balance without anybody watching.

 

Ravensight asks for two read permissions and no write permissions: **Contents** and **Metadata**, both read-only. That is enough to read files, the commit tree and a diff between two commits, and it is not enough to push a branch, open a pull request, comment, or change a setting. Nothing in the scanner writes to GitHub.

 

Then attach a repository to a game, on the same screen. One repository belongs to one game: that is what lets a push know whose telemetry to read it against. A game with a client repo and a server repo keeps a separate model of each, and a change to one is never priced as a change to the other.

 

**Only the default branch scans.** A push to a feature branch is acknowledged and ignored, on purpose: the question the scan answers is what your shipped game reports, and a branch is not that yet. If nothing happens after a push, this is the first thing to check.

documents.section_title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.title: What a push spends, and how to stop it
documents.content:
### What a push spends, and how to stop it

 

A push scan charges the balance by itself, up to **$3 a day per repository**. Past that ceiling the scan is queued instead and waits for somebody to approve it in the dashboard, where the price is shown before you agree to it. You can raise the ceiling per repository, or turn auto-charge off entirely with **Scan every push automatically**, in which case every push queues and nothing is ever charged unattended.

 

The ceiling is deliberately lower than the cheapest whole-repository price, and the reason is worth knowing. Usually a push is a diff, and a diff costs $2. Sometimes there is no diff to read: the first push after connecting, a force push, or a rewritten history all leave us nothing to compare against, so the scan reads the whole repository and is priced accordingly. That is exactly the case that must not be charged while nobody is looking, so it goes past the ceiling and waits for you.

 

Disconnecting is on the same screen, per repository or for the whole studio. Pushes stop immediately. Your notes are kept, because you paid for them and they are what keeps the next scan at the rescan price rather than a first-scan price, so reconnecting later does not mean buying the same reading twice. Deleting the game is what deletes them.

documents.section_title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.title: What you get back
documents.content:
### What you get back

 

Findings, not patches. Each one names a kind (`instrumentation_gap` or `risk`), a severity, the file and lines, a short evidence quote, a hypothesis and a suggestion. Nothing rewrites your code, and nothing is committed anywhere.

documents.section_title: The gap between what your game does and what it reports
documents.title: What it costs
documents.content:
### What it costs

 

The first scan of a repository is a fixed price by the size of the source that survives the filter, drawn from your prepaid balance: $5 under 250 KB, $10 under 1 MB, $25 under 4 MB and $50 under 16 MB. Past 16 MB of surviving source a scan is refused rather than priced.

 

Every scan after that is priced on what actually changed. We compare a hash of each file you send against the hash in our notes, and only the files that differ are read and paid for: $2 while the changed source is under 250 KB, and otherwise the tier that change set belongs to on its own. Nothing is taken on trust here, and there is no flag you can set to claim a discount. Two consequences follow, both in your favor. Resubmitting a repository with nothing changed in it is free and does not run, because there is no work to do. And a change set is measured against our notes rather than against the last submission's size, so a 900 KB edit to a 1 MB repository is priced as 900 KB of work instead of as a second full scan.

 

Pricing is per repository, not per game. A game with a client repo and a server repo keeps a separate model of each, and a change to one is never priced as a change to the other.

 

Sizing is free: ask for a quote first and you see the price, what changed, and the token estimate before any money moves. Scanning needs an admin role or above, because it spends the balance. Connecting a code host so that pushes can scan on their own is a step further and is owner only: a scan spends a quoted amount once, while a connected repository is standing permission to spend. Whether that connection is available at all depends on how the deployment you are using is configured, so treat a visible connect button as an offer rather than a promise.

 

If a run stops early on its token budget you pay for the source it actually read, at that size's tier and never more than you were quoted, and you keep the findings and notes it produced. If a run fails outright you are refunded in full and its notes are unwound, so the next scan is priced honestly as a first scan rather than as a cheap diff against a half-written model.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.content:
20. Playtest

 

## Send an AI persona through your build before a player does

 

Ravensight Playtest is a CLI you run against your own build. It hands your game to a handful of AI personas, each with a different way of playing, and brings back a written report per persona: what worked, what they got stuck on, and whether they would have kept playing. The personas' sessions land in the same dashboard as your real players, tagged so they never touch your real numbers unless you ask for them.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Before you start
documents.content:
### Before you start

 

You need Node 22 or later, a Ravensight game with an ingest key already set up, and a balance on your account. A playtest run spends from the same prepaid balance as everything else here: no card, no subscription, and nothing runs without balance to cover it.

 

Install the current runner

 

```
npm install --global ravensight-playtest
```

 

That puts the `ravensight-playtest` command on your path, and every example below runs it directly.

 

Registering a run spends money, so it needs an admin role or above. Reading past jobs, findings and reports needs only a read-only role, and writing a brief or marking a finding needs a member role.

 

Playwright is an optional dependency, so `login`, `check`, `init` and `brief` work on a machine with no browser installed; only a web-driver run asks for one. The credential store is optional too, which is why a machine with no keychain still installs cleanly.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Sign in and point it at a game
documents.content:
### Sign in and point it at a game

 

The CLI never asks for a password and never holds a model provider key. Signing in mints a short device code, which you approve from the dashboard rather than typing anything back into the terminal.

 

Sign in

 

```
ravensight-playtest login
```

 

This prints a short code and a link. Open the link, or go to [app.ravensight.io/cli](https://app.ravensight.io/cli) and enter the code yourself, then pick which of your games the CLI should be able to touch. The terminal picks up the approval on its own once you confirm it.

 

The token lands in your operating system's credential store: macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, libsecret on Linux. With none available it falls back to a file readable only by you, and says which store it used. For CI, set `RAVENSIGHT_TOKEN` and skip `login` entirely. `logout` revokes the token on the server and forgets it locally, and deliberately leaves a token that came from `RAVENSIGHT_TOKEN` alone, because that is probably a CI secret other jobs share. An org owner can revoke every token a member holds in that org at once from Settings.

 

A CLI token starts with `gt_cli_`, and only that kind works with the CLI, in `RAVENSIGHT_TOKEN` as well. An MCP token (`gt_mcp_`) is refused with a `401` that says so and tells you to run `ravensight-playtest login` for a CLI token. A game's ingest key (`gt_live_`) is refused with `403 ingest_key_not_allowed`.

 

Connect a project to a game

 

```
ravensight-playtest init --game <gameId>
```

 

Run this once per project. It writes a small local config file next to your code so every later command knows which game it is talking about.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Connect your build
documents.content:
### Connect your build

 

Ravensight Playtest plays web builds, in the cloud or on your own machine, and Godot projects on your own machine. With ravensight-playtest 0.12.0 or later it also plays native Android games on an emulator and native iOS games on the iOS Simulator, on your own machine; read [Mobile games](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-mobile) for what that needs. Native desktop builds are experimental and need an automation server you install and run yourself. Console builds need your own authorized tooling.

 

Choose a build type on the dashboard's Playtest page for its run command. The experimental desktop adapters, and a mobile setup you already run through your own automation server, talk to a local server that speaks the WebDriver protocol. Custom bridges exchange bounded game controls through JSON-RPC, with no model access to a shell. [Read the complete adapter setup and protocol guide](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest-adapters.txt).

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Which builds play where
documents.content:
### Which builds play where

 

A cloud playtest opens your build's HTML page in a browser on an isolated machine, so it plays web builds only. A local playtest runs on your own machine and plays web builds, Godot projects, and native Android and iOS builds on an emulator or simulator; for a native desktop build it has only the experimental adapters above. To play an exported web folder locally, pass `--build-dir` with the folder (CLI 0.7.6 or later): the CLI serves it with the headers engine exports need (WebAssembly, Brotli and gzip files, and the isolation a threaded build needs). `--build-url` still plays a build you serve yourself.

 

| Engine | Cloud playtest (upload a ZIP) | Local playtest (CLI) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Godot 4 | Web export, with or without threads. The entry file is its page, `index.html` or the name you exported it under. | The web export with `--build-dir`, or the project itself with `--driver godot_driver`. |
| Unity | Web build. Use the export settings in [Playtest a Unity game](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-unity). | The web build with `--build-dir`. An Android or iOS build plays on an emulator or simulator, as in [Mobile games](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-mobile). A desktop build only through the experimental `--driver unity_driver` adapter with your own automation server. |
| LÖVE | The [love.js](https://github.com/Davidobot/love.js) output, standard or compatibility mode. | The love.js output with `--build-dir`. A desktop build only through an experimental adapter: `--driver desktop_driver` with your own automation server, or a custom bridge. |
| JavaScript and HTML5 | The built site, with its HTML page as the entry file. | `--build-dir` or `--build-url`. |
| C++ | An Emscripten build: its page, JavaScript and `.wasm`, threaded or not. | The Emscripten build with `--build-dir`. A desktop build only through an experimental adapter: `--driver desktop_driver` with your own automation server, or a custom bridge. |
| Odin | A `js_wasm32` build with its page and `odin.js`. | The web build with `--build-dir`. A desktop build only through an experimental adapter: `--driver desktop_driver` with your own automation server, or a custom bridge. |
| Unreal | Not available: Unreal has no supported web export. | Not supported today. `--driver unreal_driver` is an experimental adapter that needs your own automation server. |
| iOS | Not available. Upload a web export instead. | A simulator build (`.app`) on the iOS Simulator, on a Mac with Xcode, with CLI 0.12.0 or later. See [Mobile games](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-mobile). |
| Android | Not available. Upload a web export instead. | An `.apk` on an Android emulator, on a computer with the Android SDK, with CLI 0.12.0 or later. See [Mobile games](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-mobile). |

 

A cloud upload that is a desktop, mobile or Unreal build is refused before anything is played, with the engine named and what to upload instead. An entry file that is a program or a package (such as `.exe`, `.apk` or `.ipa`) is refused before the validation hold is taken; any other such build is refused at its archive check and the hold is returned after cleanup. No playtest is quoted or charged for a refused build.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Playtest a Unity game
documents.content:
### Playtest a Unity game

 

A Unity game is playtested as a web build: export it for the Web platform and play that folder locally, or upload it as a ZIP for a cloud playtest. Both run the same build in a browser.

 

**Export settings.** In Player Settings for the Web platform:

 

- **Compression Format**: Disabled or Gzip. The local and cloud runs also serve Brotli files with their encoding, but a Brotli Unity export has not been checked end to end, so Disabled or Gzip is the safer choice.
 
- **Decompression Fallback**: off.
 
- **Data Caching**: off.
 
- **WebGL Template**: Default or Minimal, so the export has its `index.html` at the top of the folder. Zip the folder's contents, so `index.html` is at the root of the ZIP.
 
- **Resolution**: a canvas around 960 by 600, so it fits the 1280 by 800 browser window the playtester uses.
 
- **Run In Background**: on, so the game keeps running when the page loses focus.
 
- **No requests to other sites.** The page may load only its own files. A cloud playtest has no network, and a build that loads anything from a web address is refused at its archive check.

 

Play the exported folder on your own machine

 

```
ravensight-playtest run --driver playwright_web --build-dir ./Builds/WebGL
```

 

Check the ZIP before a cloud upload (free, nothing is uploaded)

 

```
ravensight-playtest build preflight ./my-game-web.zip --format web
```

 

Then upload it with `ravensight-playtest build upload` or from the dashboard, and start a run as in [Cloud playtests](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-cloud). The limits for a cloud upload:

 

- One standard ZIP under 4 GiB, with no ZIP64, at most 5,000 files and folders at most 16 deep.
 
- Up to 4 GiB unpacked. The unpacked size picks the smallest tier that holds it: Jam up to 50 MiB, Small up to 250 MiB, Medium up to 1 GiB, Large up to 4 GiB.
 
- The dashboard uploads a ZIP of up to 300 MiB; a larger one goes through `ravensight-playtest build upload`, which sends it in parts.
 
- The entry page is an HTML file of at most 64 MB.

 

**Everything is inside the canvas.** Unity draws its whole interface inside one canvas, so the page has no buttons or text the playtester can read directly; it plays from screenshots, as it does any canvas game. The run's own win check reads win wording in the page's text, so a win shown only inside the canvas is not detected by it. To tell the run your game is won, set `window.__ravensightWon = true` from a small `.jslib` plugin when the whole game is won. Play ends there, so set it only for the final win, not a level clear.

 

A jslib plugin, saved under Assets/Plugins/WebGL

 

```
mergeInto(LibraryManager.library, {
  RavensightMarkWon: function () { window.__ravensightWon = true; }
});
```

 

Call it from C# in the web build only

 

```
#if UNITY_WEBGL && !UNITY_EDITOR
[System.Runtime.InteropServices.DllImport("__Internal")]
private static extern void RavensightMarkWon();
#endif

void OnGameWon()
{
#if UNITY_WEBGL && !UNITY_EDITOR
    RavensightMarkWon();
#endif
}
```

 

A Unity web build keeps its saves where the address it is served from decides, so a save file is not placed for it: read `window.RavensightPlaytest.save` at boot instead (see *A save to start from* in [Cloud playtests](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-cloud)).

 

**What is not supported.** A native Unity desktop build cannot be playtested today. A native Unity Android or iOS build plays locally on an emulator or simulator, as in [Mobile games](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-mobile). The cloud accepts web builds only and refuses a native Unity build, and no playtest is charged for it. The CLI's `unity_driver` is an experimental adapter that needs an automation server you install and run yourself, and Ravensight does not provide one.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Mobile games
documents.content:
### Mobile games

 

A native mobile game plays on your own machine, on an Android emulator or the iOS Simulator, with ravensight-playtest 0.12.0 or later. Cloud playtests still need a web build: for a cloud run, export the game for the web as described below.

 

- **Android**: an installable `.apk` on an emulator, on a computer with the Android SDK, its emulator and platform tools.
 
- **iOS**: a simulator build (`.app`) on the iOS Simulator, on a Mac with Xcode. An App Store `.ipa` or a build for a physical iPhone is not a simulator build.
 
- **No physical devices.** Runs use an emulator or simulator only, so they do not measure performance on a real phone.

 

**Set up a device.** `ravensight-playtest device setup android` asks before it downloads the SDK parts it needs (about 1 to 2 GB) and creates one emulator for playtests; it never replaces an emulator you already have. `ravensight-playtest device setup ios` builds the small input helper the CLI uses on the simulator, with your installed Xcode. The first time, the simulator can need a visible window and Xcode automation permission. `ravensight-playtest device list` shows your emulators and simulators, and `device boot` and `device shutdown` start and stop one. Video needs `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` installed; `--no-record-video` needs neither.

 

Free checks: they install, open and close the app, with no job and no charge

 

```
ravensight-playtest check --driver android_driver --native-build ./game.apk --device emulator-5554
ravensight-playtest check --driver ios_driver --native-build ./Game.app --device YOUR_SIMULATOR_UDID
```

 

Play on an Android emulator; replace the path and the emulator serial

 

```
ravensight-playtest run --driver android_driver --native-build ./game.apk --device emulator-5554 --controller geri
```

 

Play on the iOS Simulator; replace the path and the simulator UDID

 

```
ravensight-playtest run --driver ios_driver --native-build ./Game.app --device YOUR_SIMULATOR_UDID --controller geri
```

 

The device is required: give its exact emulator serial, simulator UDID or name with `--device`, or save it in the project's configuration. `--package` (Android) and `--bundle-id` (iOS) check the app's identifier against the build; they cannot pick another installed app. `--portrait` is the default and `--landscape` asks for landscape. The usual price confirmation, brief and per-run budget apply.

 

**How a native run plays.** Geri plays, one persona at a time on the selected device; Freki and comparisons are not available for native builds. The game runs in real time: its timers keep counting while Geri decides, and the game cannot be paused between actions. Geri taps, double taps, long presses and drags in straight lines, and types text. Pinch and other two finger gestures are not available. On Android, the system Back key is available; on iOS, Geri uses the game's own navigation.

 

**Video and privacy.** The recording shows only the selected emulator or simulator display, without audio; keep private content off that display. Video stays on your machine unless you pass `--upload-video`. Reports and screenshots follow the usual upload flow. Use a test build with analytics turned off, or mark these sessions as synthetic in your game's SDK setup.

 

**A web export still helps.** When your engine exports for the web, a web build plays in the cloud and with Freki. It tests the game's logic and flow, not native touch feel, phone performance, every screen size or platform features such as purchases and notifications. For Unity, use the export settings in [Playtest a Unity game](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-unity).

 

**Your own automation server still works.** If you already run one, supply `--driver-config ./ravensight-driver.json` instead of `--native-build`; the two cannot be combined. That connection remains experimental.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Cloud playtests: one playtester per persona
documents.content:
### Cloud playtests: one playtester per persona

 

**Web builds only.** Upload a self-contained ZIP with its HTML entry page, JavaScript, WebAssembly and all other assets. It must work without external downloads, authentication services or multiplayer servers. APK, AAB, IPA, `.app` folders, desktop executables, engine projects and source code are not cloud-playtest builds. A mobile game's web export can be tested here; that tests the web build, not the native package. Native Android and iOS builds play locally, as in [Mobile games](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-mobile).

 

A cloud playtest plays your uploaded web build on our machines with one playtester per persona: **Geri and Freki play your game together**. Geri thinks: it reads each new screen, sets a goal and plans the next few inputs. Freki acts: it plays the routine steps of the plan and the repeats, and hands back to Geri when the screen surprises it. Each persona plays on its own cloud machine, at the same time as the others, and one report covers them all, with each persona's own report beside it.

 

- **Personas.** `fresh-eyes`, a first time player, is always included. Tick any others in the dashboard, or name them with `--personas`; each adds its own price to the quote, which updates as you choose.
 
- **Tiers.** Jam (builds under 50 MB, 5 minutes of play), Small (under 250 MB, 8 minutes), Medium (under 1 GB, 15 minutes) and Large (up to 4 GB, 30 minutes on a bigger machine). The default is the tier your build's unpacked size needs; a smaller one is refused before any hold or charge, with the build's real size and the tier to choose.
