The dashboard uploads a ZIP of up to 300 MB; a larger one, up to 4 GB, uploads with `ravensight-playtest build upload`, which sends it in parts.
 
- **Video.** A run of ten minutes or less saves one video. A longer run saves one part for each ten minutes it started, and the report plays them in order. Each is kept 90 days.
 
- **Play length.** Choose any length from the tier's own up to 120 minutes per persona. Geri's thinking budget and the action limit grow with it, and Geri's budget is spread over the whole run rather than spent in the first minutes.
 
- **Focus.** A start query or hash on your build (such as `?level=3`), up to five goals that go to the top of every persona's plan ("beat the first boss"), and up to five things to stay out of ("the settings menu"). They are plain text with no links, and the report shows them at the top.
 
- **A save to start from.** `--save <file>` on `hosted quote` and `hosted run` starts every persona from your save file, at most 1 MiB. `--save-target` says where your game reads it: `godot:user://saves/slot1.sav` for a Godot web export, `localstorage:<key>`, or `idbfs:/mount/path` for another engine's browser file storage. The save is placed there before the game loads. Without a target, or for a game that keeps its save somewhere else (a Unity web build does), the game reads the file itself from `window.RavensightPlaytest.save`, which has its `name`, `bytes` and a `url` to fetch. The dashboard does not upload a save yet.
 
- **The quote.** One line per persona and a total, reserved in full from your prepaid balance before anything starts. When the cloud is busy, each persona shows its own queue place and expected start; a funded run is queued, not refused.
 
- **Refunds.** Each persona settles on its own under the ordinary refund rules. A persona that never gets a machine is refunded in full. The Large tier carries a non-refundable setup fee, a separate line in the quote, kept even when that persona is refunded, unless it never got a machine.
 
- **A build too large for its tier.** If a persona runs out of memory on its machine, or its frame rate stays under 3 frames a second for most of a minute of play while the game is drawing, that persona stops early and the report says what was measured. It keeps the machine time and model spend it used plus the under-scope fee shown on the quote, the rest of its price is refunded, and the report names the tier to choose.

 

A cloud playtest with two more personas, focused

 

```
ravensight-playtest hosted run --personas speedrunner,completionist \
  --minutes 10 --start '?level=3' --focus "beat the first boss" \
  --avoid "the settings menu" --wait
```

 

This needs CLI 0.9.0 or later; a ZIP over 300 MB and `--save` need CLI 0.10.0. The dashboard's **Run in the Ravensight cloud** page offers the same choices, with the live total. Prices are in [Usage rates and limits](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/limits/).

 

To play your game where it already runs, on your staging or production site, instead of an uploaded build, see [Playtest a live URL](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest-live-url/).

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Read a cloud playtest report
documents.content:
### Read a cloud playtest report

 

Each persona's report has two lists. **Findings** are only what the run verified: the runner measured it (a control that did nothing when the page got the click, a script error, a crash, a blank screen), a check of the frame at that moment showed it, or a replay with no input showed the screen standing still. **Playtester impressions** are what the playtester felt and said that the run could not verify, in its own words: a matter of taste ("the icon is unclear") kept only when a check of the frame showed what it rests on, and its own liking. An opinion nothing the run saw supports is not kept, and a judgement of its own play ("too hard") is listed as a limit of the run. An impression can be wrong, and the report says so beside each one. What the frame or the run's record showed to be false is in neither list: it is listed with the reason under "Raised by the playtester, not confirmed".

 

- **Top issues.** The findings, each with its severity, its evidence (a screenshot or a time in the session video) and, where the persona said something, its own words. When there is none it says "None confirmed" and points to the lists below.
 
- **Playtester impressions.** Each impression with its step, the playtester's own words, the frame at that moment, its grade (the playtester's, except that a blocker the run's record does not support reads major, as a finding's would) and a note saying why it is not a finding. Impressions are never counted with the findings, never ranked, never put in what to fix first, and never kept as studio memory. The dashboard shows them after the findings, in a quieter list, and `report.json` carries them as `impressions`.
 
- **Checks on the findings.** Each issue is shown once against the frame at its moment and asked whether the frame shows it (for something the playtester says the game did, whether the game is at fault), shows the opposite, or cannot tell, and the recorded inputs are played again with no model to see whether the same thing happens. A claim that nothing happens counts as reproduced only when the screen stayed still while game time ran for two seconds with no input. A replay that could not test a claim says "not verifiable", and a check that was not made says so: neither is counted as passed.
 
- **Raised by the playtester, not confirmed.** What the playtester said that is neither a finding nor an impression, each with the reason: the run's own record or the frame contradicts it (it called the game stuck while the screen changed, or said something was missing that the run read on screen), the game was doing what it is meant to, it did not come back when tried again, it states a fact about the screen that nothing confirmed, or it is an opinion nothing the run saw supports. A false statement of fact is never relabelled as an impression. None of these is a finding about the game.
 
- **Test charter.** The areas to test, the risks for this kind of game and what a failure would look like, written before testing from the brief and the first screens. About one plan in four is a testing turn once play is under way, and the charter says how many turns each area got; an area that got none is listed as not tested.
 
- **What was and was not tested.** A table of the techniques a hired tester uses, each marked tested or not with the reason: rapid input on one control, every control play never pressed, controls out of order, text fields given nothing and far too much, a menu left and entered again, pause and resume, opposite keys held together, the edges of the play area, text cut off, sound output, input while the game loads, then focus loss, a resize, a mashed key, idling, the browser's Back button and a reload. These probes are scripted and ask no model. It then lists how a bug was recognised (script errors, a crash or a blank screen, a soft lock, the frame rate, the game's own numbers, placeholder text, a control that does nothing) and the screens and controls the run reached and did not. Not tested never means healthy.
 
- **Limits: What this run didn't cover.** Where the session never got to, and what the playtester could not read, press or confirm. Read it before the findings.

 

The job's own page has a Report tab beside the written reports. It rebuilds the same run, with no model call, as a list of what to fix first, each finding at its moment in the video, its checks, and the inputs that lead to it.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Record and compare local playthroughs
documents.content:
### Record and compare local playthroughs

 

A local run can also be played by Geri alone or by Freki alone, or by both separately for comparison. These options exist for evaluation and are no longer listed in `--help`; a cloud playtest is always the combined playtester above. **Geri** reads each screen and chooses every action itself. **Freki** proposes up to three actions on each screen and lets a separate selector pick one. Freki proposes and never decides: when the selector is unsure or cannot be reached, CLI 0.10.0 plays Freki's most likely candidate, or else the first action proposed for that screen, and the step log says which. Both play the same persona from the same brief at the same price.

 

These options require CLI 0.5.0 or later and a compatible server; the `geri` and `freki` flag values below need CLI 0.8.0. The dashboard's local setup reads the server's current CLI release and playtester capabilities before offering a comparison. Install the runner it names; the CLI checks support again before registration or charge. Web and Godot builds support this flow. For cloud playtests of web builds, see [Which builds play where](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-engines). The existing hosted Linux headless simulation flow and its separate quote are unchanged.

 

Compare one persona with Geri and Freki, keeping video local

 

```
ravensight-playtest run --driver playwright_web \
  --build-url http://localhost:3000 --personas <persona-slug> \
  --compare-with freki --record-video
```

 

Choose a persona from your game's pack. Each selected persona gets two independent paid playthroughs and two reports, one with Geri and one with Freki. Two personas mean four runs. The server quotes all runs together at the existing per-run prices, and the CLI asks you to confirm that total before charging your prepaid balance. At the current standard price, one persona with both playtesters costs $12.80 for Playtest, or $16.40 with `--long`. Freki's selections are included in its run; comparing the reports does not add a model call or fee.

 

For a single explicit playtester, use `--controller geri` or `--controller freki` instead of `--compare-with freki`. Do not combine those flags. Omitting both preserves the configured default. An unavailable playtester is refused before charge, rather than silently replaced.

 

Record a rendered Godot project

 

```
ravensight-playtest run --driver godot_driver \
  --godot-project ./your-game --personas <persona-slug> \
  --compare-with freki --record-video
```

 

Godot needs the Ravensight addon, a rendered viewport and local FFmpeg. Web video records the selected Playwright page as WebM; Godot samples the selected viewport and creates an MP4. Neither records audio, your desktop or unrelated windows. Browser recording stays on the selected page and same-origin top-level navigation. A headless Godot process has no rendered scene to record.

 

`--record-video` keeps video on your computer. `--upload-video` also records and explicitly opts in to sending it to this game's dashboard. Alternatively, review a local recording first and upload it later:

 

```
ravensight-playtest upload <jobId> --video
```

 

Reports and screenshots still follow the normal upload flow when video upload is off. A persona run also uploads its step log (`transcript.jsonl`: the inputs sent, what each screen showed and the persona's notes) so the dashboard can show the evidence report, and it is kept 90 days. This applies to projects set up before CLI 0.10.0 too. To keep it on your machine, set `"uploads": { "step_log": false }` in `.ravensight/config.json` or pass `--no-upload-step-log`. Keep real credentials and unrelated private content out of the test scene. Uploaded videos use existing game-scoped access, short-lived playback links and 90-day retention. A local-only recording does not appear in the dashboard's Recording tab.

 

Capture is bounded to 15 minutes, 1280 by 720 and 200 MiB per run, within the existing 500 MiB total artifact limit. A graceful stop or crash may leave partial video; forced termination or machine loss may prevent finalization. Missing video and incomplete reports remain missing or partial. They do not become successful playthroughs.

 

On the job page, select each playtester's playthrough for its separate report. Open **Recording** for uploaded video and supported finding timestamps; **Screenshots** is separate. A comparison stays incomplete if either report is incomplete. Each playtester starts a fresh game process or browser session, but saved game progress and randomness may differ. Use the same build, persona, goals and reset or seed settings where supported, and treat shared findings as evidence to review, not proof of identical starting state.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Write the brief
documents.content:
### Write the brief

 

Before the first run, a persona needs to know what your game is and what you actually want to learn. The quick brief asks for three things: your goals for the session, what would count as success, and how to get the build running, meaning the controls and how to start it.

 

```
ravensight-playtest brief
```

 

Four fields make a brief complete: at least one goal, what success looks like, how the game is controlled, and how to start it. The brief is versioned, so every save keeps the version before it and you can see what changed between runs. If someone else saved a newer version while you were editing, the CLI tells you rather than overwriting it. A job registered with an incomplete brief is refused, except a game-profile-only run, which does not need one. `brief --show` prints the current one, `--open` hands you the dashboard form instead, and `--from <file>` reads the fields from JSON for an unattended setup.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Check, then run
documents.content:
### Check, then run

 

`check` confirms the CLI is signed in, your token is valid, the game is visible to it, your balance covers what you are about to ask for, and that anything the run needs locally, such as Godot or a browser, is where it expects. Run it any time something seems off, and it costs nothing.

 

```
ravensight-playtest check
```

 

`run` is the one that spends money. It prints the price before charging anything: how many persona runs, whether a game profile is included, and the total against your balance. Nothing is debited until you confirm that number, and if the price has moved since you last checked, the CLI shows you the new one instead of silently charging it.

 

```
ravensight-playtest run
```

 

Unless your project config or `--personas` names others, a run uses one persona, `fresh-eyes`, a first time player. One job allows up to 100 persona/playtester runs; a comparison counts each playtester separately. Past eight runs, the price comes with a note about the clock: a job has 90 minutes of wall time in total and one run can take up to 15 of them, so the later runs in a very large job may never get to play. Nothing is lost if they do not, because a run that did not play is refunded when the job settles; split it into two jobs if you want everything played. Asking twice for the same persona, or for one this game does not have, is refused before anything is charged.

 

`--driver` chooses between the web and Godot drivers, with `--build-url` or `--godot-project` naming the target, `--concurrency` setting how many personas play at once (two by default, while Geri and Freki comparisons run sequentially, and `check` recommends a number for your machine), and `--max-actions` capping one persona's turns. From CLI 0.10.0 a web or Godot run keeps a silent video on your machine by default; `--no-record-video` turns it off. Video is sent only with `--upload-video`. The step log (`transcript.jsonl`: the inputs sent, what each observation read, the persona's notes and the checks made on its findings) uploads by default, including for projects set up before CLI 0.10.0, because the evidence report in the dashboard is built from it; it is kept 90 days. To keep it on your machine, set `"uploads": { "step_log": false }` in `.ravensight/config.json` or pass `--no-upload-step-log`. `--dry-upload` prints every file and byte that would be sent and sends nothing. `--json` and `--yes` are the pair CI wants, since a confirmation prompt with no terminal counts as no.

 

CLI 0.10.0 gives the persona a full set of inputs on web and Godot builds: drags, right, middle and double clicks, a held mouse button, hover, the scroll wheel, held keys that repeat, chords, timed key sequences, and dropdowns and sliders. `--phone` plays a web build on a phone sized screen (390 by 844) with touch and no mouse, and a web game that reads a gamepad is offered a virtual one. An input a driver does not have is refused by name and listed as a limit of the runner, never as a finding.

 

After play, a web or Godot run makes edge checks and tester probes with no model call: focus loss, resizes, rapid input, a short idle and a reload or second start on the game's save, then, on a web build, fast clicks, untried buttons, empty and oversized text, pause and resume and opposite keys (a Godot game gets the four a keyboard can make: rapid input, opposite keys, the edges and pause). A measured problem is a finding with a screenshot. `--no-edge-pass` turns both off. A run then plays its findings' recorded inputs again with no model, in a second browser or a second Godot, and says whether each came back; `--no-replay` skips it. Every report ends with what was and was not tested, kept by the runner, and a control that was never tried is listed as not tested, never as working.

 

`ravensight-playtest profile` is the other billed command: it has a persona read your codebase alongside the brief, with the same price-then-confirm step, and is priced and refunded the same way a persona run is.

 

Exit codes are meant for CI. 0 is success, 1 a failure, 2 a budget exceeded with partial results written and uploaded, 3 a failed environment check, 4 a failed authentication, 5 a model error after retries, and 10 canceled. Treating 2 as a success with a warning is usually what you want.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Fix a finding
documents.content:
### Fix a finding

 

Attempt a fix on a branch

 

```
ravensight-playtest fix <jobId>/<label>
```

 

A fix is one attempt at the smallest change that removes one finding, made on a branch in your own checkout, for $18.60. The CLI checks your repository first, refusing a dirty tree unless you pass `--allow-dirty`, then creates a branch (`--branch` names your own), plans the change against actual files, edits only those, and replays the persona that found the problem against your edited working tree so the server can judge whether the same failure came back. `--no-verify` skips that replay and `--max-actions` caps the edit loop. Nothing under `addons/`, `.godot/` or `.ravensight/` is ever edited.

 

It never commits and never pushes. What you get is a branch, the files it changed with their line counts, the verdict, and the exact command to open a pull request. You read the diff and decide.

 

Two outcomes cost nothing: a fix that concluded the right edit was no edit, and a finding that turned out to be the game working as designed. Both refund the whole $18.60 when the job settles, and the ledger names which one it was.

 

A fix attempt does send source to the model: the files it reads, and the edits it proposes, go through Ravensight's metered proxy, which keeps how much each call used and what it cost, never the text. What it uploads to Ravensight is the changeset summary (the branch, the changed paths with their line counts, and the verdict) and the pull request text, never the diff.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: When something stops halfway
documents.content:
### When something stops halfway

 

A run that was interrupted, by a sleeping machine, a crashed build or your own Ctrl-C, is picked back up by `resume`. It keeps the runs that finished, replays the rest, and never charges twice: the registration is replayed under the job's own idempotency key, which answers with the stored job rather than pricing a new one. `resume` with no job id lists the jobs this project has a journal for, and `--status` reports without restarting anything.

 

```
ravensight-playtest resume
ravensight-playtest upload <job>
```

 

`upload` drains whatever finished locally but did not finish uploading. It is safe to run repeatedly, because each file is matched by checksum and one already sent is skipped. After one online fetch the content pack is cached and verified by hash, so a run survives the network going away for everything except the model calls themselves; uploads and progress reports queue and flush when the server is reachable again.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Get a full run
documents.content:
### Get a full run

 

A run is charged whether it covered your game or stalled on its second screen. A run comes back short for five reasons: the model budget runs out early on heavy screens, the playtester cannot read or press something, it stops before the session is over, the brief does not say how to start or which choice to make, or nobody asked for a video. Work through this list before the first paid run.

 

1. Run `ravensight-playtest check` and fix every failed row. It is free.
 
1. In the brief, write how to start as a menu path, and name every choice on the way: the faction, character, mode or difficulty to pick. A playtester that has to guess may pick the wrong one.
 
1. List every input and what it does, including the one that moves time on, such as End Turn or Next.
 
1. Give three to six success criteria, one per line, each something a screen can show. With only one, the session may end when it is met.
 
1. List known issues and anything you did on purpose, so the run does not spend actions reporting them back to you.
 
1. Put text on every button. Give an icon or a coloured region a named node with a label inside it, and give web controls visible text or an `aria-label`.
 
1. In a Godot game, add a node to the `ravensight_state` group with a `_ravensight_state()` method that returns the screen, the chosen faction or character, the turn and the score. The playtester reads it with every screen, so it can confirm a choice took effect.
 
1. If the part worth testing is behind a sign-up or a long intro, add a `test_account` to the brief file, or a level select or debug start, and say so under how to start.
 
1. Ship a font that covers your game's language and set it as the project font. Text drawn as boxes is reported as a broken game.
 
1. Keep the video. CLI 0.10.0 records one on your machine by default for a web or Godot run; pass `--upload-video` to send it too. With an older CLI, pass `--record-video`.
 
1. Use `--long` when screens are heavy or the goal is far in. It doubles the actions and the time and raises the AI budget from $0.90 to $1.50, for $8.20 where a standard run is $6.40. For a set play length, use `--tier` and `--minutes` instead.

 

After the run, read "What this run didn't cover" in each report before the findings. It lists where the session never got to and what the playtester could not read, press or confirm. Fix those, then run again.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: While a run plays
documents.content:
### While a run plays

 

Each persona plays your build for as long as its budget allows, then writes a report: a markdown write-up, structured findings with severities and repro steps, and the screenshots it took along the way. Those upload automatically as each run finishes, and appear on the job's page in the dashboard.

 

A persona plays through your own Ravensight SDK, so its session writes real events into your events table, exactly like a player's would, tagged `synthetic`. Every reader in the dashboard, the analyst, `run_sql`, the rollups and your own MCP tools excludes those rows by default, so a pack of personas running overnight never moves your retention or your funnel numbers. Change the **Real players** select on Overview, Player insights or Events to **Real + AI personas** or **AI personas only** when you want to look at them on purpose, on their own or alongside real players. Those are the three pages that carry it.

 

A web build driven through Playwright has no SDK of its own to play through, so the CLI emits that session itself and needs the game's ingest key to do it: put it in `.ravensight/config.json` as `ingest_key`, or export `RAVENSIGHT_INGEST_KEY` for the run. Without one the run still completes and reports; it just sends no telemetry. A Godot build talks to the SDK it already ships, which carries its own key.

 

To check what one run's session actually sent, open the job in the dashboard and expand **Events** on that run's card. Your own tools can read the same list with the CLI token, and it is never charged:

 

```
GET /api/v1/playtest/cli/jobs/<job>/runs/<run>/events
```

 

It answers up to 500 events in time order, each with its time, name, the `synthetic` flag and its top-level properties, plus the run's session id. A game server session that joined the run's session counts as the run's too. The token needs the `playtest:read` scope, and a job outside the token's games reads as not found.

 

A run that never gets far enough to produce anything useful, or ends early with no findings, is not kept at its price. It is refunded in full when the cause is ours or it used no AI time, and otherwise billed at what it cost us, as "What it costs" below explains. You are billed for runs that happened, not for runs you paid to start.

 

One limit applies once the model has been used. An account gets 20 refunds of a persona run that used model time in any 30 days, and 5 of a game profile. Past that the unit is kept, and the job says so. Work that used no model time always comes back.

 

Every run the API returns says where its refund stands, in four fields. `refund_expected` is true before the job settles when the run has not earned its unit, so settling would give it back. `refund_expected_cents` is the amount that would come back. `refunded` is true only after the job has settled and the credit for this run has landed on your balance. `refunded_cents` is the amount credited for this run: 0 when nothing came back, and null when the run was refunded but its price is set on the job rather than on the run.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Findings, marks, and what to remember
documents.content:
### Findings, marks, and what to remember

 

Open a finished job from the dashboard, or jump straight to it from the terminal:

 

```
ravensight-playtest open <job>
ravensight-playtest review <job>
```

 

Each finding can be marked as you go through it: confirmed real, intended behavior, a duplicate of another finding, one you could not reproduce, wrongly rated on severity, or too vague to act on. Marking something **intended** offers to remember it, and remembering it turns it into a design-intent note attached to your game. The next brief a persona reads includes that note, and the next run's findings suppress the same thing again under "suppressed as intended" instead of reporting it as new.

 

A fix job's own page shows a Fix card above its runs: the finding it targeted, the branch, the files it changed, and the verify verdict in words. Its "Copy pull request text" button reads the same pull request body the CLI printed and copies it, so the terminal is not the only place to get it from.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Simulation Runner: mechanics and balance
documents.content:
### Simulation Runner: mechanics and balance

 

Simulation Runner is a Playtest mode using the existing Ravensight API and prepaid balance. A local headless adapter runs bounded episodes with random, scripted or scored strategies. Persona playtests remain the mode for observing the screen, controls and player experience.

 

Run Simulation Runner on macOS or Linux, including a Linux environment under WSL. Native Windows execution is rejected before purchase because process-tree cancellation is not supported there yet. The adapter is trusted local code running with your account's permissions, not a sandbox.

 

One batch uses the same standard `playtest_run` price as one persona run (32 AI units, $6.40, paid from prepaid balance). No monthly allowance or event-meter charge replaces that payment. The CLI quotes before registration; an unproductive failed batch is refunded. Local replay is free debugging and uploads no new server report.

 

```
ravensight-playtest simulate --config simulation.json --driver-config bridge.json
ravensight-playtest simulate --resume path/to/state.json
ravensight-playtest simulation-replay path/to/trace.json --driver-config bridge.json
```

 

Example `simulation.json`:

 

```
{
  "version": 1,
  "seed": "balance-2026",
  "runs": 1000,
  "max_steps": 100,
  "workers": 4,
  "strategies": [
    { "name": "random", "policy": "random" },
    { "name": "aggressive", "policy": "scored" },
    { "name": "opening", "policy": "scripted", "actions": ["buy", "end-turn"] }
  ]
}
```

 

Use the existing `cli_stdio` bridge configuration to launch your own game process. The example paths below are local placeholders. You may instead set `driver_config` in the simulation file to a path relative to that file.

 

```
{
  "command": "/absolute/path/to/game",
  "args": ["--headless"],
  "cwd": "/absolute/project"
}
```

 

The engine-agnostic adapter exchanges newline-delimited JSON over standard input/output. Implement `simulation.start` and `simulation.step`, expose legal actions and game-defined action scores for scored strategies, and return a `state_hash` for replay comparison. Scripted action lists stay local. A seed alone cannot guarantee identical results: your adapter must seed its own randomness and control nondeterministic state. See the [Playtest CLI installation guide](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-install); use the matching CLI protocol and adapter examples before running a paid batch.

 

Each protocol message is one JSON line. The runner supplies an episode seed and strategy name. A minimal exchange looks like this (your adapter supplies the actual state hashes):

 

```
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"simulation.start","params":{"version":1,"seed":"episode-seed","strategy":"aggressive","max_steps":100}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"done":false,"state_hash":"state-0","actions":[{"id":"buy","scores":{"aggressive":3}},{"id":"end-turn","scores":{"aggressive":1}}],"metrics":{"coins":4}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"simulation.step","params":{"action":"buy"}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"result":{"done":true,"state_hash":"state-1","actions":[],"outcome":"win","metrics":{"coins":2}}}
```

 

Strategy names use lowercase slugs of up to 64 characters (letters, digits, underscores and hyphens, starting with a letter). Metric values must be finite and between −1015 and 1015. Only terminal, completed episodes contribute outcomes and final metrics. Keep standard output for protocol messages and send diagnostics to standard error. The CLI includes a runnable `examples/simulation/economy.mjs` adapter. Use your game rules and legal actions in its place; this protocol does not simulate a game from a design document by itself.

 

A batch allows up to 10,000 episodes, 10,000 steps per episode, 16 workers and 16 strategies, additionally bounded by one million total actions and 15 minutes. At most 10 selected traces stay local for replay. A probe initializes the protocol only; it does not run a free batch. Resume uses the existing paid job rather than registering a second batch.

 

Replay checks captured state hashes, completion flags, outcomes and metrics. `fully_replayed: true` means the complete recorded window matched, which may still end at a step limit rather than a terminal game. A size-capped or failed trace can instead report `matched_prefix: true` with `fully_replayed: false`. When a failed action was captured, replay retries it; `failure_reproduced: true` requires the same sanitized protocol error. A successful retry is a divergence, not a reproduced failure. An initial-start failure has no prefix to verify, and an exhausted or illegal strategy can verify only its captured prefix.

 

The Playtest job page shows requested, completed, failed and truncated counts, total steps, outcomes per strategy, and metric count/minimum/maximum/mean. Metric names and units come from your game. A truncated episode reached a limit and must not be read as a completed win or loss. Comparing strategies can suggest questions to investigate; it does not establish that an exploit exists or automatically recommend a balanced design.

 

Only bounded summaries are sent to Playtest: sanitized strategy names/policies, seed, config hash, counts and metrics. Local commands, paths, action scripts and raw per-tick state are not uploaded as simulation summaries. This evidence stays separate from real-player analytics. Your agent can find it with `list_playtest_jobs` and read it with `get_playtest_report`; it is not automatically promoted into studio findings or memory.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Hosted Linux simulations
documents.content:
### Hosted Linux simulations

 

Upload a Linux x86_64 headless ZIP from [Playtest](https://app.ravensight.io/playtest), wait for validation, then request and accept a price quote. Hosted runs use a repeatable random strategy and return a simulation report. This mode does not include graphical gameplay, Geri or Freki runs, video recording, or human player feedback.

 

**Qualify once with $10 in verified prepaid funding on the studio owner's account.** Confirmed prepaid payments totaling $10 qualify the account. This is usable credit, not a setup fee or an extra charge. After qualifying, you can spend the credit down below $10; each new hosted request needs the start balance on its quote (see [Starting a Labs job](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#labs-start-balance)), and only the amount due is charged. If funds are short, the owner can choose **Add funds** in [Billing](https://app.ravensight.io/settings/billing), then return to Playtest and refresh. Included monthly AI units do not pay for hosted runs. A valid paid build deposit from before this rollout remains usable for that build's first run when its remaining quote is covered; new uploads and later runs still need the initial verified funding.

 

Uploading reserves **$0.49** from that balance for the build's first hosted run. The quote shows one total, the Playtest cost, then any build deposit already held and the remaining amount due. The held deposit is credited once toward that first run, so it is not a second fee. For the current standard $6.09 quote, a held $0.49 deposit leaves $5.60 due. A later run has its own full quote; always review the amount shown before confirming.

 

Known never-started runs, hosted-service failures and customer-build failures refund hosted compute. Cancellation after confirmed execution start retains the $0.49 compute charge. The Playtest portion follows its existing refund policy. An unused build deposit is returned after the build is deleted or expires and safe cleanup is confirmed; pending or unknown work must be reconciled before a refund is final.

 

**The time limit.** A hosted run or comparison that reaches its time limit is refunded in full, machine and comparison charge alike. The quote states this before you accept, and a purchase keeps the terms it was accepted under.

 

A busy service does not refuse paid work. An accepted run is charged, waits in line for a machine, oldest first, with its place and expected start on the run, and starts on its own; a run that never gets a machine within six hours, or is canceled or loses its build while it waits, is refunded in full. Funding does not bypass upload limits: an exhausted allowance requires waiting for the stated limit to clear, not another payment. You can still view existing runs, request cancellation and delete builds when new work is blocked. Only studio owners and administrators can submit hosted work; funding uses the owner's billing account.

 

The initial hosted release permits one active run and ten new run admissions per UTC day across the service. Validation is limited to two attempts per studio and ten across the service per UTC day. Upload grants are also bounded: eight grants or 512 MiB per studio, within 64 grants or 4 GiB across the service. Upload allowances are cumulative and do not reset daily; deletion does not replenish them.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: How a persona plays your build
documents.content:
### How a persona plays your build

 

For a web build, a persona plays through a driver built on Playwright: it sees the running page, clicks and types the same way a person would, and reads back whatever your game reports.

 

For a Godot project, the CLI copies your project into a temporary directory, injects a driver addon into that copy only, and launches it there. Your project on disk is never modified. If you implement `_ravensight_state()` on a node in the `ravensight_state` group, the driver reads it too, so a finding can cite the exact level, menu, or scene your persona was looking at. See "Playtest mode" in the Godot SDK guide for the details.

 

The addon only ever activates deliberately. It needs a flag on the command line or an environment variable, it binds to localhost and nothing else, it demands a per-run token before it will answer any other call, it takes one client at a time, and it frees itself the moment any of that fails. A release export does not contain it unless the preset asks for it by feature tag.

 

**Do not run a persona UI playtest of a Godot game headless.** Headless Godot routes no synthesized mouse or GUI input, so a click on a button does nothing and nothing takes keyboard focus. That makes headless a smoke test mode rather than a playtest mode for anything with a user interface. The Simulation Runner above instead calls your explicit mechanics adapter and does not synthesize GUI input. On a machine with no display, run a windowed Godot under a virtual framebuffer such as Xvfb instead. The CLI prints this in the run's console log when it launches headless.

 

Video from the Godot driver is a sequence of frames rather than a container, so stitching it into one file needs ffmpeg, and ffmpeg stays optional.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: What leaves your machine
documents.content:
### What leaves your machine

 

Your build is never uploaded, and a persona run never sends your source code. The prompts a persona reads, including your brief, and what it observes while playing transit Ravensight on the way to the model provider named on the [subprocessors page](https://www.ravensight.io/legal/subprocessors/), metered but not kept. A game profile or a fix attempt also sends the source files it reads, the same way and equally not kept. Your art and audio files never leave at all: see [Your own art and audio](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#labs-assets) for exactly what a feature sends about them. What uploads to Ravensight is exactly the reports, screenshots, and bookkeeping named on a fixed allowlist, nothing else. The dashboard's [What leaves your machine](https://app.ravensight.io/playtest/what-leaves-your-machine) page lists that allowlist against the code that enforces it, so it never drifts out of date with what actually ships.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Retention
documents.content:
### Retention

 

Reports, findings, marks, and briefs are kept for as long as the game exists. Session video, which is opt-in, and a persona run's step log are kept for 90 days and then dropped.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: What it costs
documents.content:
### What it costs

 

Playtest spends from your prepaid balance, the same one as everything else on this page. Each persona run is currently $6.40, a long persona run is currently $8.20, a game profile is currently $8.40, and a fix attempt is currently $18.60. Each price covers everything the work can cost at its limits, from the models to storing and serving its screenshots, video and reports, doubled, plus a margin of at least a dollar, and the quote shows it as one total. The price is charged when a job registers and refunded, up to the limit below, for any run that never produced a report, or that ended early (out of budget, out of time, an error, or stuck behind a blocker) with no findings, so what you keep paying for is what you actually got. A run that played to the end and found nothing is a clean pass and is charged.

 

A thin run is billed at what it cost us. When a persona run ends with fewer than 15 actions and the game is not the reason (the AI budget ran out, the playtester met a tool or driver limit, or it stopped early with nothing blocking it), you are charged only what the run cost us to run: its AI spend and its storage and transfer, rounded up to the cent. The rest of the price is refunded when the job finishes, and the run says why it was thin and what to try next. A run the game itself cut short, such as a blocker the persona reported with evidence or a persona that quit in character, is charged in full, because that run did its job. So is a finished tiny game: when the persona reaches the goal in a few actions and the run's report confirms the goal was met, you got what you asked for.

 

A run that did not earn its price is billed the same way when it still used AI time: a run of fewer than five actions, a run that ended early and found nothing, or a run that failed on the game's side and still left a report. You are charged what it cost us and the rest is refunded, with the reason on the run. It still comes back in full when the cause is ours: a failure of the AI provider or of our service that our servers recorded on the run, one of our own limits stopping the run before any play, or no report produced. A run that stops on an error on your machine, such as a driver or tool failure, is billed at what it cost us like any other run that did not earn its price. A run that used no AI time also comes back in full. An account gets 20 runs billed at cost in 30 days, counting both kinds; past that a run is kept at its price and says so.

 

A long run, `ravensight-playtest run --long`, is for a game whose first screen is heavy. It gets $1.50 of AI budget where a standard run gets $0.90, twice the actions and twice the wall clock, for $8.20 where a standard run is $6.40, and the price is quoted and confirmed exactly like a standard one. `check` on a web build measures the first screen and suggests `--long` with both prices when it is heavy; it never charges anything.

 

A local run can also play on one of the cloud tiers' allowances: `ravensight-playtest run --tier medium --minutes 30` gives every persona the Medium tier's model budget and action count for thirty minutes, on your own machine. Each tier has its own shortest length (Jam 5, Small 8, Medium 15, Large 30 minutes) and a local run may go up to 240. The price is quoted and confirmed like any other, for example $5.60 for Jam at 5 minutes and $16.20 for Medium at 30. `--focus` and `--avoid` give every persona goals to put first and things to stay out of, and `--start` opens a web build at a query or hash.

 

A fix attempt includes the persona replay that verifies it, and is refunded in full when the fix changed nothing, the finding turned out to be design intent, or the game did not boot for the verify replay (up to twice in any 30 days per account, with CLI 0.6.0 or later, which is what reports it).

 

An account gets 5 refunds in any 30 days of a fix attempt that used model time, and a cancel or any other failure counts the same as those answers. Past that the attempt is kept and the job says so. An attempt that used no model time always comes back.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Or fix it with your own agent over MCP
documents.content:
### Or fix it with your own agent over MCP

 

If you would rather your own coding agent make the change than run a fix attempt, it can read the same findings. With an MCP token (see [Analytics MCP](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/mcp/)), your own coding agent can find the job with `list_playtest_jobs`, list its findings with `list_playtest_findings`, read the full report with `get_playtest_report`, then edit the code and open a pull request itself, exactly as it would for any other change. Ravensight never writes to your repository: those three tools are read-only, and everything from there is your agent working in your own checkout with your own tools.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Starting a Labs job
documents.content:
### Starting a Labs job

 

Fix v2, Validate changes, Build a feature, Create a game and hosted runs each ask two things of an account before anything is charged.

 

- At least $10 of top-ups over the account's lifetime. A promotional balance does not count, and spending the money does not undo it. Without it, a fix runs as an ordinary fix.
 
- A start balance: the price of the whole plan plus 25 percent, at least $2 extra, rounded up to a whole dollar. A $18.60 Fix v2 needs $24.00, and Validate changes at three runs a side, $52.80, needs $66.00.

 

Only the price is charged. The extra stays in your balance, so a refund that lands when the job settles does not leave you stranded before you can try again. The CLI and hosted quotes show the figure before you confirm. An ordinary persona run, game profile or fix starts on its price alone.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Create a game (Labs, Experimental)
documents.content:
### Create a game (Labs, Experimental)

 

Create a game starts a small playable 2D Godot prototype from a brief, on your own machine. It is Experimental: it may not produce a game you want, so read the design before you approve it and read the code before you ship it. It is off until the platform switches it on, and only an owner or admin can start one. Ravensight never holds or writes your source, and nothing is pushed.

 

```
npx ravensight-playtest create "A keeper walks a dark hall and lights each lamp in turn" --name "Lantern Sweep" --milestones 3 --size medium
# read the design and approve it on the plan's page, then, from the project folder:
npx ravensight-playtest create <job-id>
```

 

**What it costs.** You declare how many milestones to buy and the largest size each may be. The account must have added at least $10 in top-ups, the balance has to reach the plan's start balance (see [Starting a Labs job](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#labs-start-balance)), and the CLI shows both before you confirm. Part of it is charged at the start, for the design, the scaffold and one persona run. Each milestone is then an ordinary [Build a feature](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#labs-feature) job, charged when it starts, with that feature's own refund rules. The balance is checked, not held, so a milestone your balance can no longer cover stops there. The Labs page states the current price.

 

**The design.** The first command makes a new game, with its key in a file git ignores, and writes a game design with a milestone list, core loop first. It is saved among your [design documents](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/design-studio/). A person approves or rejects it on the plan's page. Rejecting it gives the whole charge back, and so does a brief the model declines, within the refund limit below. There is no editor: to change a design, reject it and start again from a better brief.

 

**The scaffold.** A Godot 4 2D project with the public Ravensight SDK unmodified, a key loader, a player opt-out in its settings, build-time key injection for a public build, events that always set `rs_kind`, and a `_ravensight_state()` node a playtest reads. It is checked in Godot to import and start before the charge for it is kept. Every visual is a placeholder primitive. Studios bring their own art and audio: nothing is generated. The first command says where the files go in the new project, `assets` or the folder you name with `--assets-dir`. Put them there before you carry on, and each milestone can use them, as in [Your own art and audio](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#labs-assets).

 

**Milestones.** One at a time, each on its own branch, landing on `main` when its test scenarios pass. The next is bought only when the last validated, and the run stops at the count you declared, whatever the design lists. A milestone that does not validate stops the run: its branch holds the attempt, and running the command again tries it once more, which uses up another declared milestone if the attempt kept its charge.

 

**Playable.** When every declared milestone has validated, a persona plays the finished game. It reads as playable when Ravensight's own records show that run finished cleanly and the game itself reports at least one completed core loop. A persona is a model playing the game, not a player, so play it yourself before you ship it.

 

**Stopping.** Ctrl-C, or `create <job-id> --stop`, closes the plan. What finished stays paid for, and what never started comes back: the in-flight milestone by its own rules, the persona run if it was never played. A milestone that never started was never charged. If the process dies instead, the same command carries on, and a plan left alone closes after 14 days.

 

**The refund limit.** Once the model has been used on a plan, an account can get its first charge back twice in any 30 days. Past that, a brief that is declined, a design you reject and a plan that stops before its scaffold boots all keep that charge, and the plan's page says so. The persona run that never played still comes back. The CLI states how many you have left before you confirm.

 

**The hourly limit.** A studio has an hourly limit on model spend, and a large milestone's budget can pass it. The job pauses until the top of the next hour, says how long, and carries on. A pause costs no model time and Ctrl-C ends it. It does count toward the run's own time limit, so a run that passes that limit while it waits stops there, and that job's refund rules apply.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Build a feature (Labs beta)
documents.content:
### Build a feature (Labs beta)

 

Build a feature turns a short brief into a specification a person approves, then builds it on a new branch on your own machine and checks it against that specification. It is for 2D Godot projects and one bounded gameplay system or a few of them: movement, health, stamina, inventory, scoring, simple enemy behaviour or a HUD widget. It is off until the platform switches it on and an owner or admin turns on Labs for the game on the Labs page. Ravensight never holds or writes your source: the server stores paths and line counts.

 

```
npx ravensight-playtest feature "Hold shift to sprint, draining stamina that refills at rest"
# read, edit and approve it on the Labs page, then:
npx ravensight-playtest feature <spec-id> --godot-project .
```

 

**The specification.** It lists requirements, acceptance criteria, affected systems, proposed files, the SDK events to add and up to three test scenarios, and it is saved as a brief among your [design documents](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/design-studio/), so Huginn, the AI analyst, and the partner can read it. Writing one is one AI unit, which the included monthly allowance can cover. A brief bigger than the large size, outside those systems or needing 3D is declined and costs nothing. Only a person can approve a specification, in the dashboard, and an edit takes the approval away.

 

**What it costs.** A job needs an account that has added at least $10 in top-ups, and a balance at the plan's start balance (see [Starting a Labs job](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#labs-start-balance)). The plan is a price set by the specification's size, plus one persona run for each test scenario. The CLI shows both before you confirm, it is charged once from your prepaid balance, never from the included allowance, and an empty balance is refused before anything starts, with nothing charged.

 

**What it does.** On a clean working tree, it checks that the project starts, then plans, edits at most 40 files, runs the named checks (import, script check, the three asset checks and, if you allow them, your own tests) and has a persona play each test scenario. A failed check or a failed scenario starts a repair, at most two. The approved specification is frozen on the job, so nothing during the job can change what counts as done. It never commits or pushes unless you pass `--open-pr` and say yes at the prompt, and that only happens for a verified feature.

 

**What you get back.** If nothing changed, or the change does not pass its checks, the whole job is refunded, up to three times in any 30 days per account for a job that had already used model time. Past that the feature's own price is kept, the job says so, and unplayed scenario runs still come back. A job that used no model time is always refunded. Once a change is delivered the unit is kept, verified or not, and the report says which. Verified means Ravensight's own records show that every scenario's persona run finished with an accepted report, logged no script errors and filed no blocker or major finding. A scenario run that did not earn its unit is refunded on its own. These are model players, not real ones, so play it yourself before you ship it.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Godot 3D proof of concept (Labs, Alpha)
documents.content:
### Godot 3D proof of concept (Labs, Alpha)

 

Labs beta is Godot 2D. The Alpha is one small 3D template for trying [Build a feature](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#labs-feature) and Validate changes on a 3D project, and nothing more. [Create a game](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#labs-create) does not make a 3D game from a brief, and refuses to try. How well a model builds 3D has not been measured. It has no switch and no price of its own: the same Labs opt-in applies, and the jobs cost what they cost on a 2D project.

 

```
npx ravensight-playtest template godot-3d --game <game-id> --dir beacon-walk
cd beacon-walk
npx ravensight-playtest feature "Each beacon is worth two points" --alpha-3d
# read, edit and approve it on the Labs page, then:
npx ravensight-playtest feature <spec-id> --alpha-3d
npx ravensight-playtest validate <branch> --base main --alpha-3d
```

 

The template is placeholder meshes with the public SDK and no key, and writing it costs nothing. Without `--alpha-3d`, both commands refuse a 3D project for free. A persona plays with keys and input actions and can click a node by its path, but it cannot steer a camera with the mouse, so a feature that needs mouse look cannot be played by a persona. Your own models are listed by type and size and are never sent to the model.

documents.section_title: Send an AI persona through your build before a player does
documents.title: Your own art and audio (Labs beta)
documents.content:
### Your own art and audio (Labs beta)

 

Ravensight does not make art or audio. You supply the files, they stay in your project, and using them has no separate price: it is part of the [Build a feature](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#labs-feature) unit. Put them in a folder inside the project, `assets` unless you name another with `--assets-dir`, and see what is there:

 

```
npx ravensight-playtest assets
npx ravensight-playtest assets --assets-dir art --grid 32
```

 

This runs on your machine. It needs no login, costs nothing and sends nothing. It lists every file by type and size. For a PNG it adds the dimensions, transparency, measured pixel pitch and a guess at the layout: one picture, a tile, a strip or a sheet. For WAV and Ogg it adds the format and the length. Other formats are listed by type and size only.

 

**The warnings say what will go wrong in the game.**

 

- The real pixel pitch is measured from the pixels. A file described as a 32 grid can be 100 or more art pixels across, and `--grid` warns when it differs from what you expected.
 
- Faint, nearly invisible pixels can reach the edge of the canvas, so threshold alpha before trimming. The warning gives the box both ways.
 
- A tile with its own frame draws a grid across the floor. Use tiles with no per-tile frame, or one seamless texture.
 
- Godot does not import Opus in an Ogg file, compressed WAV, or WAV saved with the extended header.
 
- Pixel art blurs when the project's default filter is smooth, unless the node drawing it sets the nearest filter.

 

**During a feature job.** The model reads that list and uses the files by their `res://` paths. It cannot read, search or write an art or audio file, or write anything else in the declared folder except the `.import` settings beside a file. Anything the feature needs that you have not supplied stays a placeholder primitive, such as a `ColorRect` or a `Label`, and is named in the report. Nothing is generated.

 

**Three more checks.** `asset_references` checks that every asset the change names exists, with that exact case, inside the project. `asset_import` imports the project in Godot and reads what it made for each of them. `pixel_art_settings` checks that pixel art the change names has the nearest filter and clean import settings. Only what the change names can fail a job. A reference that does not resolve or a file that does not import starts a repair, and after the repairs blocks the change, so the whole job is refunded. A pixel art setting that stays wrong starts a repair too, and is then listed as a remaining risk.

 

**What you get back.** The report says how many files the change wired in, how many the project uses and how many are unused, and names the placeholders left for you to supply. Which files is in `assets-report.md` in the run directory, on your machine.

 

**Exactly what leaves your machine.**

 

| What | Where it goes |
| --- | --- |
| The content of an art or audio file | Nowhere. Not to Ravensight, and not to the model. |
| The `assets` command's output | Nowhere. It prints on your machine. |
| Each file's path, type, size, measurements and warnings, during a feature job | To the model, through the proxy, which does not store it. |
| How many files, how many wired in, used and unused, how many of each kind of warning, and each asset check's name and result | Uploaded in the feature's report. This part names no asset file. |
| Placeholders left to supply | Uploaded by name, because they are what you are being asked to supply. |
| The pull request text | Uploaded in the report. The model writes it, so it may name a file the change used. Read it before you merge. |
| `assets-report.md` and `assets.json`, which list every file | Nowhere. They stay in the run directory, because they are not on the upload allowlist. |

documents.content:
### Getting help

 

Report an issue with the CLI, or ask anything else, at [support@realityse.com](mailto:support@realityse.com).

documents.section_title: Playtest a live URL
documents.title: Playtest a live URL
documents.content:
Playtest

 

## Playtest a live URL

 

A cloud playtest can play your web game where it already runs, on your staging or production site, instead of an uploaded build. You prove the site is yours with a DNS record, save the address a playtest starts from, and say how the playtester signs in if your game needs an account. Then you start it exactly like any other [cloud playtest](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/#playtest-cloud): the same personas, tiers, play lengths, quote and report.

 

Everything below is on the **Playtest** page, under **Test a live URL**, in three parts: Domains, Targets and Start a playtest. Only an owner or admin of the studio can add, change or start anything there; every member can read it.

documents.section_title: Playtest a live URL
documents.title: Verify a domain
documents.content:
### Verify a domain

 

A playtest only ever reaches hosts this game has verified. To verify one, add it under **Domains**, copy the TXT record it shows into your DNS settings, then press **Verify**.

 

- **One host.** Add `play.example.com` and put the TXT record on `play.example.com`. Its value is `ravensight-verify=` followed by the token the page shows.
 
- **Every subdomain.** Add `*.example.com` and put its record on `example.com`. Once verified it covers every name that ends in `.example.com`, such as `play.example.com` and `eu.play.example.com`, but not `example.com` itself. Add `example.com` as its own domain if the game runs there too; a second TXT value on the same name is fine.
 
- **Each game verifies its own.** Domains belong to one game, not the whole studio. A second game adds its own, and one TXT name can hold both tokens.
 
- **Checking.** A new record can take a few minutes to appear. If Verify says it could not find the record yet, wait and press it again. One domain can be checked once every 10 seconds, and a game up to 60 times an hour, counting the checks the CLI makes before a local run; the page says when you can try again.
 
- **Checked again at every start.** The record is looked up again when you get a quote, when you confirm, and just before each persona starts. Keep it in place. If it is gone, the domain shows **Record removed**: a quote or a confirm is refused before anything is charged, and a persona due to start does not start and is refunded (see [below](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/#live-url-failures)). A playtest already playing is not stopped.
 
- **What cannot be added.** Addresses written as numbers, `localhost`, names under `.local`, `.internal`, `.test` and other names that are not on the public internet, and a host that does not point to a public address. A game can have up to 20 domains.

documents.section_title: Playtest a live URL
documents.title: Add a target
documents.content:
### Add a target

 

A target is where a playtest starts and how it signs in. Most games have one for staging and one for production. Under **Targets**, press **Add a target** and give it:

 

- **A name**, such as Staging.
 
- **A start URL.** It begins with `https://`, uses the standard port, and has no name or password in it. Its path, query and anchor are kept, so `https://play.example.com/play?level=3` starts every persona on level 3. Its host must be verified.
 
- **Extra hosts** (optional): other hosts your game loads from, like its API or its asset host, up to 8. Each must be verified, and each is an exact name, not a wildcard. Together with the start URL's host they may take at most 584 characters.
 
- **Sign in**: none, a test account, or a session (below).

 

A target shows **Ready** when every host is verified and any session has not expired. Otherwise it shows **Needs attention**, and opening it lists each problem with the host it is about and what to do. A target stays usable for 30 days after it was last saved; saving it again renews it. A game can have up to 10 targets.

documents.section_title: Playtest a live URL
documents.title: Sign in: a test account or a session
documents.content:
### Sign in: a test account or a session

 

**Test account.** Give the email and password of an account made for testing. Before the playtester starts, a script opens your sign in page (the start URL, or the sign in page you name), types the email and password, and submits. The playtester then begins already signed in. If the form is not found on its own, name its fields under **Field selectors**: a CSS selector or `text=Label` for the email field, the password field, the submit button, and something that only shows once signed in. Use this when your game has its own sign in form on a verified host.

 

**Session.** Sign in as a test user in your own browser, then paste what your site set: the cookie (as it appears in the `Cookie` header, such as `session=...; other=...`) or one header (`Authorization`, or a name that starts with `X-`, at most 100 characters). A cookie may hold up to 50 `name=value` pairs. Choose the date it expires, at most 30 days ahead. The cookie is set only for the start URL's host; a header is sent only to the target's hosts. Use a session when your game signs in through another company's sign in page, or with a magic link sent by email, which a script cannot type. After the expiry date, playtests of that target are refused until you paste a new one.

 

Either way, the saved value is never shown back. The page shows **Saved** with **Replace** and **Remove**, and an edit that leaves it alone keeps it.

documents.section_title: Playtest a live URL
documents.title: What is never shown or kept
documents.content:
### What is never shown or kept

 

- **Stored encrypted.** The email, the password and the session value are stored encrypted. The dashboard, the API and your MCP tools never return them; they show only whether one is saved, and for an email its first two characters and its domain (`qa•••@example.com`).
 
- **Never seen by the playtester.** The sign in is typed by a script in a separate browser step that records no video, screenshot or log, and the AI playtester is never given the values.
 
- **Never in a report.** If your site prints the email or password on the page, it is replaced on screen before each screenshot and video frame, and every report, log and finding is checked and cleaned before it is saved. A file that still holds one is not kept.
 
- **One gap.** Text your game draws as a picture, inside a canvas or an image, cannot be rewritten. If your game draws the account's email that way, it will show in screenshots and video. Use a test account whose address is not sensitive, never a real person's.
 
- **Deleted when you say.** **Remove** deletes the saved sign in at once. Deleting the target or the game deletes it too.

documents.section_title: Playtest a live URL
documents.title: What the playtester can reach
documents.content:
### What the playtester can reach

 

The playtester's browser can load only the target's hosts, over `https` on the standard port, and only at the public addresses they had when the playtest started. Anything else the page asks for (a font service, an analytics script, an ad, another company's sign in page) is blocked, and the report lists each blocked host and how many requests it had, such as "Not a verified host: fonts.example.net (12 requests). Verify it to let playtests load it." If the game needs one of them to play, verify it and add it to the target's extra hosts.

documents.section_title: Playtest a live URL
documents.title: Playtests are test traffic
documents.content:
### Playtests are test traffic

 

A playtest is never counted as a player or a website visitor. When your game's own Ravensight SDK runs in the playtest, its session is marked as a playtest, so its events are tagged `synthetic` and left out of your numbers by default, as for any [playtest](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/). Website page views, heatmap summaries and form views are not sent from a playtest at all.

 

The page can tell it is being playtested: it carries `window.__RAVENSIGHT_PLAYTEST__` with the run, the job and the persona before your own scripts run.

 

Events your own game server sends for the test account do not pass through the playtest browser, so they are not marked unless you mark them. Open your server's session with the browser's session token as `joinToken` (see [POST /api/v1/session](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/http-api/)): a session joined to a playtest session is a playtest session too, and its events are tagged `synthetic`. Or leave the test account out of what your server sends.

documents.section_title: Playtest a live URL
documents.title: From your own computer
documents.content:
### From your own computer

 

The [Playtest CLI](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/playtest/) can play a live URL too, on your machine, with the same sign in and the same rules for what the browser may reach. A public host must be verified for the game first; the CLI checks before it registers the run, and refuses with the record to add, charging nothing. A local address, such as `http://localhost:3000`, is your own dev server and needs no check.

 

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--url <url>` | Play the game at this address. |
| `--login-email <email>` | The test account's email. |
| `--login-password-env <NAME>` | The name of an environment variable that holds the password. The password is read only from there; a flag that carries the password itself is refused. |
| `--session-cookie-env <NAME>` | An environment variable holding a `Cookie` header value. |
| `--session-header-env <NAME>` | An environment variable holding one header, as `Name: value`. |
| `--sign-in-url <url>` | The sign in page, when it is not the start URL. |

 

A local playtest of a staging site, signed in as a test account

 

```
export PLAYTEST_PASSWORD='the test account password'
ravensight-playtest run --driver playwright_web \
  --url https://staging.example.com/play --personas fresh-eyes \
  --login-email qa@example.com --login-password-env PLAYTEST_PASSWORD
```

 

On your computer the password and session never leave your machine: they are not sent to Ravensight and not written to the run's folder.

documents.section_title: Playtest a live URL
documents.title: When the site is down or the sign in fails
documents.content:
### When the site is down or the sign in fails

 

If the start URL does not load, the sign in is refused, the sign in form is not found, the sign in sends the browser to a host that is not verified, or the session has expired, the playtester stops before it plays. The run fails with a report that says what happened and what to change, and no AI time is spent on it. It is billed under the usual cloud playtest rules for a game that failed to run, which the quote states before you agree. A sign in that leaves your verified hosts (another company's sign in page) needs a session instead.

 

A host that is not verified, or no longer points to a public address, is refused before anything is charged when you get a quote and when you confirm. It is checked once more just before each persona starts. A persona refused then never starts and is refunded in full at once, even when another persona of the same playtest is already playing. The cloud run's page says which host was refused and why. If the host cannot be looked up at that moment, the check is tried again for up to 10 minutes before the persona is refused. The same applies when the target was changed or removed after you confirmed.

 

A target not saved for 30 days, or a session past its expiry date, is refused at the quote with nothing charged. Save the target again, or paste a new session, and ask for a new quote.

documents.section_title: Playtest a live URL
documents.title: What it costs
documents.content:
### What it costs

 

A live URL playtest is priced exactly like a cloud playtest of an uploaded build, from the same prepaid balance: the price per persona for the tier and play length you choose, shown in the quote before you agree. It plays on the smallest tier unless you choose a larger one. There is no extra fee for a live URL, and nothing to upload, so there is no build check hold. Prices are in [Usage rates and limits](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/limits/).

documents.section_title: Playtest a live URL
documents.title: Getting help
documents.content:
### Getting help

 

Ask anything at [support@realityse.com](mailto:support@realityse.com).

documents.section_title: What you meant, what players did, what you decided
documents.title: What you meant, what players did, what you decided
documents.content:
21. Studio features: Studio Intelligence

 

## What you meant, what players did, what you decided

 

Analytics tell you what happened. Player Reports tell you what it felt like. Studio Intelligence is where those meet a question you actually care about, and where the answer stops being a browser tab.

documents.section_title: What you meant, what players did, what you decided
documents.title: An investigation
documents.content:
### An investigation

 

You start with a question. Against it you gather evidence: analytics results, player reports, playtest findings, feedback, notes you write yourself. Every piece keeps its provenance, so months later you can see where a claim came from rather than having to trust it. When you have enough, you record the decision and the follow-up you are trying next, and that stays attached to the question rather than being lost in a chat log.

documents.section_title: What you meant, what players did, what you decided
documents.title: Release comparison
documents.content:
### Release comparison

 

Inside an investigation you can put one release beside another and see the same metrics for both. Read it as what changed, not as what caused it: a comparison shows a difference between two windows, and it has no way to know what else you shipped in between.

documents.section_title: What you meant, what players did, what you decided
documents.title: Analysis
documents.content:
### Analysis

 

Asking Ravensight to analyze an investigation is a bounded AI action, metered exactly like an analyst question. It reads the evidence you gathered, not the whole account. The decision stays yours: nothing here marks a question resolved on its own.

documents.section_title: What you meant, what players did, what you decided
documents.title: Where it connects
documents.content:
### Where it connects

 

A player report can be sent into an investigation from the Player Reports page. Findings the investigation produces are kept in the same studio context graph as the analyst's, so the next game starts from them, and the analyst can search them with `search_studio_intelligence`. A playtest finding needs no such step: once a run finishes, its worst findings already sit in the analyst's memory and in the studio graph as evidence, ready for an investigation to cite.

documents.section_title: What you meant, what players did, what you decided
documents.title: Market research and publisher drafts
documents.content:
### Market research and publisher drafts

 

Market research on the Studio Intelligence page works three ways: you collect sources you name, you ask a question and get a quick look in seconds, or you start deep research that keeps digging in the background. Starting a quick look or deep research needs a member role or above.

 

#### Collect the sources you name

 

A research run collects up to five comparable sources you name: a game's store page, or any public HTTPS page you are permitted to collect. Each comes back as a dated excerpt with its limitation stated, a relevance estimate and a category. You choose which passages to include, up to five, and only those are used as context, labelled as external research rather than facts about your game.

 

#### Quick look

 

Ask a market question of up to 1,000 characters and the answer arrives in seconds. Ravensight answers first from the shared market fact base (below), which is free, and two AI providers research the same question in parallel with a small number of web searches each. The answer shows each claim with its status and its sources. If one provider times out, the other still answers. A quick look is one shared AI unit, the same as a research run, and may use the included monthly allowance. When neither provider returns anything usable it is refunded, and the fact base hits are still shown.

 

#### Deep research

 

Deep research is a background job for a question that deserves more than a quick look. Pick one to four focus areas (competitors, player needs, opportunities, pricing) and, if you like, the quick look it follows from. The run moves through stages you can watch: queued, researching, extracting, reconciling, merging, then complete. A project runs one deep research job at a time, and collecting sources can run while it does.

 

It costs **25 AI units ($5.00)** from the prepaid balance only, never the included allowance. An empty balance is refused before anything runs, and so is a run when no provider can run at all, so nothing is charged. A provider kept out by a platform limit is shown on the run as skipped. When one provider fails, the run finishes as **partial** on the other provider's results, keeps the charge, and says so on the report. When neither provider returns anything usable it is refunded in full. A run whose charge is uncertain is held for billing review rather than retried or refunded blindly, and an owner can settle or refund it from the run itself. A studio also has a daily research limit.

 

When a deep run follows a quick look, it lists what changed: claims it added, claims it confirmed, claims it now disputes, and quick look claims it dropped. Each provider's raw report can be read in full from the run when it was kept. A report too large to keep, or one from a run where report storage is not configured, is not kept, and the run says so.

 

#### What a claim's status means

 

- **Corroborated.** Both AI providers found the claim, each citing public sources. (A fact in the shared fact base is also corroborated when a person added it.) This is agreement between two AI providers on cited public sources, not independent verification.
 
- **Single source.** Only one provider found the claim.
 
- **Disputed.** The two providers contradict each other. Read both sources before relying on either.

 

Player reviews quoted in a report are samples, not a measurement of every player. Nothing from a quick look or deep research enters your studio's context by itself: a person still accepts what is used.

 

#### The shared market fact base

 

Reports stay private to the studio that asked. The public facts drawn from them go into a market fact base that Ravensight keeps for every studio. A fact is only ever about a public subject: a public game on Steam, a genre, a tag or a platform. Each one carries a public source link, a short quote that supports it and the day it was collected. Facts are written by a separate extraction step that sees only the cited source quotes and titles, never your question, your notes or your studio's names, and a fact the quote does not support is dropped. Anything naming your studio, your projects, your games or a phrase your question puts in quotes is filtered out and stays in your private report, and a fact never says who asked.
