Because the fact base needs no AI to answer, it keeps answering during an AI provider outage. Reading it needs a read-only role or above.

 

Facts change in a few plain ways. Finding the same fact again strengthens it in place, adding its sources, rather than writing a copy. Facts that disagree are both marked disputed. A research finding can dispute a fact both providers found only when both providers agree on it from two different sites, and a fact Ravensight added by hand is never disputed by research. A newer figure for the same measure replaces the older fact only when both providers found it; the older fact is kept, marked superseded. A fact can also be retired, after which it no longer appears in search and cannot be cited.

 

A market fact can be cited as evidence in an investigation, on a [Brainstorm](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/brainstorm/) card and in a [Strategy matrix](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/strategy/) cell. When a fact a cell cites is disputed, superseded or retired, the cell is flagged for you to look at. It is never re-scored on its own.

 

#### Publisher drafts

 

From the included passages you can generate a draft in one of six formats: a positioning brief, a store description, a launch announcement, a trailer outline, a publisher pitch, or the questions and evidence gaps a buyer would raise. Every external claim cites its source by number, a draft that cites nothing is refused and refunded, and the export carries the source list with it. A research run and a draft are one shared AI unit each, and a project keeps up to 50 research runs.

documents.section_title: What you meant, what players did, what you decided
documents.title: Background work, on a ceiling you set
documents.content:
### Background work, on a ceiling you set

 

The work Ravensight does without being asked each time, weekly digests, pattern synthesis and feedback enrichment, runs under a monthly budget in cents that the owner sets and that is stated against the current rate before it is accepted. It is a ceiling on spend, not a subscription: nothing renews, and switching it off stops the work. Each of the three can be enabled on its own.

 

Each environment also has its own **Write a weekly digest** switch on its card under **Settings > Projects**. Each digest is 1 AI unit. A new production, early access or demo environment starts with it on, and every other new environment starts with it off, so a development or staging build does not spend an AI unit every Monday unless you turn it on.

 

Reading an investigation needs a read-only role or above. Creating one, gathering evidence and recording a decision need a member role or above. Setting the background budget is owner only.

documents.section_title: Muninn, studio memory
documents.title: Muninn, studio memory
documents.content:
22. Studio features: what your studio knows, kept and reusable

 

## Muninn, studio memory

 

Analytics answers a question and then loses the answer. Muninn, studio memory, is the other half: the studio context graph where every conclusion Huginn reaches is kept as a dated finding, owned by your studio rather than by the game that produced it. It lives under **Understand > Muninn**.

 

What the analyst is told to trust over its own reading, the game context and studio notes you write yourself, is described under [Analyst context](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/analyst/#analyst-context).

documents.section_title: Muninn, studio memory
documents.title: Findings
documents.content:
### Findings

 

When an analyst answer finishes, a cheap background model distils it into at most four standalone findings. A finding is one sentence with numbers in it, stored with the date the data was observed and a link back to the conversation that produced it, so you can always go and read the reasoning behind it.

 

Two deterministic guards run before anything is stored. A finding whose numbers do not appear verbatim in the answer is dropped, and a finding that restates one you already have is suppressed. Neither is a prompt instruction; both are code.

 

Every finding carries a status you control:

 

- **active**, the default: extracted and in use.
 
- **confirmed**: you vouched for it. Confirmed findings lead the game brief and outrank recency.
 
- **archived**: it was wrong or has gone stale. It stops being used and stops being returned, but it is kept rather than deleted, because knowing what the analyst once believed is itself useful.

documents.section_title: Muninn, studio memory
documents.title: Teach and correct Muninn
documents.content:
### Teach and correct Muninn

 

On the Muninn page, use **Teach Muninn** to add an observation and choose the game it belongs to. You can edit a finding when its wording or conclusion needs correcting, confirm one you trust, or archive one that no longer holds. A saved observation belongs to the studio; it is not a replacement for the evidence behind a claim.

 

An owner-enabled MCP write token can use `add_studio_fact` to add a fact within its permissions. Adding a fact through MCP is a metered operation; use the dashboard when you want to review and correct findings directly.

documents.section_title: Muninn, studio memory
documents.title: The weekly studio digest
documents.content:
### The weekly studio digest

 

The Muninn page shows the latest weekly studio rollup: game digest headlines, recorded sales by currency, marketing touchpoints, proposed patterns and upcoming publisher reporting or goals. It covers the previous Monday through Sunday in UTC. Missing figures stay unrecorded rather than becoming zero, and monthly sales rows are not divided into an invented weekly amount.

 

The studio rollup combines existing records without another model call or a separate generation charge. This is different from the per-game AI digests. Owners and admins with an email address can receive the studio rollup by email; change the studio digest email preference in Settings. Reading it through `get_studio_digest` still uses the MCP event meter.

documents.section_title: Muninn, studio memory
documents.title: Patterns
documents.content:
### Patterns

 

Once your studio has more than one game, a weekly pass reads your active findings and proposes the lessons that held across several of them, each with the findings it was distilled from attached. A pattern is only proposed when findings from at least two different games support it, and that rule is enforced in code after the model answers, not asked for in the prompt.

 

Proposed patterns are shown as proposed. Nothing synthesized becomes part of what your studio knows until a person confirms it.

documents.section_title: Muninn, studio memory
documents.title: The design risk check
documents.content:
### The design risk check

 

Describe something you are about to build. Ravensight retrieves your own relevant findings first and asks the model to grade the plan against them, so it is reading evidence rather than recalling anything. It answers `repeat`, `caution` or `clear`, with the findings that justify the verdict cited by name. A citation it cannot map back to a real finding of yours is dropped rather than shown, and if your studio has no relevant history yet, it says so instead of inventing a verdict. You can run it from Muninn or from the Design studio.

 

This is the one part of studio context that calls a model, so it is metered exactly like an analyst question. Browsing saved context in the dashboard uses no AI units. MCP reads are metered separately.

documents.section_title: Muninn, studio memory
documents.title: For your own agents
documents.content:
### For your own agents

 

The same context is available over the [Analytics MCP](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/mcp/) through `search_studio_context`, `get_game_brief`, `list_touchpoints`, `list_sales`, `summarize_sales`, `list_brainstorm_sessions`, `get_brainstorm_board` and `get_starting_context`. All eight are bounded MCP reads, each weighted as 100,000 events on the shared event meter, so a coding agent can pull your studio's findings, what you did to market them, what they earned and what you are thinking about next, on every task it picks up.

documents.section_title: Muninn, studio memory
documents.title: Who can see it
documents.content:
### Who can see it

 

Findings are the most sensitive thing in your account: they are your conclusions about your own games, not raw numbers. The tenancy filter is part of the query rather than applied to the results, in the database read and inside the semantic search stage alike, so another studio's context is not merely hidden from you, it is never retrieved. Every member of your org can read the context graph; confirming and archiving findings needs a member role or above.

documents.section_title: Plan the next game against what you already learned
documents.title: Plan the next game against what you already learned
documents.content:
23. Studio features: Design studio

 

## Plan the next game against what you already learned

 

The analyst tells you what happened. The design studio is where you decide what to do about it, with your studio's own history in the room.

documents.section_title: Plan the next game against what you already learned
documents.title: Documents
documents.content:
### Documents

 

Write and keep your design documents here. Each one keeps its recent versions, so you can see what a draft replaced. The studio chat can propose an edit to the document in front of you, and proposing is all it does: the markdown comes back to you and nothing changes until you accept it.

documents.section_title: Plan the next game against what you already learned
documents.title: Reference documents
documents.content:
### Reference documents

 

Upload a Markdown, plain text or PDF file from Design or from a brainstorm and it is kept as a reference document: source material your studio did not write here, which the studio chat and the brainstorm partner can read and cite. Text files up to 256 KB and PDFs up to 5 MB and 200 pages are accepted, and the body is kept up to 100,000 characters, with the upload telling you when the end was left off. There is no OCR: a PDF that is only scanned images has no text to read, so it is refused rather than guessed at.

documents.section_title: Plan the next game against what you already learned
documents.title: The risk check
documents.content:
### The risk check

 

Describe a plan in the Design studio and it is graded against your own findings. How that works is under [The design risk check](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/studio-context/#risk-check).

 

Design chat and risk checks each use one shared AI unit per completed bounded action, including internal tool steps. Failed, undelivered work is refunded. Ravensight manages provider keys; reading and editing saved documents does not use AI units.

documents.section_title: A board to think on, with your studio in the room
documents.title: A board to think on, with your studio in the room
documents.content:
24. Studio features: Brainstorm

 

## A board to think on, with your studio in the room

 

A brainstorm is a board you think on, next to a partner that has read what your studio already learned. Open one in **Build > Brainstorm**. The list follows the game switcher, and a board started under All games has no game until you move it to one. A board starts with five columns, Ideas, Questions, Risks, Keep and Drop, which you can rename, re-order or add to, up to eight. A card is one thought in one of those columns, written by you or by the partner, and a card can cite what it rests on: a pattern from your studio context, one of your documents, a touchpoint, a playtest finding, a row in the sales ledger, a Pulse post or a public fact from [market research](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/studio-intelligence/#market-research). Every citation is checked when the card is written, against your own studio or, for a market fact, against the public fact base, so a card cannot point at evidence you do not have.

 

The partner reads your studio's own history before it answers: the findings across every game you have shipped, the patterns you confirmed, the touchpoints that moved players and what they cost, and what your playtests keep finding. Ask it a question and it answers in the thread, cites what it used, and can put cards on the board it is sitting at, up to twelve per question. It writes to that board and nowhere else, and nothing it writes is hidden from you: a card it adds is a card you can edit, move or drop. The thread is kept with the board, so a brainstorm you reopen next month picks up where it stopped. Attach one of your documents, a design document or an uploaded Markdown, plain text or PDF reference, and the conversation is scoped to it: the partner is told which documents this board is about and reads them by name. When you are done, promote one card or the whole board to a Design brief, which lands in Design as a document you own.

 

**Start with what the studio knows** fills a new board from your own record: your confirmed patterns, your best touchpoints by measured lift, your sales by storefront and your findings by category. The starting context it reads is a plain digest of that record and it is free, built without a model call, and you can read it beside any board. Turning it into cards is one shared AI unit, the same unit a Design chat turn uses, and the dialog names that unit before anything is spent. If the partner could not produce cards, the unit comes back and the page says the board is empty rather than claiming it was filled.

 

Each question to the partner is one shared AI unit. For a design question that would benefit from the deeper model, the partner may offer the deep tier as a choice with its price shown, five units from your prepaid balance and never from the included allowance, and nothing is charged unless you choose it. The board itself, its cards, its attachments and promotion are all included. What ships today is the board: there is no freeform canvas.

documents.section_title: See what a decision does to every kind of player
documents.title: See what a decision does to every kind of player
documents.content:
## See what a decision does to every kind of player

 

A decision rarely lands on one player. A port, a price change or a new mode helps one group, costs another and leaves a third untouched. A strategy matrix puts that on one page before you commit: your player segments down one side, the directions you are weighing across the top, and a score in every cell for each lens you care about. Open one in **Build > Strategy matrix** with a title, and optionally the question it answers, how far ahead it looks, and one of your titles and one of your games it is about. The list follows the game switcher, and All games shows every matrix, including one with no game. Start it blank, or seeded with your studio's own starting context, which calls no model and costs nothing. Read it as a sheet, one lens at a time, or as a stack with every lens layered, where each layer has a text summary.

documents.section_title: See what a decision does to every kind of player
documents.title: Segments, directions and lenses
documents.content:
### Segments, directions and lenses

 

A **segment** is a group of players you name yourself, such as players who finished the campaign or players on a handheld, with an optional description and a weight for how much it matters to this decision. A **direction** is one option you are weighing, including doing nothing, with an optional description and, set in the dashboard, parameters such as a price. A **lens** is what you score it on, with an optional description and a weight. Every matrix starts with five: fit, revenue, friction, feasibility and risk, and you can add your own. Fit, revenue and feasibility count for a direction; friction and risk count against it. A matrix holds up to 12 segments, 10 directions and 10 lenses, and a studio can keep up to 100 matrices.

 

Each cell is a whole score from 1 to 5 with a confidence of low, medium or high and a rationale of up to 1,000 characters. The rollup for a direction is a weighted mean, lenses inside each segment and then segments, and it carries what it rests on: its confidence, how much of it is assumption, how many cells are contested and which cells contributed most. The gaps list what to look at next: cells not scored yet, assumptions, low confidence and contested cells, heaviest first. The rollup and the gaps count accepted cells only. Every cell shows its score as a digit, its confidence as a word and its basis as a letter and a shape, so nothing depends on colour.

documents.section_title: See what a decision does to every kind of player
documents.title: Evidence, inference or assumption
documents.content:
### Evidence, inference or assumption

 

Every score says what it rests on. **Evidence** means it cites at least one record: an insight from your studio context, one of your documents, a touchpoint, a playtest finding, a row in the sales ledger, a Pulse post, a brainstorm card, or a public fact from [market research](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/studio-intelligence/#market-research). A score cites up to eight sources, and each citation says whether that source supports the score or contradicts it. **Inference** means the score was derived from cited evidence rather than read straight off it. **Assumption** means nobody has evidence yet, and it is allowed to cite nothing. Every citation is checked when it is written, against your own studio or, for a market fact, against the public fact base, and only a reference is kept, never the source text, so a cell cannot point at evidence you do not have. When a market fact a cell cites is later disputed, superseded or retired, the cell is flagged so you can look again; its score is not changed for you.

documents.section_title: See what a decision does to every kind of player
documents.title: Scenarios and diffs
documents.content:
### Scenarios and diffs

 

A scenario is a branch of the matrix: a what if, such as the port slipping a quarter or the price landing lower. It can rescore cells of its own, and it can carry up to 20 rules that move every cell they name by a whole number of points, up to 4 either way, such as raising risk by one everywhere. A moved score stays between 1 and 5, and everything else stays on the base matrix. Compare a scenario with the base and the diff lists every cell that moved, from what to what and why: rescored in the scenario, moved by one of its rules, or scored only in the scenario. It also shows every direction's rollup and rank before and after. A matrix holds up to 20 scenarios.

documents.section_title: See what a decision does to every kind of player
documents.title: Record the decision, then the outcome
documents.content:
### Record the decision, then the outcome

 

When you choose, record the decision: the direction, the scenario it was made under if any, your reasoning, and up to ten predictions. A prediction is a metric, a comparison (at least or at most), a threshold, a date to judge it by and how likely you think it is. Resolve each prediction once. Day 1 and day 7 retention and new players are read from one of your games' events, and a touchpoint's lift from that touchpoint, over the time from the decision to the prediction's date, or to today if that date has not come yet. Any other metric is entered by hand, and so is a prediction that names a segment or has no game, title or touchpoint to read: the decision marks it as one Ravensight cannot pull.

 

Units sold and net revenue come from one title's sales ledger, the prediction's own or the matrix's, so they cannot name a segment, and they are pulled only once the prediction's date is over. Net revenue names one currency, its threshold and its outcome are whole minor units of that currency, and it is never converted and never typed in. The pull refuses rather than guesses when the ledger rows in the window mix daily and monthly periods, when a monthly row is only partly inside the window, or when some rows did not report the figure. Correct the ledger, or for units sold, enter the actual by hand.

 

Calibration compares what you predicted with what happened, as a hit rate and a Brier score across your resolved predictions. It needs at least five resolved predictions before it reports a number, and says so rather than showing one from too few. It is a check on your own judgement over time, not a forecast.

documents.section_title: See what a decision does to every kind of player
documents.title: Partner suggestions, one AI unit
documents.content:
### Partner suggestions, one AI unit

 

The partner can suggest segments for a matrix, or suggest scores for one direction at a time, from what your studio already knows. Each suggestion is one shared AI unit, the same unit a Design chat turn uses, it draws the included allowance first, and the dialog names the unit before anything is spent. Suggested segments are not stored: each one joins the matrix only when a person adds it. Suggested scores are stored as the partner's and stay proposed until a person accepts them, and a cell a person has already accepted is never overwritten. A suggested score that does not cite one of the sources it was shown is stored as an assumption. If the partner suggests nothing new, the unit comes back. Filling the whole matrix in one step is not offered.

documents.section_title: See what a decision does to every kind of player
documents.title: Over MCP
documents.content:
### Over MCP

 

Your own agent can read matrices, compare a scenario with its base and list decisions with `list_strategy_matrices`, `get_strategy_matrix`, `diff_strategy_scenario` and `list_strategy_decisions`. With a token an owner has allowed to write, it can also create a matrix, add segments and directions, set a score and record a prediction's outcome with `create_strategy_matrix`, `add_strategy_segment`, `add_strategy_direction`, `set_strategy_score` and `record_prediction_outcome`. Partner suggestions, scenarios, recording a decision, a direction's parameters and deletes stay in the dashboard. See the [MCP tool cards](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/mcp/).

documents.section_title: See what a decision does to every kind of player
documents.title: The open core
documents.content:
### The open core

 

The scoring core is a separate MIT package, ravensight-matrix: the schema, the rollup, the gaps, the scenario diff and calibration, with no I/O and no dependencies, so the dashboard and the server compute the same numbers. It ships a CommonJS entry and an ES module entry and runs on Node 18 or later. The source is on [GitHub](https://github.com/Reality-Software-Entertainment/ravensight-matrix) and the package on [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ravensight-matrix) (`npm install ravensight-matrix`). Evidence checks, the partner, metering and MCP stay in the hosted service.

documents.section_title: What you did outside the game, and what happened next
documents.title: What you did outside the game, and what happened next
documents.content:
25. Studio features: marketing memory

 

## What you did outside the game, and what happened next

 

Analytics can tell you that Tuesday tripled. Only you can tell it that a video went out on Monday. A touchpoint is that record: one thing you did outside the game, written down by you, so the platform can measure what happened next.

 

Record one in **Studio > Marketing** with a kind (ad, video, stream, post, press, launch, update, sale or other), a title, when it happened, and optionally a link, a channel name of your own, a spend and some notes. Or import a spreadsheet export as CSV with a header row naming `kind`, `title` and `occurred_at`, plus any of `url`, `channel`, `spend`, `notes` and `tags`. Column order does not matter. Tags are separated by a vertical bar so a tag can contain a comma, `spend` is a plain amount like 129.99, and every row that validates is imported while every row that does not comes back with its line number and the reason. One bad date does not refuse the file.

 

Each night, and on demand from the touchpoint itself, the platform measures the lift for every game in your studio that has events. In plain words: it counts the devices whose very first event for that game arrived in the 72 hours after the touchpoint, works out how many new players a 72 hour window would have seen anyway (the average day over the previous week, times three), and reports both numbers and their ratio. If your game had no new players at all in that previous week there is no ratio, and you get an empty one rather than an invented multiple.

 

Lift can only be measured while that baseline week is still inside the 90 day event window, which means touchpoints from roughly the last 83 days. An older one, such as a historic campaign imported from a CSV, gets no lift, and asking for it answers `422 lift_outside_retention` without changing anything. Moving a touchpoint's date clears the old measurement and measures the new moment, or leaves it with no lift when the new date is too old.

 

Read it as correlation, not proof. Two touchpoints inside the same 72 hours each show the whole lift, and a storefront feature you never recorded shows none of it. The number tells you which week to look at; you still decide what caused it. Touchpoints appear as markers on the game's history chart, on the Studio Intelligence evidence map with their strongest lift, and they can be cited as evidence in an investigation. The weekly digest names any touchpoint whose 72 hour window covers a day it calls a spike.

 

When filling the form in, the platform can offer a suggested kind and channel from the link's host and your own title and notes. It is only ever a suggestion: nothing is filled in for you, nothing is stored until you save, and when that helper is unavailable the form works exactly as it always does. Deleting a project keeps its touchpoints, because the money you spent and the lift it produced happened whether or not the project is still in your account.

documents.section_title: What each title earned, in your own numbers
documents.title: What each title earned, in your own numbers
documents.content:
26. Studio features: sales ledger

 

## What each title earned, in your own numbers

 

Marketing memory says what you did. The sales ledger says what it earned, in your own numbers. A row is one storefront, one period and one line item for one title: the storefront, whether the period is a day or a month and which one, the currency, a region if the export splits by region, the line item (the base game, a DLC, an edition or a bundle, with your own name for it), and then whatever the report gave you: units and refunded units, gross, net, refunds, chargebacks, fees, payout, the price and discount at the time, wishlist adds, and a note. Record one by hand in **Studio > Sales**, or import a store export. Nothing is recomputed from anything else: net is what the payout report said, even when it disagrees with gross minus fees, because the report is the fact.

 

Importing is two steps. Upload the CSV and the platform reads the header row, matches the columns it recognises to the ledger's fields, and shows you the mapping beside the first few rows parsed exactly as the import will parse them. A column it could not place is offered with a suggestion, marked as a suggestion, and you confirm or change every mapping before anything is stored: the preview stores nothing, and the suggestion helper never decides. An amount like `4.990`, which some exports mean as four thousand and others as four point nine nine, is flagged above the table so you can say which it is. A weekly export is refused with a one line reason rather than spread over seven days. Every row that validates is stored and every row that does not comes back with its line number and the reason. Importing the same file twice changes nothing; importing a corrected one updates the rows in place.

 

Totals are per currency, always. A studio selling in dollars and euros sees two blocks, and there is no combined figure anywhere, because a conversion rate would have to come from somewhere and would be wrong for the period it was applied to. For the same reason a monthly row is never added to a daily one: the summary says so when a group carries both, and you read the two rows apart. Nothing that nobody recorded is shown as zero.

 

Give a title its release date in **Settings > Projects** and the Sales page draws its launch curve: cumulative units and net for the first ninety days after release, from daily rows, in one currency at a time. Without a release date the curve anchors on the first recorded sale instead, and monthly rows are counted beside the chart rather than smeared across it. On Overview and Player insights, the **Show units sold** switch draws units per day over the players line for that game's title, so a sale and the players it brought sit on the same axis; it is off by default and costs no extra request.

 

Plainly: these are recorded numbers. The only thing read from a store on your behalf is a [connection](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/connections/) you add yourself, which never overwrites a row you entered or imported, and the platform never infers a sale from telemetry. The analyst, the weekly digest, cross-game synthesis and your own agents over MCP all read the ledger you keep, with the same rule attached: minor units, never converted, a month never added to a day.

documents.section_title: Keep publisher goals and reporting with your titles
documents.title: Keep publisher goals and reporting with your titles
documents.content:
## Keep publisher goals and reporting with your titles

 

Open **Studio > Publishers** to record a publisher relationship, its status, linked titles, contract dates and notes. Add goals and reporting obligations so the next due date stays visible beside the relationship.

documents.section_title: Keep publisher goals and reporting with your titles
documents.title: Progress from your records
documents.content:
### Progress from your records

 

Goal progress is computed from the sales ledger and player rollups rather than entered by hand. Revenue stays in the goal's currency. A goal without enough data says why instead of showing a false zero. Review progress and update the goal's status as your work changes.

documents.section_title: Keep publisher goals and reporting with your titles
documents.title: Prepare a report
documents.content:
### Prepare a report

 

Select a publisher and reporting period to generate a Markdown report. It brings together linked titles, goal progress, sales by title and currency, marketing touchpoints with their measured lift, and reporting obligations. The report is assembled from records without a model call. Marketing lift is correlation, not proof of attribution.

 

Downloading or generating a report does not send it to the publisher. Review it and send it through your chosen channel, then mark the relevant obligation as sent. Private notes are excluded from the MCP publisher reads.

 

Your own agent can use [MCP](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/mcp/) tools `list_publishers` and `get_publisher_report` with the appropriate studio access. These are metered reads. Generating a report through MCP does not mark it sent.

documents.section_title: What people said back
documents.title: What people said back
documents.content:
26. Studio features: Pulse

 

## What people said back

 

Marketing memory records what you put out. Pulse keeps what came back: your own posts, how their engagement moved over time, the comments, replies and quotes people left, and the people behind them. Every post you record in Pulse is also a marketing touchpoint, so the new players it was followed by sit right beside the conversation it started.

 

A post gets into Pulse four ways. Record it by hand in **Studio > Pulse** with its platform, its link or id, when it went out, its text and, if you have them, its numbers. Import a spreadsheet export as CSV, up to 2,000 rows a file, through a column mapping you confirm before anything is stored, as with the sales ledger. Add a **source**, a Bluesky handle, a YouTube channel or a Reddit account (up to ten per studio), and Pulse finds your new posts once a day and reads them on a schedule. Or **watch a link** to any public page, up to ten at a time, and Pulse reads that page for you (see [the crawler](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/pulse/#pulse-crawl) below). **Refresh** reads a polled or watched post again right now.

 

A polled post is read hourly for its first two days, every six hours to a week, daily to thirty days and weekly to ninety, then left alone, and at most fifty posts per studio are read on that schedule at once, the newest first. A reading only becomes a new snapshot when a number moved or a day has passed. Pulse keeps up to 500 comments and 1,000 reactions per post; past that, the post's own counters still say how many there were.

documents.section_title: What people said back
documents.title: What each platform lets Pulse see
documents.content:
### What each platform lets Pulse see

 

Platforms do not all say the same things, and Pulse never fills a gap with a guess. A number a platform does not report is shown as not reported, never as zero.

 

| Where | Comments and replies | Who reacted | Numbers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bluesky | Yes, and quote posts | Yes: likers and reposters by handle | Likes, replies, reposts, quotes |
| YouTube | Yes | No: YouTube never says who liked | Views, likes, comments |
| Reddit | Yes | No: Reddit never says who voted | Score, comment count |
| A watched link | Where the page shows them, such as Steam store and community pages and itch.io pages | No | What the page publishes |
| Anywhere else | By hand or CSV | By hand | By hand or CSV |

 

LinkedIn and X show most posts only to signed-in readers, so a link to one usually comes back as behind a login, and you record that post by hand instead. Pulse holds no account of yours on any platform and asks for no sign-in: a source is a public handle you type in.

documents.section_title: What people said back
documents.title: Huginn's summary of what they said
documents.content:
### Huginn's summary of what they said

 

Ask Huginn to summarise the comments on one post, or every post in a date range (the newest 50 in it), and it answers in a short paragraph with the themes, the questions people asked, the features they requested, their objections and an overall sentiment. Each summary is one shared AI unit from the included allowance, then the prepaid balance, and asking again about a post with no new comments returns the stored summary for free. What Huginn reads is bounded (up to 200 comments or 40,000 characters, newest and most-replied first) and anonymous: each comment is labelled by a number, never by a handle or name, and it is read as material to summarise, never as instructions. Each summary is also filed as a dated finding in Muninn, so the analyst and your brainstorms can cite what people asked for. That finding belongs to the newest game of the post's project, or your studio's newest game when the post has no project, so deleting that game deletes the finding with it (the summary on the post stays), and a studio with no game yet gets no finding. In the dashboard, **Summarize** on a post and **Summarize this period** on the Posts tab say what they will use before you click. Over the API it is `POST /api/v1/org/pulse/posts/<id>/summary`, or `POST /api/v1/org/pulse/summary` with a date range. It is never available over MCP, because it is a model call.

documents.section_title: What people said back
documents.title: People, and matching them across platforms
documents.content:
### People, and matching them across platforms

 

Everyone who commented on, replied to, quoted or (where the platform says) reacted to your posts becomes a person in Pulse, with how many times and on how many of your posts. The people who came back to the most posts are listed first, and you can keep your own notes and tags on each. When the same handle appears on two platforms, or two profiles link to the same page, Pulse proposes that they are one person. Nothing is merged until someone in your studio confirms it, a rejected pair is never proposed again, and a confirmed merge is permanent.

 

Posts can be cited as evidence in a Studio Intelligence investigation and on a brainstorm card, and Studio Intelligence's search reads post and comment text beside your documents and touchpoints. The studio graph holds only how often repeat engagers came back to which posts: no handle, name or comment text ever goes into it.

documents.section_title: What people said back
documents.title: How Pulse is charged
documents.content:
### How Pulse is charged

 

There is no Pulse price. Everything Pulse stores is weighted events on the same monthly event meter as your player events, charged once for each row actually stored, so reading a post again that has not changed costs only the read. The weights per post, snapshot, comment and reaction, and the per-byte rate for watched links, are in [Rates](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/limits/#rates). People, matching and reading what you stored are free.

 

Anything you ask for (recording, importing, adding a link, Refresh) is charged to the studio's owner and can use the prepaid balance. Scheduled reading in the background uses only the included monthly events unless the studio owner opts in, and then only up to the studio's background budget. Without that opt-in, a source or link that would need the balance pauses and says so, and it picks up again after a top-up, a new month or the opt-in.

documents.section_title: What people said back
documents.title: Other people's handles, and deleting
documents.content:
### Other people's handles, and deleting

 

Pulse stores what was public on your own posts: each person's handle, display name and profile link on that platform, and the text of what they wrote to you. It reads nothing about them beyond your posts, and it is shown only to your own studio. Treat it as you would any correspondence you keep.

 

Deleting a post deletes its snapshots, its comments and reactions and its marketing touchpoint. Deleting a source stops reading it and keeps every post it found. Stopping a watched link keeps what it read. A person record (the handle, display name, profile link and your notes) stays after their comments are deleted. To remove someone entirely, open them in Pulse, People and choose **Delete person** (the API is `DELETE /api/v1/org/pulse/people/<id>`). Their comments and reactions are removed from Pulse, the counts on your posts drop to match, and it cannot be undone. Deleting is not charged, and it does not refund what was charged to store those rows.

documents.section_title: What people said back
documents.title: The crawler: RavensightPulse
documents.content:
### The crawler: RavensightPulse

 

If you run a website and found `RavensightPulse` in your logs: it reads one public page that a studio using Ravensight saved as a link, usually a post, an announcement or a thread about their own game, to keep track of the replies to it. It identifies itself as:

 

```
RavensightPulse/1.0 (+https://ravensight.io/docs/#pulse-crawl)
```

 

- It fetches only pages a studio saved, over https, with a plain GET: no sign-in, no cookies, no forms and no scripts run.
 
- It reads a saved page at most once a day for its first thirty days, then once a week until ninety days, then stops. It stops sooner after three unchanged reads, or three refusals, missing pages or login pages in a row.
 
- It visits a host at most once every five seconds from each of our servers (robots.txt and the page are one visit), runs at most two visits at once, and reads at most 2 MB of a page.
 
- It reads `/robots.txt` first (cached for up to a day) and honours every `Disallow` under `User-agent: *` or any user agent containing `ravensight`. A disallow with a wildcard blocks the whole host for it, and `Allow` lines are not read, so a disallow always wins.
 
- A page behind a login or consent wall is not read: the studio is told to record it by hand.

 

To keep it off your site entirely, add this to robots.txt:

 

```
User-agent: RavensightPulse
Disallow: /
```

 

Questions, or a problem with it: write to [support@realityse.com](mailto:support@realityse.com) with your host name and we will look into it.

documents.section_title: Your store numbers, pulled in
documents.title: Your store numbers, pulled in
documents.content:
27. Studio features: Connections

 

## Your store numbers, pulled in

 

A connection links one of your store accounts to the records you already keep. Whatever it reads goes to one of three places: money in goes to the [sales ledger](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/sales-ledger/), attention goes to [Pulse](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/pulse/), and money out is reserved for your [marketing touchpoints](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/marketing-memory/) (no connection writes ad spend yet). Steam is the first provider.

 

**Connecting Steam.** Create a Financial Web API group key on the Steamworks partner site and add it in **Settings > Connections**. Only the studio owner can add, change or remove a connection. The key is checked against Steam once, stored encrypted, and never shown again, not to you, your team, your agents or our logs: you see only its last four characters. Steam lets you restrict a key to IP addresses. That is optional; if you do, ask us at [support@realityse.com](mailto:support@realityse.com) for the addresses to allow. Ravensight then lists the apps the key can see, and you map each app to one of your titles. An app you have not mapped is skipped and named in every sync result, never guessed.

 

```
POST /api/v1/org/connections
Cookie: gt_session (dashboard sign-in, studio owner)

{ "provider": "steamworks", "key": "<your group key>",
  "publisherKey": "<optional Publisher Web API key>",
  "feeds": ["revenue", "attention"], "label": "Steam" }
```

 

**A second key for Steam players.** Steam has two kinds of Web API key. The Financial Web API group key above reads sales and wishlists and nothing else. Checking Steam tickets ([Require a Steam ticket](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/#public-steam)) and syncing Steam leaderboards and stats need a [Publisher Web API key](https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/webapi_overview/auth), which you create on the same Steamworks page; put it in a group that covers only your games. Add it when you connect, or later with **Publisher key** on the connection (over the API, `PATCH /api/v1/org/connections/<id>` with `{ "publisherKey": "..." }`, and `null` removes it). It is checked against Steam once, stored encrypted, shown only by its last four characters and only to the owner, and Steam's own list of the apps it covers is shown beside it. **Test** checks both keys. Until you add one, those checks use the first key, which Steam may refuse; the connection then says that it needs a Publisher Web API key, and so does the answer your game gets.

 

**What it brings in.** Once a day, after Steam's previous day is complete, a connection reads the dates whose sales changed and writes one ledger row per title, day, country and line item (base game, DLC or bundle), and reads wishlists into Pulse as one post per mapped store page with a daily snapshot of wishlist adds, deletes and purchases. The first sync reads the 90 most recent changed dates and the last 30 days of wishlists; bring older history in with Steam's own CSV export through the sales import. A sync that stops part way carries on from where it stopped the next time, and reading the same day again updates its rows rather than doubling them.

 

**Two choices worth knowing.** Every Steam row is in US dollars, from Steam's own dollar figures: nothing is converted, and rows you import in another currency stay separate rows in that currency. Units are units sold before returns, with returned units beside them, so returns are never subtracted twice. And your own records win: a synced row that matches one you entered by hand or imported is not written, and the sync result counts it.

 

**How it is charged.** A sync is weighted events on the same meter as everything else: a flat amount per sync, one event per byte read from Steam, and each new ledger row, snapshot or post at its own weight (see [Rates](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/limits/#rates)). Rows a sync only updates cost nothing. The daily sync follows the same background opt-in as Pulse, and **Sync now** is charged like anything else you ask for. Adding and testing a key are free.

 

**Deleting a connection** keeps every row it wrote, in Sales and in Pulse, and deletes the stored key. AdMob and other ad revenue come in today by CSV, through the sales import with the `admob` storefront and the `ads` line item, not by a connection.

documents.section_title: Your analytics as tools for your own agents
documents.title: Your analytics as tools for your own agents
documents.content:
18. Analytics MCP

 

## Your analytics as tools for your own agents

 

Ravensight runs an MCP server at `/mcp` so you can ask Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or anything else that speaks MCP about your game's data directly, without opening the dashboard.

documents.section_title: Your analytics as tools for your own agents
documents.title: Connect it
documents.content:
### Connect it

 

**What a call costs, before you make one.** Every analytics read over MCP costs 100,000 events on the shared event meter, about $0.05 past the included allowance; discovery (listing the tools) and `get_usage_rate` are free. MCP also needs an account that has loaded a prepaid balance at least once.

 

Mint a personal access token from the dashboard's **Settings > MCP access** tab. It looks like `gt_mcp_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx` and is sent as a Bearer token.

 

```
claude mcp add --transport http ravensight https://api.ravensight.io/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer gt_mcp_..."
```

 

The endpoint is a stateless streamable HTTP transport: every request is handled independently, with no session to resume and nothing to clean up between calls.

documents.section_title: Your analytics as tools for your own agents
documents.title: Tools
documents.content:
### Tools

 

The game analytics tools are Huginn's own toolset, the same read-only tools the AI analyst reaches for in the dashboard. Every tool below that takes a `game_id` checks it against the games your token's owner actually has, on every single call rather than once when the token was minted: a token can never read another tenant's game, and a teammate removed from your studio loses access on their next call.

 

A token is bound to the studio that was selected when it was minted. Every `game_id` is checked against that studio and, when the token is limited to some projects, against those projects, whatever the billing mode. If you were invited to another studio, switch to it in the dashboard before minting a token for it; a token minted in your own studio cannot read the other studio's games.

 

MCP calls are metered usage on the same event meter as everything else: one call weighs 100,000 events, which is $0.05 once the included million is spent, and a write costs exactly what a read costs. MCP needs an account that has loaded a prepaid balance at least once. A token has no spending cap of its own unless you set one in **Settings > MCP access**: without one it stops only when your included events and balance run out. A cap guards against an agent stuck in a loop, which matters most with auto-recharge on, and a token that has spent its cap is refused rather than charged further. Because each call weighs 100,000 events, the included million covers about ten calls a month when nothing else is sent, and the usage page and the sidebar meter show MCP calls as their own bar, apart from your games' player events (see [usage, billing and limits](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/limits/)). A call that fails is not charged. Your external AI client may charge separately for its own model usage.

 

Every metered answer carries `_meta.remaining`, read after that call was charged: `eventsUsed`, `includedEvents`, `eventsRemaining` (included events left this month, never below zero), `callsRemaining` (how many more calls those cover) and `balanceCents`. The balance is shown to the studio owner only and is `null` for anyone else. The free `get_usage_rate` tool returns the same numbers as `allowance` and `balanceCents`, so an agent can pace itself before it spends. MCP calls draw the included monthly events first, then the prepaid balance. The `includedAllowance` field in a rate refers to AI units only, so it is `false` for MCP even though calls use the included events.

 

**A token reads by default.** The write tools below need a token an owner has switched **Allow writes** on for, on the token's own form in **Settings > MCP access**. A write-capable token can record marketing touchpoints, keep the sales ledger, configure websites in its permitted scope, store reference documents, record Pulse posts, put cards on a brainstorm board, teach Muninn a fact, manage traffic blocks, and build a [strategy matrix](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/strategy/) and resolve its predictions. The separate [Allow organization management](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/organization-api/) switch enables game, project, invitation and member operations subject to the holder's role. Money and tokens remain outside these write surfaces, and ingest keys are issued only through the separate [key permission](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/organization-api/#agent-keys). Every studio-context write is written to your audit log with the tool name and how many rows it created, updated or rejected, never the rows themselves.

 

The studio-wide comparisons are not MCP tools. Asking the same metric, funnel or property of every game at once is something Huginn does in the dashboard, and the API exposes under `/api/v1/studio/analytics/...`; an MCP client asks `list_games` and then one game at a time.

 

Some of them are written to your org's audit log: `run_sql`, every studio-context read, and every write. Those are the calls that can pull the most out of an account, or put the most into it, in one request, so if a token ever goes astray you can see exactly what was taken and what was added. The log records the tool name and the game, never your query text and never what a write said.

 

#### list_games

 

List your games: game_id, name, environment, the title each belongs to (project_id and project_name), and whether tracking is enabled. Every other tool takes a game_id from this list. Each entry also carries gameId, the same value under its older name; it is deprecated, so read game_id. One entry per environment, so a title with a production and a development build appears twice, with the same project_id and project_name and a different environment.

 

#### get_integration_status(game_id, session_id?, hours?)

 

One bundled check of whether a game's integration is working, priced as one call: use it after wiring an SDK instead of several separate reads. It returns `usage` (`remaining` included events this month, the `allowance`, and `balance_covers`, how many more calls the prepaid balance pays for, shown to the billing owner only and otherwise null); `implementation`, the Implementation health card's status and warnings, each with its title and the detail naming its fix; `events`, what arrived in the last `hours` (default 24, at most 168): the top 20 event names with counts, real and playtest session counts and the latest event time; with `session_id`, the first 200 events of that session in order; and `detection`, the game's detection profile. For a game with [public keys](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/public-builds/), `implementation.public_keys` lists each live key (paused included, revoked and expired left out) with its `prefix`, `label`, `state`, this month's `accepted`, `ceiling`, `remaining` and the ceiling's cost in event blocks, its refusal `counts`, its most frequent unlisted names and its `signals`; each signal is also one of the `warnings`, with the id `public_key:<code>:<prefix>`. Counts and names only, never a key. `traffic` holds today's ten busiest [connecting addresses](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/traffic/), masked, each with its shape, and the game's block list; a `many_devices` or `rejections` address is also a warning with the id `ip_concentration:<hash prefix>`.

 

**Budgeting agent reads.** Every metered answer, this one included, carries `_meta.remaining` read after the call was charged, with `callsRemaining` among its fields. An agent that checks it after each call, or asks the free `get_usage_rate` first, can stop before it spends past what you meant it to.

 

#### get_overview(game_id, granularity?, from?, to?)

 

Headline analytics for one game: daily active players, totals, median session length, top events, and `detection`: the game's detection profile with the number of sessions in the window (`sample_sessions`). `granularity` is `day` (the default) or `hour`; hour needs `from` and `to` at most 14 days apart and labels each point `YYYY-MM-DD HH:00:00` in UTC. The answer names its `granularity`, and both series are sparse: a day or an hour with no events has no point.

 

#### query_players(game_id, from?, to?, limit?, skip?, link_id?)

 

Per-session behavior rows with rage-quit, stuck, and engaged flags and the indicators behind them. The flags are inferred under the game's [detection profile](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#detection-profile), and the answer says so with `inferred: true` and `sample_sessions`. With rage quit detection off, or deaths as outcomes, `rageQuitLikely` is null. With `link_id`, a [campaign link](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/campaign-links/#campaign-links-player-insights) id from `list_campaigns`, only the players who arrived by that link in the window, with every session they played there, and `campaignLink.players` says how many players that is.

 

#### query_levels(game_id, from?, to?)

 

Per-level funnel: starts, completions, deaths, completion rate. `levelEvents` names the events behind those counts, read as a start, completion, run end, death or fail under the game's [detection profile](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/dashboard/#detection-profile), each with its count and top-level property keys, so a death sent as `ember_out` with a `cause` key shows as one.

 

#### get_retention(game_id, days?, mode?, cohortBy?, startEvent?, returnEvent?, cumulative?, from?, to?)

 

Retention overall and by first-seen cohort, with day 1 and day 7 always present, and `activity`: daily active players (the last 24 hours), weekly (7 days), monthly (30 days) and stickiness (daily over monthly) for the 30 days ending at `to`. `days` is day 0 to 90, up to nine days; `mode` `classic` means returned on that day, `rolling` means on or after it. `cohortBy` groups by `day` or `week`. `startEvent` and `returnEvent` take an event name; write `kind:purchase` for a typed kind (also `kind:resource`, `kind:progression`, `kind:error`, `kind:health`, `kind:level_start`, `kind:level_complete`, `kind:death`), and a bare name is an event name. A typed event stored with `rs_invalid` is never counted. With any option the answer adds `overall`, a rate per day counting only cohorts whose day is over (`null` when none is), and each cohort's `retained` players and rate per day, `null` for a day the cohort has not lived through yet. `cumulative` adds each cohort's sessions, playtime in seconds and revenue per currency, in minor units of that currency and never added across currencies.

 

#### get_metrics(game_id, from?, to?)

 

Players, sessions, new versus returning, and session length as both an average and a median. New means first seen ever, not first seen in the window you asked about.

 

#### get_monetization(game_id, from?, to?)

 

What players spent, from purchase events: active players, payers, paying conversion, first purchases and the time from a player's first event to their first purchase (median and average, null when nobody made one). Then `byCurrency`, one row per currency with its revenue, transactions, payers, revenue per paying player (`arppu`) and per daily active player (`arpdau`, one currency's revenue divided by all daily active players), a daily series of the latest 30 days (`truncated` counts the days dropped) and the top items. Every amount is an integer in minor units of the row's currency, never add two currencies; divide by 10`minorUnitDigits` to display one. A repeated transaction id is counted once, in revenue, transactions, payers and items alike, and a purchase without one counts each time. A purchase stored with `rs_invalid` is never counted.

 

#### get_ad_revenue(game_id, from?, to?)

 

Revenue with ads included, one row per currency in `byCurrency`: `purchaseRevenue` is purchases in minor units, the same number `get_monetization` gives, and `purchaseMicros`, `adMicros`, `totalMicros`, `arpuMicros` (over active players) and `arpdauMicros` (over daily active player-days) are whole micros of that currency as digit strings. A million micros is one major unit, so `"1500"` is 0.0015. Purchases are scaled from minor units by the currency's own exponent; nothing is converted and two currencies are never added. Then `ads`: shown, clicked, failed and rewarded counts, ads shown per session, and per placement, network and format the same counts with revenue per currency. An ad stored with `rs_invalid` is never counted.

 

#### get_campaigns(game_id, from?, to?)

 

Paid acquisition per campaign: `installs` (players whose attribution was touched in the window), the sources and networks that reported them, and per currency `revenueMicros` (purchases and paid ads in the window by players attributed to the campaign), `spendMicros` (the spend you imported, null when none was, which is not zero) and `roas`, revenue over spend in that one currency, null without spend. Campaign `""` is attributed players whose source named no campaign. Needs the studio read permission, because it carries spend.

 

#### get_ltv_forecast(game_id, campaign?, from?, to?)

 

Lifetime value per player by day since first seen, per currency, and a forecast. `pooled` is the observed cumulative revenue per player, counting only the cohorts that have lived through each day. `forecast` fits `a * (day + 1)^b` on those days and answers `perPlayerMicros` with an approximate 95% interval (`lowMicros`, `highMicros`) at 30, 60, 90, 180 and 365 days. Events are kept 90 days, so a day past the observed curve is an extrapolation, and `tooFew` is true when there were fewer than 7 days with revenue or fewer than 50 players to fit. `campaign` narrows the cohorts to one campaign's players.

 

#### get_progression(game_id, p1?, p2?, from?, to?)

 

How players move through the game's own hierarchy, from `progression` events. With no `p1` it answers for the top level (`rs_p1`); pass `p1` to list what is inside that node (`rs_p2`), and `p1` with `p2` to go one deeper (`rs_p3`). Each value is at most 100 characters. Every node has `attempts` (starts), `completes`, `fails`, `players`, `winRate` (completes over completes plus fails, 0 when neither happened), `medianSecondsToComplete` (from a session's first start to its first completion, null when no session did both) and `medianScore` (the median `rs_score` on completes, null when none was sent). Up to 100 nodes, most attempted first. A progression event stored with `rs_invalid` is never counted.

 

#### get_economy(game_id, resource?, from?, to?)

 

The virtual currencies a game creates and removes, from `resource` events. Each resource lists `earned` and `spent` (plain numbers in the game's own unit, never minor units), `net`, `earners`, `spenders` and `events`, busiest first, up to 20. The chosen `resource` (at most 64 characters; the busiest when omitted) also gets a daily series of earned, spent and net over the latest 30 days (`truncated` counts the days dropped), and its top sink and source items by amount, up to 20 each. A resource event stored with `rs_invalid` is never counted.

 

#### get_health(game_id, from?, to?)

 

Errors and performance, from `error` and `health` events. Errors carry the total, the players who hit one against the active players, errors per affected player, a daily count per severity (`debug`, `info`, `warning`, `error`, `critical`) over the latest 30 days (`truncated` counts the days dropped), the 20 most frequent messages (cut at 200 characters), each with its five busiest builds and their exact counts, newest build first, the 20 builds that raise the most, each with its sessions, and the five biggest open error issues. Performance lists, per platform and build (20 at most), the sessions with the median and slowest-tenth frames per second, median memory in megabytes and median boot time in milliseconds, using the latest sample from each session and `null` where no session sent a metric, then the sessions per frame rate bucket (0-15, 15-30, 30-45, 45-60, 60+). An event stored with `rs_invalid` is never counted.

 

#### get_hardware(game_id, by?, from?, to?)

 

Which hardware is hurting the game. `by` is `device_model` (the default), `os_version` or `gpu`. Per value and platform, the 50 with the most sessions, each with at least five players: `sessions`, `healthSessions` (those that sent a health sample), `errorSessions` and `errorRate`, then the median and slowest-tenth frames per second, median memory in megabytes and median boot time in milliseconds, from each session's latest sample. `unknownSessions` counts sessions with no value. Groups with fewer than five players, and any past the 50, are one `other` row that is shown but never judged, and `smallGroups` counts the small ones. `minimumSpec` judges only groups with at least 20 health sessions, against a target of a median of 30 frames per second or more with at most 5% of sessions raising an error. For device models and GPUs it lists the groups below the target, slowest first. For OS versions it gives, per platform, the lowest version from which every version meets the target. Device names are text sent by players' devices.

 

#### get_dimension_breakdown(game_id, dimension, limit?, from?, to?)

 

Players by `country`, `device_model`, `os_version` or `gpu`, ranked by players (20 values by default, 50 at most): `players`, `sessions`, `events`, `payers` and payer `conversion` (`count`, `n`, `value`, `interval95`, `lowSample`), and the rest in `other`. A value with fewer than five players is never shown on its own: it is counted in `other`, and `smallGroups` says how many such values there were. A player who played from two countries counts in both rows, so `totalPlayers` is the real total. `unknownPlayers` had no value.

 

#### get_distribution(game_id, metric, buckets?, min?, max?, currency?, filters?, from?, to?)

 

How a measure is spread across sessions or players: the statistics (`count`, `mean`, `p50`, `p90`, `min`, `max`) and a histogram of equal-width buckets, each `{ from, to, count }`, the last closed on the right. `metric` is `session_length` (seconds per session), `events_per_session`, `sessions_per_player`, `playtime_per_player` (seconds) or `revenue_per_payer`. Revenue is whole minor units of one `currency`, which it requires, and is never added across currencies. `buckets` is 5 to 50 (10 by default). `min` and `max` cut the values themselves, so the statistics and the buckets describe the same population. `filters` keeps whole sessions that touched the property values given. A purchase stored with `rs_invalid` is never counted. With no values the statistics are `null` and every bucket is zero.

 

#### get_level_map(game_id, level?, event?, xKey?, yKey?, bins?, from?, to?)

 

Where things happen in a level, from `x` and `y` top-level properties, or the keys you name. `event` is `kind:death` by default, `all` or an event name. Cells are square in your game's units, 8 to 30 on the longer side (`bins`, 20 by default), the busiest 40 first, each with `column`, `row`, `x` and `y` (its low corner), `events` and `players`. `withoutPosition` counts events of that kind with no usable position, and `levels` lists what else can be mapped. `level` defaults to the one with the most positioned events.

 

#### get_retention_split(game_id, by?, days?, mode?, from?, to?)

 

Retention per value of one thing a player has. `by` is `game_version` (the default) or `platform`, both the one they started on; `country`, `device_model`, `os_version` or `gpu`, the first known value (empty when none is known); or `prop:<key>`, the first value they sent of a property; an empty value means they never sent it. The five biggest values get a row and the rest fold into `other`, so the rows are disjoint and sum to the cohort. `days` is up to nine days from 0 to 90, [1, 7] by default. `retained` per day has `count`, `n` (players whose day is over), `value` (`null`, not 0, when none is), `interval95` and `lowSample`.

 

#### get_data_quality(game_id, from?, to?)

 

Whether the numbers can be trusted. `lateness` has `late` (an hour or more after the event's own time), `veryLate` (a day or more), `clockAhead` (a device clock a minute or more ahead), and `medianLagSeconds` and `p90LagSeconds`, `null` with no events. `duplicates` has `droppedAtIngest` for this month and `storedRepeats`, the same `rs_event_id` stored more than once. `schemaDrift` compares the two most recently seen builds: `newEvents`, `goneEvents`, `addedKeys` and `removedKeys`, 20 each at most, with `truncated`. `sdks` covers the last 24 hours and `rejections` this month. `visitorSessions` is for web games and counts real players only: `newWebDevices`, the devices first seen in the window that sent a web event, and `sessionOnly`, those that never sent more than 3 events in a session. Its `reading` is `flagged` when we are 95% sure at least 60% of them did nothing past a session start, the shape website visitors leave when the game SDK starts on every page, `clear`, or `not_enough_data` under 10 devices. A flagged reading carries a `finding` with the fix and a link to [Web games: your website and your game](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/web-games/). `visitorSessions` is `null` when it could not be read; the rest of the report still answers. Every share has `count`, `n`, `value`, `interval95` and `lowSample`. It needs the same permission as `get_integration_status`.

 

#### explain_metric_change(game_id, metric, from?, to?, baselineFrom?)

 

How much a metric moved between a window (7 days by default, 90 at most) and an equal baseline, the one right before it unless `baselineFrom` says otherwise, and where the change sits. `metric` is `players`, `new_players`, `sessions`, `session_seconds`, `events`, `errors`, `errors_per_session` or `progression_fails`. `change.reading` is `clear`, `could_be_noise` or `not_enough_data`; a count's noise is read per session, so one spammy session does not make a change look clear. `dimensions` lists up to eight rows each for platform, build, level, new or returning and up to three properties, each row with `baseline`, `current`, `delta`, `shareOfChange` and `lowSample`. `shareOfChange` is `null` when `additive` is false, because a player can sit on two rows. `session_seconds` and `errors_per_session` are means per session (`measuredAs` says so, and a mean can move differently from a median); their rows add `mix`, the group growing or shrinking, and `rate`, its own average changing, which sum to `delta`. This says where a change sits, not what caused it. Money is not explained here.

 

#### list_builds(game_id, from?, to?)

 

The `game_version` values seen in the window, most recently seen first (50 at most), each with `players`, `sessions`, `firstSeen` and `lastSeen` in unix seconds. An empty string is a game that sent no version.

 

#### compare_builds(game_id, a, b, steps?, windowSeconds?, from?, to?)

 

Two builds side by side over one window. `metrics.retentionD1` and `retentionD7` follow players who started on the build and count a return on any build; a return day that is not over yet counts neither way. `errorPlayers`, `medianSessionSeconds`, `fpsMedian` and `fpsP10` read what happened on the build. `steps` adds a `funnel` on each build's own events. Each side carries `n`, `value`, `interval95` and `lowSample` (under 30). `value` is `null`, not 0, when nothing was measured. `verdict` is `b_higher`, `b_lower`, `no_clear_difference` or `not_enough_data` (under 10 on a side, or no interval). A share uses a Wilson interval and its difference Newcombe's; a median has no interval under six values, the slowest tenth none under 35, and a verdict on either means the two intervals do not overlap. `sharedPlayers` counts players seen on both builds.

 

#### get_funnel(game_id, steps, windowSeconds?, countBy?, filters?, filterScope?, from?, to?)

 

An ordered conversion funnel over 2 to 8 event names: how many reached each step, the share lost from the step before, and the gap into each step as an average and a median. Steps must happen in order inside the conversion window, so doing step two first does not count as converting. Count players or sessions, and filter by event property. `filterScope` is `event` by default, which keeps only step events that carry the property, so a step that does not send it reads 0; `session` keeps every step event of a session that touched it. Each step after the first has `conversion`, and the funnel has `overall`: `count`, `n`, `value`, `interval95` (a Wilson 95% range) and `lowSample` (under 30). `value` is `null`, not 0, when nobody reached the step before.

 

#### get_property_breakdown(game_id, property, event?, level?, limit?, from?, to?)

 

How one event property's values are distributed: ranked values with event and player counts, plus a daily series. Reads the top-level keys of the payload your game sends, so ask for the key name. `event` and `level` narrow it to one event name and one level, for example the cause of deaths in one room. An unknown key returns an empty breakdown, which is an answer.

 

#### get_usage_rate()

 

What a metered MCP call costs, the result and byte ceilings a tool answer is held to, the header to send when you retry one, and what is left of the month: `allowance` (included events, events per call, used, remaining and calls remaining) and `balanceCents`. Free: ask it first if your agent wants to know the price before it spends.

 

#### get_history(game_id, from?, to?)

 

Lifetime totals and long-range trends from stored rollups, beyond the default 90-day raw window: lifetime players, sessions and events, a daily active player series, summable totals and merged top events for the window you ask for. This is the tool for month over month, year over year, and all-time questions.

 

#### search_studio_context(query, game_id?, limit?)

 

Search everything your studio has learned, across every game you have shipped: findings the analyst distilled from past questions, weekly digest findings, and confirmed cross-game patterns. Ask it before you design or change a system, to find out whether you have already hit the problem you are about to walk into. Pass a `game_id` to narrow it to one game, or leave it off to search the whole studio.

 

#### get_game_brief(game_id, limit?)

 

The compact "what we know about this game" brief: the findings you have confirmed or most recently recorded about one game, human confirmed first and newest after that.

 

#### get_code_brief(game_id, limit?)

 

What the last code scan understood about the repositories behind one game: the architecture, the modules, and which telemetry the code actually sends against which is missing. For a coding agent that last part is the pairing worth having, because a funnel that stops dead at a step nothing in the repo fires is an instrumentation gap rather than a player behaviour. Our notes, never your source. Empty until a scan has run.

 

#### list_playtest_jobs(game_id, state?, limit?)

 

Ravensight Playtest jobs for one game: AI persona playtests, not real players. Each row is one priced job, its state, which modules and personas ran, how many findings it produced and their severity split, and what it cost. Newest first.

 

#### list_playtest_findings(game_id, severity?, category?, persona?, job_id?, q?, limit?)

 

Findings from Ravensight Playtest: what an AI persona hit while playing your game, each with repro steps and evidence references, a screenshot, a video timestamp, a transcript step or a file line, rather than a bare claim. Filter by severity, category, persona or job, or search title and description with q.

 

#### get_playtest_report(game_id, job_id, run_id?, format?)

 

Read a Ravensight Playtest report, an AI persona's notes on playing your game, as markdown or JSON. Omit run_id for the job's aggregate report across every persona that ran, or give a run_id for that one persona's own report. A run that ran out of budget may have a partial report: its JSON carries `partial: true`, and its sentiment and would_continue are placeholders, not the persona's view. When the run stored its step log, the answer also carries `evidence`: what to fix first, and each finding with its video second, its confidence and the reasons for it, what was expected and what happened, and the recorded inputs that lead to it. Each finding also says where it comes from (`basis`: measured by the runner, measured from the input log, or the playtester's own judgement, with `why_severity` when the playtester gave a reason), what the claim check answered when the finding was shown against a picture of its moment (`claim_check`), and whether playing its recorded inputs again brought it back (`replay`, with how many replays matched). A check that was not made says so and is never counted as passed. For a job it lists each issue with how many personas reported it. Its `health` is `issues_found` or `not_tested`: no findings means not tested, never that the game is fine. Limits of the playtest tool are counted there and are never findings. A run's answer also carries `impressions`: what the playtester felt and said that the run could not verify, each with its words, step, evidence and a note saying it is an impression. Impressions are never findings and are not in `list_playtest_findings`.

 

#### list_design_docs(kind?, game_id?, project_id?, limit?)

 

List your studio's design documents: id, kind, title, gameId, version count, and when each was last touched. Filter by kind (gdd, brief, note, or reference), by the gameId label on a document, or by the title it is filed under with `project_id`. Bodies are not included here, read one with `get_design_doc`.

 

#### get_design_doc(doc_id)

 

Read one design document by id: its header plus the current markdown body, capped at 40,000 characters with a note when a document runs longer. Never returns version history, a coding agent wants the doc as it stands.

 

#### list_touchpoints(game_id?, project_id?, from?, to?, kind?, limit?)

 

Your studio's marketing memory: the ads, videos, streams, posts, press mentions, launches, updates and sales you recorded, with what you spent and the measured 72 hour lift. Pass a `game_id` to get that one game's lift per touchpoint, or leave it off for every game's. Pass a `project_id` to read only the touchpoints filed under that title; each row names its own `project_id`, null for a studio-wide one. A null ratio means there was no baseline to compare against, not that the lift was zero. This is correlation you can explain, not attribution.

 

#### search_market_facts(query?, subject?, status?, limit?)

 

Search the shared market fact base: public facts about public games, genres, tags and platforms, each with its source link, a short quote and the day it was collected. Filter by `subject` (such as `steam:<appId>` or `genre:<slug>`) or by status (unverified, corroborated, disputed, superseded). Corroborated means two AI providers agreed on cited public sources, or a person added the fact; it is not independent verification. Facts come only from cited public sources, through an extraction step that never sees your question or your studio's names. A retired fact is not returned. Needs a read-only role or above, and is priced as one MCP call (100,000 events).

 

#### get_market_research(research_id)

 

Read one of your studio's own market research runs: a quick look or a deep research job, with its stage, each provider's status, the summary, every claim with its status and sources, and for a deep run what changed against the quick look it followed. A run from another studio answers as not found. Read only: starting a quick look or deep research is a dashboard action and is not available over MCP. Priced as one MCP call (100,000 events).

 

#### describe_studio_data(project_id?)

 

What your studio holds, as counts and dates only, never row contents: for each kind of data in [what data Ravensight holds](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/data-products/), how many records, when something was last added and how long it is kept, and the tools that read or write each kind, plus the [hints](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/studio-data/#studio-data-hints) Studio data shows (a connection that needs attention: repeated failed syncs or a key to re-enter; a game whose oldest events reach its retention limit within 30 days; an unfunded account). Pass `project_id` from `list_games` to count one title's games; studio-wide records such as sales, Pulse, brainstorms and touchpoints are then left uncounted. A count that could not be read is null, meaning not counted, never zero. Results are cached for up to five minutes. Needs `studio:read`; a token limited to some projects is refused. Metered as one programmatic read on the event meter. See [Studio data](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/studio-data/).

 

An agent that does not yet know what your studio has can read the free resource `ravensight://data-products` first, to learn which kinds of data exist and which tools read them, then call `describe_studio_data` once to see which of those your studio actually holds before it spends a call on any of them.

#### list_connections()

 

Your studio's [connections](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/connections/), one row each: the provider (Steam first), your label, its status (active, paused, paused because the included events ran out, waiting for the key to be entered again, or in error), when it last synced, which records it feeds, how many apps are mapped to titles, and which keys it holds (`keys.publisher` is the Publisher Web API key that checking Steam tickets needs, with the last refusal in words). Never returns a key, and nothing about a connection can be changed over MCP. Metered as a programmatic read on the event meter.

 

#### list_campaigns(game_id)

 

The [campaign links](https://www.ravensight.io/docs/campaign-links/) of one game: each campaign with its links, and for each link its short address, destination, source, medium, label, whether it is active or disabled, the tags the redirect adds and the address visitors land on. Needs a role that can read campaign links, so a viewer is refused. Nothing about a campaign link can be changed over MCP. Metered as a programmatic read on the event meter.

 

#### get_campaign_stats(game_id, campaign_id?, link_id?, source?, from?, to?, tz?)
